about: Learn 2: a page for every variety, species, process, country and region. Each claim cites its sources (sources.json). Checked against those sources Oct 28, 2026.

records.name: Australia
records.summary: A tiny, machine-harvested Arabica crop from Queensland and northern NSW.
records.lede: Australia grows under 300 t of Arabica a year, mainly on Queensland's Atherton Tablelands and in northern New South Wales, and imports about 99% of the coffee it drinks. Hand-picking was too expensive, so the modern industry was built on machines: the Jaques family near Mareeba helped build what is described as the world's first mechanical coffee harvester, and SBS dates the modern industry's birth to 1985.

regions.name: Atherton Tablelands
regions.teaser: Around Mareeba in Far North Queensland: about 70% of the crop. Higher, frost-free and rainy; a grower calls the coffee nutty, almost biscuity

regions.name: Northern Rivers (NSW)
regions.teaser: Lower and cooler, with farms from the Byron Bay hinterland to Coffs Harbour. Slower ripening and a chocolatey cup, says grower Rebecca Zentveld

harvest.text: On the Atherton Tablelands, picking happens in the southern winter: in mid-June 2023 Skybury's harvest was in full swing, with six to eight weeks of picking ahead.

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: Almost all Arabica. No ranking was found: a roaster lists Typica, Catuai and Mundo Novo as among the most commonly grown, plus the Kenyan K7 and SL6, which suit Australia's drier climate; K7 is the benchmark the national variety trial set out to beat, and Skybury grows Bourbon. Cherries are machine-picked, machine-dried and colour-sorted; no source found says how much is washed or natural.

cup.text: Northern NSW grower Rebecca Zentveld says her region's cooler climate stretches ripening and gives a chocolatey cup, while Far North Queensland coffee tends nutty, almost biscuity. Skybury's own customers most often call its coffee earthy, SBS reported in 2021.
cup.why: Zentveld puts northern NSW's chocolatey side down to its cooler climate and longer ripening.
cup.watch: Price and scale. Production costs make Australian coffee dearer than imports, and K7, a high-quality variety, grows too tall for the harvesting machines, which cuts yields and raises costs.

story.text: Coffee is first believed planted at Kangaroo Point, Brisbane.
Plantations spread across northern NSW and Queensland, with some 46 growers around Cairns.
Growing fades out: the end of indentured South Sea Islander labor in 1901, cyclones, droughts, sugarcane and cheap imports all take their toll.
Australia's modern coffee industry is born, SBS says, helped by Coffee Shuttle One, the mechanical harvester the Jaques family built with a local shipping company near Mareeba.
Southern Cross University and World Coffee Research begin variety trials; by 2025 three new royalty-free varieties were reported to beat K7 on yield and taste.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Australia has neither coffee berry borer nor coffee leaf rust, so farms need few chemicals. Growers use irrigation to trigger flowering so the cherries ripen together for the machines, then dry them mechanically and sort them by color. The Jaques method, in the industry's growers' manual, cuts trees back to the stump every six years.

sections.title: Right now
body: AgriFutures said in September 2025 that Australia grows under 300 t a year and that three new open-access varieties from the Southern Cross University and World Coffee Research trial beat K7 on yield and taste; growers pay no royalties on them. Early plantings are under way in Western Australia, and the cost of suitable land is the main barrier to growth.

Grower counts vary by source: about 50 in total, a northern NSW grower estimated in 2021, while a roaster counted about 30 farmers on the Atherton Tablelands and about 170 farms in northern NSW the same year. SBS describes Skybury as Australia's largest exporter of Arabica, and Jason Jaques said in 2021 that demand for local coffee had roughly doubled since COVID.

records.name: Burundi
records.summary: Washed Bourbon from 600,000 small farms in the northern hills.
records.lede: Burundi is a small, landlocked country beside Rwanda, and nearly all of its coffee comes from about 600,000 smallholder farms. Most of it is Bourbon grown in the northern mountains and washed at central stations, and importers describe sweet, clean, often floral cups. Its known weak spot is the potato taste defect, which it shares with its neighbors.

harvest.text: Picked from about March to July. Kayanza stations such as Yandaro and Mpemba pick mainly from May to July.

grows.species: Arabica, mostly Bourbon types
grows.text: Mostly fully washed at central stations; a few stations also make naturals and honeys.

cup.text: Importers describe sweet, clean cups: Cafe Imports tastes fig jam, flowers and sparkling citrus in the best lots, and Sucafina calls them very sweet and often floral. Roasters' lots add honey and orange-like citrus.
cup.why: Starbucks credits high altitude, volcanic soil and plenty of rain. Cafe Imports also describes a careful washing routine: a dry ferment, long soaks in mountain water, density sorting and drying on raised beds.
cup.prized: Cleanliness and sweetness: Intelligentsia, a roaster, calls Burundi consistently among the cleanest and sweetest coffees in Africa.
cup.watch: The potato taste defect: one bean, linked to damage by the Antestia bug, can make a whole dose smell of raw, peeled potato. You can't see it in green or roasted beans, so grind small doses (about 30 g), throw out one that has it and purge the grinder. One bad dose doesn't mean the whole bag is bad.

story.text: Belgian colonial rulers introduced Arabica coffee.
Independence; production then grew until the early 1990s.
Civil war devastated the coffee sector.
The government and international companies began investing in coffee again.
The state coffee board was replaced by a regulator, ARFIC, and private companies were allowed to buy coffee, many buying washing stations from the state.
At the Cup of Excellence, a national quality competition, 62% of Burundi's entrants withdrew because of the potato defect.
The state took back control: a new coffee office, ODECA, replaced ARFIC and took over the state-linked washing-station companies.

sections.title: How Burundi washes
body: Cafe Imports describes the usual routine: about 12 hours of dry fermentation after pulping, a 12–14 hour soak in mountain water, floating to sort by density, a second 12–18 hour soak, then drying the beans, still in their parchment husk, on raised beds. Stations also float cherry before pulping to remove damaged fruit, part of the fight against the potato defect.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: ODECA, the state coffee office, sets minimum cherry prices early in each harvest and still owns about 100 washing stations and a large dry mill in Bujumbura; private companies process about 70% of the coffee (Atlas Coffee Importers, 2023).

Stations pay one price for Cherry A, ripe cherry, and about half that for Cherry B, the floaters (light cherries that float in water), which go back to farmers to sell or process at home. Sorted, fully washed Cherry A makes the specialty grade.

sections.title: Right now
body: The latest published crop figure is Sucafina's March 2025 forecast: about 12,000 tonnes of green coffee, similar to the year before, picked from late March to July. Harvests swing between high and low years, and Atlas Coffee Importers called 2023 a particularly low one.
In 2025 Burundi merged its 18 provinces into five: Kayanza, Ngozi and Kirundo are now part of Butanyerera, Muyinga part of Buhumuza, and Karuzi part of Gitega.

records.name: Bolivia
records.summary: High Yungas coffee from small family farms, after a steep decline.
records.lede: Bolivia's coffee grows at 1,400–2,100 m (4,600–6,900 ft), about 90% of it in La Paz department, home of the forested Yungas valleys, on family farms of 1–5 hectares (2.5–12 acres). Exports fell from a peak of 125,000 bags in 1989 to about 22,000 in 2020, and coca, which pays more and is easier to pick, is a big reason.

regions.name: Los Yungas
regions.teaser: Forested, hilly valleys in La Paz department, which grows about 90% of the crop. South Yungas sits highest. La Paz coffees tend to be clean, winey and fruit-led

regions.name: Caranavi
regions.teaser: About five hours' drive from La Paz. A wet mill near the town processes coffee from the Sol de la Mañana producer program

regions.name: Samaipata
regions.teaser: In Santa Cruz, to the east. Hot days and cold nights slow ripening; Santa Cruz coffees run rich and bold, with red fruit and milk chocolate

harvest.text: Picked from June to October, by hand over many passes, because cherries ripen slowly and unevenly at altitude.

grows.text: Traditionally washed: farmers pulped coffee on the farm and took it to central processing stations; no published source says how common naturals or honeys are. For decades growers worked only with Typica and Caturra; many are now replacing Typica with the higher-yielding Catuaí, and some plant Gesha and Java. No source gives shares.

cup.text: Melbourne Coffee Merchants, an importer, calls Bolivian coffees very sweet and clean: some lean to cane sugar, toffee and dark chocolate with balanced acidity, others are winey, with berry and butterscotch notes.
cup.why: Altitude and cold nights: in Samaipata, days near 30 °C (86 °F) and nights near 8 °C (46 °F) slow ripening, which the importer says helps sugars develop.
cup.watch: Drying: La Paz's rainy, humid climate makes drying coffee hard without mechanical help.

story.text: Coffee is first grown on estates in the Yungas, a region already well known for coca.
Agrarian reform hands small parcels of 1.5–8 hectares to thousands of mostly Indigenous families.
Exports peak at 125,000 bags; by 2010 they are down to 66,000 a year, and by 2020 to about 22,000.
The Cup of Excellence competition arrives and lifts Bolivia's profile; it is replaced by the President's Cup in 2010.
The Sol de la Mañana mentoring program starts with 15 producers; it now has about 200 members across Bolivia.

sections.title: Coffee versus coca
body: Coca is the coffee farmer's biggest rival: it can be harvested year-round, is easier to pick and often pays more. Melbourne Coffee Merchants adds that coca growing clears forest and shade trees, causing erosion, and that coffee gets little government support.

sections.title: Signs of recovery
body: A mentoring program called Sol de la Mañana started in 2014 with 15 producers and now has about 200; members' average yields rose from 2.5 to 20 bags per hectare. Many farmers are also replacing Typica with the higher-yielding Catuaí.

cup.text: Chocolate turns up in most of the 12 protected-origin descriptions in Brazilian Farmers' 2022 guide, often with nuts or caramel, while acidity runs from gentle and citric (Cerrado Mineiro) to bright (Montanhas do Espírito Santo). Sucafina calls sweetness with chocolate, honey and molasses the classic Brazilian Bourbon pulped-natural profile.
cup.why: Brazil has long been known for natural coffee, dried whole on patios, and pioneered the pulped natural, which dries with the fruit pulp still on the seed. Embrapa-linked researchers say dry processing gives a fuller-bodied, sweeter cup with moderate acidity.
cup.watch: Conilon, Brazil's Robusta and about a third of the crop, tends to be fuller-bodied but more bitter, less aromatic and less acidic than Arabica, though fine lots are on the rise.
cup.prized: Sweetness and chocolate: Brazilian Farmers' summaries of the protected origins call Campo das Vertentes very sweet, with chocolate and nut, and give Cerrado Mineiro a long chocolate finish; Sucafina's classic Brazilian cup is a Bourbon pulped natural with chocolate, honey and molasses.

story.text: Army officer Francisco de Melo Palheta, sent to French Guiana over a border dispute, brings back coffee seed.
Coffee becomes Brazil's biggest export in the 1830s, and within a decade Brazil is the world's top coffee producer.
Mundo Novo is introduced and replaces Bourbon on farms; Catuaí reaches the field in 1972, and by 2012 the two were estimated at about 85% of the varieties planted.
The Cup of Excellence competition is born in Brazil, its winners sold through the first online auction for coffee.
Conab's September survey puts the crop at a record 67.6 million bags.

sections.title: Naturals, patios and machines
body: Sucafina says most Brazilian coffee in the 19th and 20th centuries was processed natural, and that many producers now also offer honeys and fully washed coffee. In a 2019 survey of 296 growers by the farm confederation CNA and the portal CaféPoint, 85% made naturals (cherry dried in its skin), 14% made pulped naturals (cereja descascado, skin off, mucilage left on), and 1% also fermented the seeds in tanks.

Drying in that survey was mostly on cement or asphalt patios (42%) and in mechanical dryers (34%), then raised beds (10%) and dirt patios (9%). Harvesting: 42% stripped branches by hand, 25% used harvesting machines, 23% handheld machines, and only 10% picked ripe cherries selectively. Sucafina adds that most Brazilian coffee is grown on large farms built to maximize output.

sections.title: Conilon, Brazil's Robusta
body: Conab's September 2026 survey counts 19.4 million bags of Conilon (down 6.6%) out of 67.6 million in all. Espírito Santo, the main Conilon state, grew 16.5 million bags of coffee in all, and Rondônia, in the Amazon, about 2.9 million bags of Conilon.
Rondônia's protected name, Matas de Rondônia, covers coffee from Conilon × Robusta plants, described as sweet, chocolatey and woody.

records.name: China
records.summary: Almost all from Yunnan, mostly washed Catimor.
records.lede: About 98% of China's coffee grows in Yunnan, a mountainous province in the southwest. Most of it is Catimor, a rust-resistant variety that Nestlé and the provincial government planted across Yunnan from 1988, and most is washed. Some farms now also grow Gesha, Typica and Bourbon for specialty buyers.

regions.name: Hainan
regions.teaser: China's tropical island province, which grows a little Robusta, best known as Xinglong coffee; growing has shrunk as farmers switch to betel nut and coconut

harvest.text: Picked mostly from December to March, by one importer's account, though the season can start as early as October. Milling and shipping mostly run from December to May.

grows.species: almost all Arabica from Yunnan; a little Robusta on Hainan
grows.text: Catimor is by far the most planted, for its yield and toughness, says the importer Sucafina; about 30 varieties are grown in all, including Caturra, Typica and SL34, and some farms now grow Gesha. Over 90% is washed; naturals often come from the first picking, with a little honey and newer experiments.

cup.text: Even most of Yunnan's specialty coffee has been simple and mild, says the importer Sucafina, scoring 80–82 points in cupping (the industry's standard tasting, out of 100). One roaster described a washed organic Catimor as very sweet, citrusy and balanced, with green apple, sugar cane and dates.
cup.prized: Consistency. Sucafina points to uniform, consistent profiles, and a buyer told Perfect Daily Grind that Catimor at 83–84 points gives a strong, repeatable flavor, while 87–88 points is hard to get from it.
cup.watch: Simplicity. Most of Yunnan's specialty coffee scores 80–82, Sucafina says, and the 83-plus lots that do exist mostly stay in China, where domestic buyers pay top prices.

story.text: A French missionary planted coffee beside his church in Zhukula, outside Dali; 24 of those century-old trees still stand.
Yunnan had about 4,000 hectares of coffee, then leaf rust, a fungal disease of the leaves, nearly wiped it out: about 270 hectares were left by 1970.
Nestlé teamed up with the Yunnan government to plant rust-resistant Catimor across the province, which brought production back.
Starbucks opened a Farmer Support Center in Pu'er.
Pu'er held its first specialty coffee expo.

sections.title: Right now
body: Yunnan typically grows 1.5–2 million 60-kg bags of Arabica a year, StoneX wrote in August 2026. In 2024, bad weather and fusarium, a fungal disease that hadn't been a big problem across most of the region, raised concerns about yields and quality. China drinks far more than it grows: USDA figures cited by StoneX put consumption at about 6.75 million bags, about 60% of it supplied by imports.

sections.title: Beyond Yunnan
body: Hainan, China's tropical island province, grows Robusta. Overseas Chinese returning from Southeast Asia brought the first seed in the 1890s, and coffee took hold at Xinglong, a farm settled from 1951 by returnees and formally founded in 1956; Premier Zhou Enlai praised its coffee in 1960. Today growing there has shrunk as farmers switch to betel nut and coconut, though young roasters are pushing for specialty quality.

records.name: Côte d'Ivoire
records.summary: Natural Robusta from the southern half, plus a little 'presidential' Arabusta.
records.lede: Côte d'Ivoire grows Robusta across the southern half of the country, most of it dried whole in the cherry and sold for blends. In the 1970s it was the world's third-largest coffee producer; USDA now puts the crop at about 1.3 million bags, after a 2024/25 harvest half that size. A little Arabusta, an Arabica–Robusta hybrid first grown in the 1960s for a milder cup, survives in the hills around Man.

grows.text: Nearly all Robusta, dried whole in the cherry and sold for blends and instant coffee; Arabusta is a small, hand-processed rarity from the hills around Man. No washed lots turned up in the sources.

harvest.text: Sources differ: PDG says cherries are picked by hand from August to January, a Scottish roaster gives November to April, and FAO's 2000 profile October to March. The official marketing season opened on 1 October in 2025.

cup.text: Scottish roaster Naked Roaster says the finest grades can show layers of dark chocolate, nut and tobacco. Arabusta is valued locally as milder and more floral than Robusta, which many Ivorians find bitter (CNN, 2018).
cup.prized: Arabusta, "the Presidential Coffee", sold in Ivorian supermarkets for three to four times the price of Robusta in 2018 (CNN).
cup.watch: Defects are common because of weak quality control and post-harvest handling, so even top grade 0 needs sorting for stones and sticks, and most goes into blends (PDG).
cup.why: The country's low, flat land suits Robusta, a high-caffeine species that many Ivorians find bitter (CNN, 2018).

story.text: Coffee arrived with French colonisation; until commercial growing took off about 30 years later, farmers grew small amounts of Liberica.
Robusta arrived from Java and the Belgian Congo.
President Félix Houphouët-Boigny asked for a sweeter, milder coffee, and Arabusta, "the Presidential Coffee", was first grown.
The world's third-largest producer, behind Brazil and Colombia; in the 1970s and 80s exports often topped 300,000 tonnes a year.
Robusta output peaked at about 380,000 tonnes in 2000; two civil wars, from 2002 to 2011, then badly hurt the sector, and production has declined since.

sections.title: Selling it
body: Buying and exporting coffee is regulated: the Coffee-Cocoa Council (Conseil du Café-Cacao) fixes the farmgate price at the start of each season, and exporters need a licence (DGE). For 2025/26 the price was set at 1,700 FCFA a kilo for coffee, at a season opening held on 1 October 2025.
Côte d'Ivoire is also one of three countries where wild stenophylla is native, and the larger sample tasted for the 2021 study of that species came from here (CIRAD).

sections.title: Where it goes
body: About a third of the 2022/23 crop was processed in the country, where Nestlé's Abidjan instant-coffee plant (capacity 9,000 tonnes) has long led the industry. Most green coffee stays in Africa: of 343,000 bags exported from October 2023 to March 2024, 82% went to African buyers, and Algeria alone takes nearly 80% of green exports (Tea & Coffee Trade Journal, 2025).
Yields are low, about 300–350 kg a hectare by one 2025 estimate, and the government plans to replant at least 400,000 hectares of old farms.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Ivorian Robusta is sold by grade, from grade 0 (the best) down to grade 2. One Abidjan exporter told PDG (2022) that even grade 0 has to be sorted for stones and sticks, and Ivorian coffee is often added to blends rather than sold as a single origin. Arabusta is known as "the Presidential Coffee" (CNN, 2018).

records.name: Cameroon
records.summary: Mostly Robusta, with washed Java Arabica from the western highlands.
records.lede: Cameroon grows mostly Robusta, largely in the coastal zones, and a small crop of Arabica on the western highland plateaus of the West and Northwest regions. In 1990, with record exports, it ranked 12th in the world; it now harvests under a tenth of its 1990s crop. Its specialty coffee is mostly washed Arabica, much of it the Java variety, and roasters often describe chocolate with some fruit.

regions.name: Northwest

regions.name: East

harvest.text: FAO's 2000 profile gives September to February for Arabica and November to mid-February for Robusta.

grows.species: Mostly Robusta (about nine-tenths of the 2024–25 crop), plus a small Arabica crop
grows.text: Robusta, most of the crop, is dried whole in the cherry. The Arabica is mainly Java and Jamaica (a local name for Typica), and nearly all of it is washed, most of it by farmers at home; honey and natural Arabica lots are few.

cup.text: AFCA describes Cameroon's coffee as full-bodied with a rounded finish and chocolate character. Sweet Maria's found a washed Java lot from near the Bamboutos mountains bittersweet and roast-toned with filbert and toasted coconut, and a UK roaster tastes dark chocolate and red fruit in Boyo coffee.
cup.why: AFCA credits the quality to altitude, rich volcanic soils and plentiful rain.
cup.watch: Most of what large exporters ship is commercial grade; specialty lots come from small groups like Cameroon Boyo (PDG, 2016).
cup.prized: Honey and cherry-dried (natural) lots from select farmers in the Cameroon Boyo group are the highest grades of specialty coffee Cameroon exports, though tiny in volume, says PDG (2016); kept from fermenting or going mouldy while they dry slowly, the naturals can be sweet and fruity.

story.text: Under German rule, coffee trial gardens were set up at Victoria, Ebolowa, Nkongsamba and Dschang.
In the West, 200,000 coffee seedlings had been planted at Dschang by 1928.
Java, brought in mid-century through the seed company Vilmorin, was released after nearly 20 years of selection; breeder Pierre Bouharmont noted it partly tolerates coffee berry disease.
Record exports of 156,000 tonnes; a long decline followed.
About 11,600 tonnes in all, under a tenth of the 1990s level; Arabica exports more than doubled in 2025, to 824 tonnes.

sections.title: Growing and processing the Arabica
body: Most Arabica is "farmer-washed": growers pulp, ferment, wash and dry it at home, then sell the dried parchment. A few large central washing stations exist, and the Cameroon Boyo group added small shared wet mills and, for some farmers, honey and natural lots (PDG, 2016).
One cooperative lot sold by Sweet Maria's in 2026 was fermented in tanks for up to 36 hours and dried for 7–10 days.
To grow more Arabica, the West's cooperative union, UCCAO, planted a 6-hectare field of Java seedlings at Bagang-Fondji in 2015, with the national research institute IRAD.

sections.title: Right now (2026)
body: Marketed output rose 9.9% to 11,637 tonnes in 2024–25, the last full season reported, and farmgate prices jumped: about 2,850 FCFA a kilo for Arabica and 1,959 FCFA for Robusta. The 2025–26 season opened on 16 January 2026.

Falling world prices then cut coffee export earnings by 17.6% in the first quarter of 2026, to CFA4.1 billion ($7.1 million). The 2014 recovery plan's goal of 125,000 tonnes of Robusta and 35,000 tonnes of Arabica by 2020 was never reached.

sections.title: Who roasts it
body: Unlike cocoa, which foreign companies largely control, Cameroon's coffee roasting is in local hands, and local roasters' coffees have won international awards (Ecofin, 2026). Still, AFCA says roasters in the country process only about 5% of the crop. Most of it is exported green, and in 2024–25 over 60% of the Robusta exports went to Italy, Algeria and Belgium.

records.regionsNote: ONCC lists seven coffee regions: West, Northwest, Littoral, Southwest, South, Centre and East. FAO's 2000 profile has Robusta in every province but the north, and Arabica on the high ground of the west, northwest and east.

records.name: DR Congo
records.summary: Volcanic-soil Arabica from Kivu and Ituri, rebuilding after decades of conflict.
records.lede: In the 1970s Congo was one of Africa's leading coffee exporters, but by 2002 decades of instability had cut its exports from about 120,000 tonnes a year to 10,000. Today's specialty coffee comes from cooperatives in the eastern highlands of North and South Kivu and Ituri, where Bourbon and Blue Mountain are two of the most popular varieties. Importers describe complex, layered cups with bright acidity.

harvest.text: Picked from April to July, says Sucafina.

grows.species: Arabica and Robusta: Arabica in the eastern highlands, and Robusta too (Grand Nord grows large volumes of both); Congo was a major Robusta producer before the 1990s
grows.text: Specialty lots are mostly Bourbon-type Arabica, with some Blue Mountain, from cooperatives in Kivu and Ituri. No recent, solid figure for how the whole crop splits between Arabica and Robusta has been published.

cup.text: A trader at Atlas Coffee Importers often finds prune, spice, chocolate, black tea and blackberry, and Sweet Maria's describes complex, layered aromatics and flavors with vibrant brightness.
cup.why: Perfect Daily Grind points to volcanic soil and high elevation in Kivu and Ituri.
cup.prized: Untapped potential: Counter Culture's buyer has called Congo one of the last few untapped regions for stunning Arabica.
cup.watch: Like coffee from Rwanda and Burundi, it can carry the potato taste defect. Slow overland export routes add risk: coffee that waits too long at a port or border can pick up moisture, which hurts the cup.

story.text: Independence from Belgium, followed by decades of instability.
Exports ran about 120,000 tonnes a year, among Africa's leaders.
Over 100,000 tonnes of coffee were grown.
After production plummeted in the 1990s, exports were down to about 10,000 tonnes a year.
Cooperatives began forming across the country, some funded by NGOs and development agencies.
The government set aside US$100 million for the coffee sector.
Almost 24,000 tonnes were grown, up from 16,700 in 2016.

sections.title: Smuggling and Lake Kivu
body: Official and unofficial taxes push some Congolese coffee over the borders to be sold as another country's, and much of Ituri's goes out through Uganda because exporting that way is easier. Sucafina cites reports that up to 1,000 people a year died, mostly by drowning, crossing Lake Kivu to sell coffee in Rwanda.

cup.text: Colombia's tourism site sketches three broad styles: fuller-bodied, low-acid coffee with chocolate tones in the north; medium body and acidity with fruity, herbal aromas in the centre; and medium-to-high acidity with floral, sweet notes in the south. The growers' federation's protected regional profiles fit that spread, from chocolate in the Sierra Nevada to caramel in Huila and Cauca and citrus in Tolima and Santander; Juan Valdez adds citrus notes for Nariño.

feel.acidity: medium to bright; softer in the north

cup.why: Coffee Review points to small farms at fairly high altitude and to coffee that is mostly picked with care and washed. Place matters too: it finds softer, sweeter, rounder cups in the northern Sierra Nevada and the most distinctive range in the south.
cup.prized: Coffee Review says the southern departments of Huila, Nariño and Cauca give the most distinctive cups, with balanced brightness and often more complex aromatics.
cup.watch: Coffee Review says the everyday cup has tended to get simpler and coarser, partly because badly adjusted demucilagers, machines that scrub off the sticky fruit layer in place of a fermentation tank, leave some fruit on the beans, which can ferment slightly and leave off-notes.

story.text: Jesuit priests bring coffee to Colombia, Cafe Imports says; commercial exports start in the first decade of the 1800s.
The national coffee growers' federation, the FNC, is founded; it sets up its research centre, Cenicafé, in 1938.
Caturra arrives from Brazil; until then Typica had been the only variety grown in Colombia, says Cenicafé.
A government-backed program starts paying for more than three billion trees to be replanted with rust-resistant Castillo; until then Caturra was thought to be nearly half of production.
Colombian authorities relax rules that for decades let only standard washed coffees that met set grades be exported.

sections.title: Washed on the farm
body: Barista Hustle says the vast majority of Colombian coffee is washed on the farm where it grows. The pulped seeds go straight into a fermentation tank, usually with little or no water, for 12–36 hours depending on climate and altitude, and growers judge the end by feel: the seeds turn gritty once the sticky fruit layer (mucilage) has broken down. Cenicafé, the federation's research centre, also calls this wet route the most frequent in Colombia.

Naturals were long discouraged for export: Coffee Review says that for decades Colombian authorities allowed only standard washed coffees out, until they relaxed the rules in 2015. In trials Cenicafé reported in 2023, whole cherries took about 19 days to dry in the sun and about 10 in a mechanical dryer, against about 4 days for washed coffee in the same kind of dryer.

These lots are a tiny share. In 2021 Coffee Review cited Luis Samper, a coffee writer and researcher, who points out that they remain the tiniest drop in the bucket for Colombian coffee: estimates he had seen put exports of alternative-processed Colombian coffees (natural, honey, anaerobic) at around 15,000 bags of 70 kg a year, against about 10.7 million 70-kg bags of Arabica exported in 2020.

sections.title: From Caturra to Castillo
body: Cenicafé released its first rust-resistant variety, Colombia, from 1983, then Tabi in 2002, Castillo in 2005 and Cenicafé 1 in 2016. Cenicafé 1 was 41% of the seed Cenicafé produced and handed out in 2020, and in 2024 it released Castillo 2.0.

Caturra, rust-prone, was thought to be nearly half of production until the 2008 replanting program. World Coffee Research puts the share of coffee land in rust-resistant varieties at 35% in 2010; the FNC put it at 88% in 2025. No published figure splits that land between Castillo, Cenicafé 1, Colombia and Tabi.

cup.text: Royal Coffee says Costa Rica's larger lots tend toward chocolate and mild citrus, while its micro-lots (small, separately processed lots) can taste wildly different. Cafe Imports says the country is known for good but often mild coffee, and Coffee Review describes the classic cup as balanced, clean and straightforward, with nut, ripe citrus, chocolate and stone fruit.

feel.acidity: crisp in high Tarrazú; softer in Tres Ríos

cup.why: Altitude and processing. Cafe Imports credits Tarrazú's high farms for its crisp acidity, and Coffee Review says the shift to small farm micromills brought honeys, naturals and a much wider range of cups than the classic washed style.
cup.prized: Buyers look to micro-lots for the most unusual cups; Royal Coffee says the micromills behind them invest heavily in natural, honey and anaerobic processing, partly because of limits on water use.
cup.watch: Micromill coffees vary: Coffee Review says they range from delicate and floral to musty and rustically rough.

story.text: Coffee growing begins in the Meseta Central, the country's central plateau.
A first shipment goes to Chile, and from there is sold on to England.
ICAFE, the national coffee institute, is created after the Great Depression's price crash.
A presidential decree allows only Arabica varieties to be planted.
A leaf-rust epidemic, a fungal disease of the leaves, hits Central America, Costa Rica included.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Mostly small farms: Cafe Imports counts 47,137 coffee families (2017) and says nearly 70% of the coffee comes from producers with fewer than 200 bags a year to export; Royal Coffee counted about 38,000 producers in 2019/20. Only Arabica is grown, under a 1989 decree, and ICAFE's rules for the national coffee name authorize Caturra and Catuaí, plus others it approves; Coffee Review puts it more bluntly: Costa Rica grows Caturra and more Caturra.

sections.title: Right now
body: USDA forecasts 1.2 million 60-kg bags for 2026/27, up from 1.16 million in 2025/26 but below 1.32 million in 2024/25, and counts all of it as Arabica.

records.name: Cuba
records.summary: Eastern mountain coffee, now about a sixth of its 1960s peak.
records.lede: Coffee reached Cuba from Santo Domingo in 1748, French planters fleeing the Haitian Revolution gave it a major boost from the 1790s, and for part of the 1800s Cuba was the main coffee exporter to Europe. The harvest peaked at 60,300 tonnes in 1961–62 but has been around 10,000 tonnes a year in the 2020s, about 90% of it from the mountains of the four easternmost provinces. Cuba now imports coffee to meet its own demand.

facts.label: a year in the early 2020s; 11,500 t in 2021
grown in the four easternmost provinces (2022)

coffee growers, all selling to the state (Reuters, 2012)

regions.name: Sierra Maestra
regions.teaser: Home of Cuba's highest peak, Turquino, in Santiago de Cuba and Granma; Santiago was the top coffee province in 2012. Source of the washed export Arabicas Turquino and Serrano
regions.alt: Serrano: up to about 915 m · 3,000 ft

regions.name: Nipe-Sagua-Baracoa
regions.teaser: The largest of the four coffee massifs, across Holguín, Santiago de Cuba and Guantánamo; Guantánamo was Cuba's second coffee province in 2012

regions.name: Guamuhaya (Escambray)
regions.teaser: Central mountains in Villa Clara, Cienfuegos and Sancti Spíritus, home of Crystal Mountain coffee. In 2022 AFP visited a Villa Clara farmer here growing eight Arabica varieties for the specialty market, about 25 km from the Jibacoa research station that trains growers

regions.name: Sierra del Rosario
regions.teaser: West of Havana. At Las Terrazas, coffee grows in shade at about 250 m (820 ft) and dries on rooftops and small patios

harvest.text: Picked from September to January, peaking in October and November, Reuters reported in 2012. A US roaster was told in 2015 that picking can start in July or August.

grows.species: Arabica (up to about 60%) and Robusta (about 40%)
grows.text: No national variety count was found. In 2024 Lavazza's Michele Cannone named the rust-resistant Isla 6-14 and Isla 6-11 as Cuba's most common Arabicas, with Bourbon and Red Caturra; a 2010 Cuban study, citing 1990 data, named Caturra and Catimors, plus Robusta. The state exporter's Arabicas are washed, and Lavazza's Cuban blend uses washed Robusta plus a small share of Robusta fermented for up to 72 hours.

cup.text: A US roaster who sourced in Cuba in 2015 found Serrano, a washed Arabica, full-bodied and nutty with a banana-like note. Lavazza says its yeast-fermented Cuban Robusta tastes of milk chocolate and almond, with a sweet, winey finish.
cup.why: Lavazza credits controlled fermentation with selected yeasts, for up to 72 hours, with adding complexity and sweetness to its Cuban Robusta.
cup.prized: In 2022 five Cuban coffees from the east and centre scored above 85 points with certified tasters, Cuba's first entries in the specialty category, said the scientific director of its agroforestry research institute.
cup.watch: Altitude. Cuban coffee grows low by specialty standards: the same scientist said Cuba reached specialty quality at about 400 m (1,300 ft), thanks to its geography and climate, while specialty coffee usually grows above 1,500 m (4,900 ft).

story.text: José Antonio Gelabert starts Cuba's first coffee farm, outside Havana, with seed from Santo Domingo.
French colonists fleeing the Haitian Revolution bring better methods and found the first big coffee estates in the south-east.
The harvest reaches a record 60,300 tonnes.
UNESCO lists the remains of the first coffee plantations in south-east Cuba as a World Heritage Site.
Hurricane Sandy leaves 20–30% of the crop on the ground; Reuters expects under 4,000 tonnes, the lowest in more than a century.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffee is grown in four mountain systems, across 8 provinces and 27 municipalities, a 2010 Cuban study says: Sagua-Nipe-Baracoa (Holguín, Santiago de Cuba and Guantánamo), the Sierra Maestra (Santiago de Cuba and Granma), Guamuhaya, also called the Escambray (Villa Clara, Cienfuegos and Sancti Spíritus), and Guaniguanico (Pinar del Río). In 2012 Reuters ranked the provinces Santiago de Cuba, Guantánamo, Granma and Holguín, in that order.
Export names include Turquino, after the peak in the middle of the Sierra Maestra, and Serrano Superior, both washed Arabicas, and Crystal Mountain from the Escambray.

sections.title: Who sells it
body: Growers must sell their coffee to the state, and the state company Cubaexport handles exports; in 2008 Japan and France were the main buyers. AFP reported in 2022 that only 1,365 tonnes had been exported, and Cuba aimed for about 2,700 tonnes in 2022, while the island needs about 24,000 tonnes a year for itself.

sections.title: Plans
body: The official goal is 30,000 tonnes by 2030, partly by planting over 7,000 hectares of coffee in the lowlands and recovering plantations hit by climate change with more resistant varieties. Since 2018 Lavazza has worked with about 250 growers in Santiago de Cuba and Granma provinces on quality and forest protection.

records.name: Dominican Republic
records.summary: Shade-grown Typica from small farms, sold mostly at home or to blenders.
records.lede: The Dominican Republic grows its coffee mostly on smallholdings in the shade, and most trees are Typica or Typica-related, says Coffee Review. INDOCAFÉ, the national coffee institute, counted a 2025 harvest of 450,713 quintales, almost all of it Arabica. Producers sell mostly at home or to blenders, and Puerto Rico is the biggest export buyer.

regions.name: Cibao
regions.teaser: One of seven official regions. INDOCAFÉ's 2025 prices put 'Cibao Altura' (Juncalito) coffee first

regions.name: Barahona
regions.teaser: Generally high-grown, fairly bright and intense but balanced, says Coffee Review. Second in INDOCAFÉ's 2025 prices

regions.name: Valdesia (Baní and Ocoa)
regions.teaser: An EU-protected name since 2016 for Typica and Caturra from Ocoa, Peravia and San Cristóbal. Coffee Review finds Baní coffees softer and rounder

regions.name: Jarabacoa and Constanza
regions.teaser: Towns that Starbucks and the trade ministry name among the main growing areas. Washed and red-honey lots from Jarabacoa's Ramírez Estate scored 90 and 92 at Coffee Review (2020–21)

regions.name: Neyba (Neiba)
regions.teaser: One of the seven official coffee regions; the trade ministry lists Neiba among the main producing areas

grows.species: Arabica, with a little Robusta (about 3% in 2025)
grows.text: No current variety census was found. Coffee Review describes mostly Typica trees, but leaf rust since 2010 hit Typica and Caturra hardest, and in 2026 INDOCAFÉ's director said practically no Typica is left. Farms have replanted with rust-resistant types from regional breeding programmes; in 2014 the research council Coniaf launched a programme to spread Catimor. Starbucks lists washed as the method; Coffee Review has also scored a red-honey lot.

cup.text: Coffee Review describes a classic Caribbean cup: full in the mouth, with quietly lively acidity and a familiar but complete range of aromas and flavors. In its 2010 island tasting, the Dominican coffees led the ratings, two of three scoring 90 or more. Recent reviews of Jarabacoa coffees found cocoa and nut notes: cocoa powder and macadamia in a washed lot (90, 2021), baking chocolate, almond and raspberry jam in a red-honey lot (92, 2020).
cup.why: Coffee Review links the classic Caribbean style to the Typica and Typica-related trees, and says a lot's microclimate and processing usually matter more than its region.
cup.watch: Wet processing and drying have long been weak points, leaving mild taints, especially a faint mustiness, which this gentle style shows readily.
cup.prized: A quiet, sweet, cocoa-toned cup with a velvety feel, as in Coffee Review's 2021 washed Jarabacoa review.

story.text: Typica reaches Santo Domingo, as the country was then called.
Coffee seed goes from Santo Domingo to Cuba.
A hurricane strikes; Coffee Review says the industry is still recovering from it.
Coffee leaf rust breaks out in Chene, María Teresa and El Maniel; by 2014 the research council Coniaf says it affects more than 75% of farms.
The EU protects the name Café de Valdesia, the first Dominican product to get such protection there.

sections.title: The official regions
body: Coffee grows on the slopes of four related mountain massifs, in seven official regions: Cibao, Barahona, Noroeste, Neyba, Sierra Sur, Sierra Occidental and Sierra Central. Coffee Review says a lot's microclimate and processing usually matter more than which region it comes from.

Starbucks's coffee academy maps Juncalito, Jarabacoa and Constanza as the main growing areas, and the trade ministry adds San José de las Matas, Ocoa, Neiba and Barahona. On retail bags, Coffee Review says, Barahona and Baní are the names you'll see most.

sections.title: Right now
body: INDOCAFÉ reports a 2025 harvest of 450,713 quintales (437,131 Arabica, 13,582 Robusta) and exports worth about US$48 million. Leaf rust, a fungus, is still a problem: about 67.9 million rust-resistant or rust-tolerant plants were set out over 2020–2025.

In July 2026 INDOCAFÉ's director said about 23,000 families grow coffee, fewer than in past years, and that about 70,000 tareas (about 4,400 ha; a tarea is 629 m²) had been renewed. Low farms were hit hardest by rust, and with climate change new planting is now recommended from 700 m (2,300 ft) up, instead of 450 m (1,480 ft). Exports grew from about US$5 million in 2018–19 to US$46 million in 2024, the same report says.

harvest.text: INDOCAFÉ's monthly figures for 2025 show picking from about October to March, peaking in November, December and January. Starbucks's coffee academy gives October to June.

records.name: Ecuador
records.summary: High Andean Arabica on the equator, beside a big instant-coffee trade.
records.lede: Ecuador sits on the equator between Colombia and Peru and grows both Arabica and Robusta, from the coastal lowlands up into the Andes. Most of what it exports leaves as instant coffee, and about half the beans its instant-coffee factories use are imported. The finest specialty lots come from highland provinces such as Loja, Zamora-Chinchipe and Pichincha.

facts.label: forecast for 2026/27 (60-kg bags)
Robusta's share: 68% in USDA's 2022/23 forecast, roughly 50% by Royal Coffee's 2026 estimate
coffee farmers in 2022, 96% on under 5 ha (12 acres)
of its 2021/22 coffee exports were instant coffee

regions.name: Loja
regions.teaser: The far south, on the Peru border. Mostly small farms, about a fifth of the country's Arabica, and a major source of its organic coffee

regions.name: Zamora-Chinchipe
regions.teaser: East of Loja, toward the Amazon. Typica and Caturra under shade, often organic

regions.name: Pichincha
regions.teaser: North of Quito. Larger, business-run farms. Cafe Imports says it was the first to export specialty coffee from here

regions.name: Imbabura
regions.teaser: Northern highlands. Softer and rounder than Pichincha, says one coffee guide

regions.name: Manabí
regions.teaser: On the coast, where coffee was first planted. About two-thirds of coastal production in 2022, and over 90% of its coffee land is Arabica

harvest.text: The main picking runs from about April to September (USDA says April to October), with a smaller fly crop, a second, lighter picking, to the end of the year. On the equator some coffee is picked almost year-round.

grows.species: Robusta (roughly half to two-thirds of the crop) and Arabica
grows.text: Sources disagree on which method leads: Royal Coffee calls natural (café en bola) the default, cheapest method, while Coffeeness says washed dominates the highlands; honey and experimental lots are small. Robusta grows mostly in the Amazon lowlands. Typica, Caturra and Bourbon are the traditional Arabicas (no source ranks them); Sidra, Typica Mejorado and Gesha are newer specialty plantings.

cup.text: Algrano, a green-coffee marketplace, says the best lots balance acidity and sweetness, with floral aromas, juicy citrus and red-apple fruit over a chocolatey base. Coffeeness adds caramel and panela sweetness, panela being unrefined cane sugar.
cup.why: Variety and altitude: Cafe Imports says Sidra can show fruity, floral character when grown higher and processed carefully.
cup.watch: Drying: Cafe Imports says some areas that used to get morning fog and afternoon sun are now foggy all day, which keeps coffee from drying evenly on patios.

story.text: Coffee is first planted, in the coastal province of Manabí.
Coffee becomes a commercial crop when disease threatens the cacao industry.
About 347,000 hectares are planted; by 2022 USDA put the area at about 60,000 hectares.
The Cup of Excellence competition comes to Ecuador; Coffeeness says the winner was a Typica Mejorado from Loja that scored 90.93.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: Instant coffee dominates: in 2021/22 about 93% of Ecuador's coffee exports were soluble. Its factories can process more than a million bags a year, nearly three times what the country grows, and about half their beans come from Vietnam, Brazil and Colombia, USDA reported in 2022.
Royal Coffee notes that Ecuador uses the US dollar, which raises costs above its neighbours', and that small specialty lots are hard to fill into containers, so importers sometimes use airfreight.

sections.title: Café en bola
body: Natural processing, drying the whole cherry, is the default and cheapest method, known locally as café en bola; Cafe Imports describes it as coffee left to dry on the tree. Washed coffees are easy to find, and experimental lots exist in small volumes.

sections.title: Where each kind grows
body: USDA's 2022 report put 86% of Ecuador's Robusta in the Amazon region, with more in coastal provinces such as Santa Elena, Manabí and Guayas. Forty percent of Arabica was grown in coastal provinces, with Manabí making 67% of the coast's coffee.

The coffee area has shrunk from about 347,000 hectares in the early 1980s to about 60,000 in 2022, and the agriculture ministry's statistics track only Arabica area. USDA also mapped where each style is made: washed Arabica in El Oro, Manabí, Loja, Guayas and Zamora-Chinchipe, and natural Arabica in Loja, Manabí, El Oro, Los Ríos, Guayas and Pichincha.

cup.text: Process sets the style. Sweet Maria's says washed Ethiopians tend toward bright acidity, citrus, florals and sweet spice, while naturals lean to dried fruit, from berry to mango and peach, with a thick body. Cafe Imports finds naturals fruitier and more chocolatey, often winey and syrupy, and washed lots lighter and brighter.

feel.body: light when washed, full and syrupy when natural

cup.prized: Sweet Maria's says the best washed Ethiopians can have sparkling-bright, citrus-like acidity, and its naturals dried-fruit flavors from berry to mango and peach with a thick body.
cup.watch: A grade isn't a taste rating: Cafe Imports notes that Ethiopian grades measure uniformity, cleanliness and defects, not flavor.

facts.label: of the crop is natural (sun-dried); 20–30% washed

where its Arabica grows (3,600–7,200 ft)

harvest.text: Picked from October to January. Cafe Imports says the new crop typically reaches buyers abroad from about April to June.

story.text: Arabica formed in Ethiopia's forests as a natural cross of Coffea canephora and Coffea eugenioides, a 2024 genome study suggests.
The Jimma Agricultural Research Center began breeding and selecting coffee; its first releases, in 1978/79, included 74110 and 74112.
The government set up the Ethiopian Commodity Exchange (ECX), through which most coffee was then sold.
The ECX voted to allow direct sales from individual washing stations, a step back toward traceable coffee.
Sidama voted to leave the Southern region and became Ethiopia's tenth region.
USDA forecasts a record 12.1 million bags, after more than half the coffee area was replanted with higher-yielding varieties over four years.

sections.title: Washed or natural
body: Most Ethiopian coffee is natural. UNIDO's 2025 study of the coffee trade puts 70–80% of it as unwashed, sun-dried coffee and 20–30% as washed, the same split USDA gave in 2021, and the lowest washed share among Africa's Arabica growers. Washing needs fresh cherry delivered to a station and cash up front, while farmers can dry cherry at home.

Areas lean different ways: Coffee Hunter lists washed as the usual process in Yirgacheffe and Limu and both in Guji, and Cafe Imports says Harrar's coffee is almost always natural. In January 2026 exporters told Algrano that washed coffee would be scarce that season, because farmers short of cash were drying more cherry at home.

sections.title: Gardens, forests and farms
body: About half of Ethiopia's coffee is garden coffee, grown by households, often among food crops like banana and beans. By UNIDO's 2025 count, semi-forest coffee gives about 30–35%, forest coffee about 10% and plantations about 5%. Yields run from about 250 kg a hectare in forest to 750 in gardens and 900 on plantations.

The farms are tiny. The national coffee authority counts 5.9 million coffee farmers, and USDA says smallholders, often on less than half a hectare, grow about 90% of the crop. The government has also set aside 100,000 hectares for modern, private coffee farms, the first time land has been reserved for this (USDA, 2026).

cup.text: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids sorted Guatemalan coffees into two camps in 2003: delicate, balanced cups with floral and fruit notes, and cups with a more intense, simpler acidity. Anacafé's eight regional profiles run from very sweet Antigua and chocolaty Nuevo Oriente to citrusy Atitlán, floral San Marcos and wine-like Huehuetenango.
cup.why: Higher farms generally give more acidity and usually more nuance, and dry weather while the fruit ripens and is picked usually makes coffee sweeter, Davids writes.
cup.prized: Huehuetenango's Geishas and Pacamaras lead the national Cup of Excellence; in 2026 Huehuetenango farms took 16 of the 27 places.
cup.watch: Davids prefers the delicate camp; the other leans on a more intense and often simpler acidity.

story.text: Coffee reaches Guatemala.
Exports start to grow after 1850, and planting gathers pace in the 1860s.
Growers form their own association, which becomes Anacafé, the national coffee association.
Leaf rust, a fungal disease, sweeps the country; USDA says about 20% of production was lost to it.
Anacafé 14, a rust-resistant variety created in Guatemala, is released.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Most growers are small. Smallholders are 97% of Guatemala's coffee growers but harvest about 44% of the crop; medium farms harvest 31% and about 350 large estates 25% (USDA figures reported in 2024). Anacafé supports about 125,000 coffee families, and in 2021 USDA said at least 93% of the coffee grows under shade trees.

Replanting is slow: about a third of Arabica plantations had been renewed with rust-tolerant hybrids by 2026. Robusta is a small crop, about 130,000 bags, but Barista Hustle says Robusta rootstock is widely used for grafting.

sections.title: Protected names
body: World Coffee Research credits Guatemala with setting up a denomination-of-origin system, a set of protected regional names, for its eight producing regions. In October 2026 the European Union added Café Antigua, coffee from the department of Sacatepéquez, to its register of protected geographical indications, which guards the name against imitations in Europe; the EU's description cites honey, caramel, apple and toasted-nut aromas.

records.name: Hawaii
records.summary: Kona's small lava-slope farms, plus Kaʻū, Maui and Kauaʻi.
records.lede: Hawaii is the only US state that grows coffee on a commercial scale: about 1,000 farms on five islands (2023-24), together growing about 0.1% of the world's coffee. Kona, on the Big Island's western slopes, is the famous name, and Kaʻū, Maui and Kauaʻi also grow coffee. Labor is short, and since 2010 two pests, coffee berry borer and leaf rust, have pushed costs up.

regions.name: Kona
regions.teaser: Western slopes of Hualālai and Mauna Loa: about 700 farms, most under 5 acres (2 ha), in a belt barely a mile wide

regions.name: Kaʻū
regions.teaser: The Big Island's south. Kona-style coffee, often cheaper and better prepared than standard Kona, says Coffee Review

regions.name: Puna
regions.teaser: The Big Island's wettest region, on the opposite side from Kona: small scattered farms, mostly Typica, Caturra and Catuai, replanted from the mid-1990s after decades of sugar

regions.name: Hāmākua
regions.teaser: The Big Island's north-east Hāmākua coast, where a handful of tiny, carefully run farms have distinguished themselves, says Coffee Review

regions.name: Maui
regions.teaser: Small boutique farms on Haleakalā's cool upland slopes, plus larger mechanized estates on the coastal plains

regions.name: Kauaʻi
regions.teaser: Kauai Coffee, a mechanized estate of about 3,000 acres (1,200 ha) on the coastal plain; Red and Yellow Catuai make up about 80% of its coffee

regions.name: Molokaʻi
regions.teaser: Malulani Estate, a large mechanized farm on former sugar and pineapple land on the coastal plain

regions.name: Oʻahu
regions.teaser: Waialua Estate, a large mechanized farm on former sugar and pineapple land

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: Two pictures: Kona's roughly 700 small farms grow the heirloom Kona Typica, first brought from Guatemala, while the big mechanized estates lean on Catuai: Red and Yellow Catuai make up about 80% of Kauai Coffee's crop, and it is common in Kaʻū, Puna, Maui and Molokaʻi too. Kona coffee is traditionally washed (pulped within a day of picking, fermented, rinsed and dried); naturals and honeys are small specialty lots, from Kona and Maui among others.

cup.text: Coffee Review's Kenneth Davids describes classic Kona as balanced, quietly complete and gently bright, with a smooth mouthfeel. In the Hawaii reviews on one Coffee Review page, chocolate and nut notes recur, while naturals and Geshas from Kona and Kaʻū add floral and tropical-fruit notes.
cup.why: The Kona Farmers Association credits the heirloom Kona Typica for the smooth, balanced cup. Kona also gets most of its rain in summer, and afternoon clouds shade the trees from the worst heat.
cup.prized: Carefully farmed lots: Hawaii's agriculture department says coffee from Kona, Kaʻū and Maui consistently scores 85 points or more.
cup.watch: Blends. For decades a bag could say Kona with only 10% Kona coffee inside; from July 2027 Hawaii-labeled blends must hold at least 51%.

story.text: Coffee reaches Kona; Wikipedia credits the Rev. Samuel Ruggles with bringing cuttings in 1828.
A state law lets coffee use a regional name such as Kona if it holds at least 10% beans from that region.
Coffee berry borer, a small beetle that Hawaii's agriculture department calls the most devastating coffee pest, is found on the Big Island, and later spreads to other islands.
Coffee leaf rust, a fungal leaf disease, is found on Maui and the Big Island for the first time.
New laws raise the minimum Hawaii-grown share in labeled blends from 10% to 51%, effective July 2027.

sections.title: Grades
body: Hawaii grades its green coffee by state standards, from Extra Fancy, Fancy and Hawaii No. 1 down to Select, Prime and No. 3. Coffee graded below Prime may not carry a regional name such as Kona or Kaʻū on the label. In 2024-25 about half of the state's crop went through certified grading, and most of it graded Prime.

sections.title: Right now
body: USDA forecast the 2025-26 crop about 20% below the year before, with bearing acreage down to 6,500 acres. Over the decade to 2024, Hawaii's yield per acre fell about 27% and green exports fell sharply, while prices rose.

cup.text: Going by Perfect Daily Grind's 2017 guide to the six regions, Honduran coffee tends toward caramel and chocolate sweetness with citrus or tropical fruit: chocolate and caramel in Copán and Agalta, citrus, peach and apricot in Montecillos, and tropical fruit, grape and berry in Opalaca. Coffee Review calls most Honduran coffee gentle, smooth and medium-bodied, balanced in acidity and often chocolaty; clean high-grown lots can add flowers, citrus, caramel and nut.
cup.why: PDG says Montecillos's cold nights slow ripening and give a sweeter cup, and Coffeeness says Copán's high farms ripen slowly too.
cup.prized: Cup of Excellence buyers pay most for Geishas: 2026's top three lots were Geishas from Intibucá, Santa Bárbara and Francisco Morazán, at $75–90 a pound.
cup.watch: Drying. Honduras is rainy, and Coffee Hunter says patios are hard to use in some regions, so coffee is prone to over-fermentation; Coffee Review says slow drying on small farms can bring heavy notes of molasses, tobacco and herbs.

story.text: IHCAFE, the national coffee institute, releases Catuaí, which for a time makes up nearly half of the Arabica grown.
Hurricane Mitch destroys about 80% of the country's agriculture.
Marcala becomes a registered appellation of origin, the first in Central America.
A leaf-rust epidemic leads to a national replanting program, so Honduran trees are now younger on average.
Production passes 5 million bags, making Honduras Central America's biggest grower.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: Small farms grow almost all of it: World Coffee Research counts more than 120,000 coffee farms, with smallholders producing about 95% of the coffee (2018 study), and Coffee Hunter says 70% of farmers work less than 2 hectares. Coffee grows in 15 of the 18 departments, and USDA says 61% of farms sit between 3,900 and 5,200 ft (about 1,200–1,600 m); all of it is Arabica (2025).

sections.title: Varieties and rust
body: Honduras breeds its own rust-resistant varieties. Lempira and IHCAFE 90 carry Robusta genes and replaced many older fields, and Parainema was released in 2004. In 2017 IHCAFE said 60% of the coffee area was improved, rust-resistant plants. That same year a new rust strain broke Lempira's resistance, and Coffee Review counts as many as four new strains since. USDA puts recent growth down to less rust, stable weather and more mature Parainema plantings.

records.name: Haiti
records.summary: Once half the world's coffee; now small, mostly Typica farms.
records.lede: As the French colony of Saint-Domingue, Haiti grew roughly half the world's coffee in the late 1780s. Today its coffee comes mostly from small farms where old Typica trees grow among food crops, and little is exported: coffee exports were worth less than half a million dollars in 2023. Coffee Review finds the classic Haitian cup low-toned, full and chocolaty.

harvest.text: Picking usually starts in September and can run into June, says Perfect Daily Grind.

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: All Arabica, about 90% Typica in a 2010 study, with some Bourbon, Mundo Novo, Caturra and Catimor. Sources split on processing: that World Bank study put about 70% as dried in the cherry (natural), most of it drunk at home, and found unwashed 'café pilé' was also most of what was exported; but an exporter told Perfect Daily Grind in 2022 that most is now washed. Haitian Blue is usually washed, and the social enterprise Singing Rooster also makes honey lots because water is short.

cup.text: Coffee Review describes the classic Haitian cup as low-toned, full and chocolaty, and in 2010 scored a Haiti Ranquitte coffee 88 for its rich, chocolaty, low-acid character. Perfect Daily Grind calls well-grown, well-processed Haitian coffee medium-bodied and mellow, with little acidity.
cup.why: A 2006 study for the Inter-American Development Bank says land above 900 m (2,950 ft) has the best potential for quality, and links acidity to altitude.
cup.watch: Careless drying. Much Haitian coffee is dry-processed with little care and sold at home, and even good lots can carry a hint of a drying fault.

story.text: Coffee probably arrives in Saint-Domingue, brought from Martinique by a French naval officer.
Saint-Domingue, worked by enslaved Africans, supplies about half the world's coffee.
A slave revolt begins; many plantations burn, and Haiti wins independence in 1804.
Production peaks at about 740,000 sacks, by the IDB study's count.
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes, one of a run of disasters that have left many farms unproductive.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffee grows in Haiti's mountain ranges, among them the Massif du Nord, the Montagnes Noires, the Chaîne des Matheux, the Massif de la Hotte and the Massif de la Selle. The 2006 IDB study names Grand'Anse, Sud-Est, Nord and Centre as the main producing departments.
Most farms are small 'creole gardens', where coffee shares the ground with bananas, cassava, papaya and vegetables. The Typica trees are often old, tall and unpruned, and give little fruit.

sections.title: Natural or washed?
body: Sources disagree on how much is dried in the cherry (the natural method). A 2010 World Bank study put about 70% as dry-processed and 30% as washed or semi-washed, but an exporter told Perfect Daily Grind in 2022 that most is now washed. The traditional 'café pilé' is dried until a black crust forms around the bean, then pounded free in a mortar.

Coffee sold as Haitian Blue, named for the blue-grey tint of its green beans, is usually shade-grown and washed, and a 1990s programme built washing stations for cooperatives. The social enterprise Singing Rooster added honey processing because water is short.

sections.title: Where it goes
body: Little leaves the country as Haitian coffee. The Dominican Republic bought about 28% of production at the time of the 2010 World Bank study, and Perfect Daily Grind reports that Haitian coffee is often resold as Dominican, which blurs the export figures. Most of the rest is drunk at home.

sections.title: On the bag
body: 'Haitian Bleu' began in the 1990s as a brand for Cafetières Natives, a federation of 7,000 farmers backed by almost US$6 million from USAID; the name referred to Jamaica Blue Mountain. Coffee Review says the effort failed. Today the importer and roaster Cafe Kreyol sells coffee as Haitian Blue, bought by direct trade.

Café pilé, the traditional coffee dried in a black crust and pounded free, is what most Haitians drink at home. In 2010 it was also the main formal export: the café pilé export chain carried about 6% of the crop, against 2% for specialty coffee, a World Bank study found.

records.name: Indonesia
records.summary: Earthy wet-hulled Sumatras, and a lot of Robusta.
records.lede: Indonesia is one of the world's biggest coffee producers, and most of its crop is Robusta from southern Sumatra and Java. Its Arabica grows on islands from Sumatra to Papua, and much of it is wet-hulled, a local method that tends to give a heavy, earthy cup. Smallholders, usually on 1–2 hectares, farm about 98% of the coffee land.

regions.name: Southern Sumatra (South Sumatra, Lampung, Bengkulu)
regions.teaser: The main Robusta belt. In 2023 these were Indonesia's first, second and fifth biggest coffee provinces, together close to half the national crop

regions.name: Aceh (Gayo)
regions.teaser: Shaded hills around Lake Tawar near Takengon, protected as Gayo coffee. A bit higher than Lintong, and Coffee Review finds them perhaps a bit brighter

regions.name: Lintong (North Sumatra)
regions.teaser: A compact area southwest of Lake Toba. Mandheling is a looser trade name for wet-hulled Sumatra

regions.name: Kerinci (Jambi)
regions.teaser: Jambi grows mainly Robusta, and has more recently begun exporting wet-hulled Arabica sold as Kerinci

regions.name: Java
regions.teaser: Big government estates in East Java's Ijen–Raung highlands, traditionally washed; smallholders across the island's highlands

regions.name: Sulawesi (Toraja)
regions.teaser: Named for the Toraja people, and sold as Kalossi under the Dutch. Washed estate coffee and wet-hulled smallholder lots

regions.name: Bali
regions.teaser: Historically washed rather than wet-hulled. Picked April to July, says Sucafina

regions.name: Flores
regions.teaser: Importers know it for clean washed lots, but Royal Coffee says most of the crop is wet-hulled, and Coffee Review says Flores coffee may be made by any of Indonesia's methods. Robusta grows here too

regions.name: Papua
regions.teaser: Indonesia's far east. Picked May to October, says Sucafina

harvest.text: Robusta in Sumatra is picked from April, peaking in June and July. Arabica is picked twice a year, around April–May and September–October, USDA reported in 2025; in the Gayo highlands the protected-name rules say picking runs from September to May or June. Islands differ: Sucafina lists Java April–August, Bali April–July, Flores May–September, and Sulawesi and Papua May–October.

grows.species: mostly Robusta (about 88% in 2026/27)
grows.text: Mostly Robusta from southern Sumatra; an Indonesian exporter says most Lampung Robusta is dried in the whole cherry (natural). Most Arabica is wet-hulled, with washed lots from East Java's estates, Bali and newer projects; importers and the Gayo rules most often list Timor Hybrid and Catimor types (Tim Tim, Ateng, P88), plus Sigarar Utang, Andungsari, S795 and some Typica, without giving shares.

cup.text: Wet-hulled Indonesian coffee tends toward an earthy, savory, herbal cup with a heavy body, often with dark chocolate and nut, says Cafe Imports. Coffee Review hears forest-floor notes in old-style Sulawesi lots, and calls newer smallholder Javas a cleaner, sweeter take on the same profile.
cup.why: Wet-hulling strips off the parchment while the bean is still wet, at roughly 25–50% moisture by importers' accounts. Coffee Review says the process shapes a Sumatra more than altitude or variety does.
cup.prized: Newer, cleaner Sumatras, which Coffee Review says bring a rich, sweet pungency, complex stone fruit, and deep floral and spice notes.
cup.watch: Old-style lots can taste musty, from damp earth to sharp mildew, a note the trade once sold as earthy, says Coffee Review. The process can also crush beans and dry them unevenly.

story.text: Dutch colonists planted Indonesia's first coffee around Batavia, now Jakarta; floods destroyed the first seedlings.
The Dutch East India Company began shipping Java coffee to Europe.
A forced-cultivation system made each village set aside a fifth of its land for export crops such as coffee.
Coffee leaf rust destroyed most of the crop, many estates were abandoned, and farmers largely switched to Robusta.
Wet-hulling probably began in Aceh, partly because farmers wanted quick payment and had no good way to dry coffee in the wet climate.
Gayo Arabica from the Aceh highlands is registered in Indonesia as a geographical indication (GI), a protected origin name.

sections.title: Right now
body: Heavy rain disrupted flowering in southern Sumatra and Java, and USDA expects Robusta to fall by 1 million bags in 2026/27. In late November and early December 2025, floods and landslides in Aceh and North Sumatra damaged farms, roads and processing sites; StoneX said nearly a third of Arabica farms were affected.

sections.title: Moving uphill
body: Coffee grows best in Indonesia at about 800–1,400 m (2,600–4,600 ft) today. One 2018 study projects that band moving up to 1,200–1,600 m (3,900–5,200 ft) by 2050 as the climate warms. Starbucks' Coffee Academy map puts Sumatra's Arabica at about 800–1,500 m (2,600–4,900 ft).

sections.title: The Robusta side
body: Robusta is most of Indonesia's coffee, and the main Robusta areas are the southern Sumatran provinces of South Sumatra, Lampung and Bengkulu. Robusta pickers often strip every cherry from the branch, ripe or not, and most of the crop goes into blends and instant coffee. Yields stay below 1 t per hectare, USDA reported in 2025.

An Indonesian exporter describes Lampung Robusta as earthy and woody, with peppery spice, roasted nut and dark chocolate. Some Indonesian producers now aim for fine Robusta, a grade that allows no primary defects and at most five secondary defects in a 350 g sample.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: About 1.77 million people work in Indonesian coffee, and smallholders farm 98% of the coffee land. Coffee moves from farmers through collectors, processors and traders to exporters, and much of the trade inside the country is in asalan, partly processed, unsorted green coffee.

In the wet-hulled chain, a farmer dries wet parchment for a few hours to about 50% moisture and sells it; it is hulled at about 25–35%, and exporters in Medan can bring it from 14–15% down to 11–12% before shipping, Sweet Maria's explains.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Mandheling is a loose trade name: it usually covers Lintong and other coffees from around Lake Toba, and sometimes any wet-hulled Sumatra. Gayo is a protected name for Arabica from Central Aceh, Bener Meriah and Gayo Lues. Kerinci is Arabica from Jambi, and Kalossi is the old Dutch-era name for Toraja coffee from Sulawesi.

records.name: India
records.summary: Shade-grown Robusta and Arabica, and the home of monsooned coffee.
records.lede: India grows coffee under shade trees in the hills of the south, mostly in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. About 70% of the crop is Robusta, and nearly all coffee holdings are small. It's also the home of monsooned coffee, beans left to swell in the humid monsoon air.

regions.name: Coorg (Kodagu)
regions.teaser: Karnataka. India's biggest coffee district: about 121,000 t in 2025–26, roughly a third of the crop, most of it Robusta

regions.name: Chikmagalur
regions.teaser: Karnataka. About 95,000 t in 2025–26, a little over half Robusta; with Coorg, one of the best-known areas, says Coffee Review

regions.name: Bababudangiris
regions.teaser: The Karnataka hills where legend says India's first coffee was planted, around 1600. Arabica, with its own protected name

regions.name: Wayanad
regions.teaser: Kerala. All Robusta, about 69,000 t in 2025–26, with its own protected name, Wayanad Robusta

regions.name: Hassan
regions.teaser: Karnataka's third coffee district: about 41,000 t in 2025–26, a little more Robusta than Arabica

regions.name: Araku Valley
regions.teaser: Andhra Pradesh, in the Eastern Ghats. Arabica grown by tribal families, with its own protected name; the state grew about 15,000 t in 2025–26

regions.name: Travancore
regions.teaser: Southern Kerala. Mostly Robusta, about 8,800 t in 2025–26

regions.name: Pulneys
regions.teaser: Tamil Nadu. Nearly all Arabica, about 8,200 t in 2025–26

regions.name: Nilgiris
regions.teaser: Tamil Nadu. Mostly Robusta, about 6,300 t in 2025–26; the Coffee Board lists the old Kents variety here

harvest.text: Arabica is picked from November to January and Robusta from December to February, says the Coffee Board, usually by hand.

grows.species: mostly Robusta (about 70% in 2025–26), plus Arabica
grows.text: About 70% Robusta, mainly the S.274 and CxR selections. For Arabica the Coffee Board calls S795 by far the most popular, but a 2024 Counter Culture visit found Selection 9 and Chandragiri most planted now; Cauvery is India's name for Catimor. Both species are sold washed and natural, with no published split, and monsooning is India's own specialty.

cup.text: Coffee Review describes the traditional Indian cup as clean, sweetly bright and balanced, often with nut, baking chocolate and ripe citrus. The Coffee Board says its Mysore Nuggets Extra Bold, a premium washed Arabica, shows full aroma, medium to good body, good acidity and a hint of spice, and describes its Robusta Kaapi Royale as full-bodied, soft, smooth and mellow.
cup.why: Leaf rust hit India so hard that almost no pure Arabicas are grown there. Coffee Review credits the clean cup to careful picking and processing, and blames its lack of distinctiveness on the hybrids planted instead, which carry some Robusta or Liberica genes.
cup.prized: Coffee Review says lots of the Selection 9 variety can show an elegant, floral-and-fruit delicacy, and ranks India's best Robustas among the world's finest, matched only by some from Uganda.
cup.watch: Sameness: Coffee Review finds many Arabicas clean and moderately bright but not very distinctive.

story.text: Legend credits the Sufi saint Baba Budan with bringing seven seeds from Mocha, in Yemen, to the Baba Budan Giri hills.
Kent, a pure Arabica selected for rust tolerance, is planted; today it survives only in rare stands.
A coffee law, the Coffee Act VII of 1942, created the Coffee Board of India.
India's coffee research station releases S795, a cross of S.288 and Kent that became its most widely grown Arabica.
The government freed up the coffee trade.
Exports reached US$1.8 billion, up about 40% on the year before.

sections.title: Monsooned coffee
body: Monsooning copies what used to happen to coffee on long, damp sea voyages. From June to September, at curing works on the west coast, natural-processed beans are spread out and then bagged loosely in open-sided warehouses where the monsoon air can reach them. Over 12–16 weeks they swell to nearly double their size and fade to a pale straw color.

The Coffee Board calls the result mellow but aggressive and musty, with little acidity and a heavy, syrupy body like an aged coffee. It's used mostly in blends. Monsooned Malabar AA is the top grade, and Monsooned Malabar Robusta has a protected name.

sections.title: Under shade
body: Most Indian coffee grows under two layers of shade trees, with nearly 50 kinds of shade tree in use. Farmers often plant pepper, vanilla and fruit trees among the coffee.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Indian bags often name a region or an estate. The government counts seven geographical indications, legally protected origin names, and names Coorg Arabica, Chikmagalur Arabica, Bababudangiris Arabica, Araku Valley Arabica, Wayanad Robusta and Monsooned Malabar Robusta among them.

The Coffee Board also promotes three premium coffees by name: Mysore Nuggets Extra Bold, very large beans from washed Arabicas of Chikmagalur, Coorg, Biligiris, Bababudangiris and Shevaroys; Robusta Kaapi Royale, made from the Robusta Parchment AB grade of Coorg, Wayanad, Chikmagalur and Travancore; and Monsooned Malabar AA, the top monsooned grade.

sections.title: Right now
body: The Coffee Board's final estimate for 2025–26 came in at 373,000 t (111,000 t Arabica, 262,000 t Robusta), well below its early forecast of 403,000 t. Heavy, drawn-out rain had brought black rot to Arabica and fruit rot to Robusta, and grower groups had warned the Arabica forecast was too high.

For 2026–27 the Board's first estimate is 404,000 t. USDA is more cautious at 6.14 million 60-kg bags (about 368,000 t), with Arabica yields down 8% after heat and a long dry spell during flowering, and it names aging trees and white stem borer, an insect pest, as drags on Arabica.

records.name: Jamaica
records.summary: Blue Mountain Typica, defined by a line on a legal map.
records.lede: Jamaica's famous coffee is Jamaica Blue Mountain. Under the regulator JACRA's 2018 rules, the name simply means coffee grown inside a boundary drawn around part of the Blue Mountains, in the east of the island. Most of it is a local form of Typica, processed by the washed method, and Japan takes about 70% of the crop, the Gleaner reported in 2023.

of the crop goes to Japan (Gleaner, 2023)
where High Mountain coffee grows, outside the Blue Mountain area (1,500–3,000 ft)
