regions.name: Blue Mountain
regions.teaser: Only coffee grown inside this legally mapped part of the eastern Blue Mountains may use the name. Often summed up as the parishes of St Andrew, St Thomas, Portland and St Mary

regions.name: High Mountain
regions.teaser: Premium grades grown outside the Blue Mountain area, in parishes such as Manchester and St Elizabeth, sold as Jamaica High Mountain Supreme. About 4,800 farmers (2026); output fell 56% from 2020/21 to 2024/25

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: Almost all washed Arabica, mostly the local Blue Mountain form of Typica; Bourbon, Caturra and some Gesha also grow. About 90% of the crop comes from the Blue Mountain region.

cup.text: Blue Mountain producers describe a mild, creamy sweetness with no bitterness, and one adds hints of nuts, chocolate and sweet herbs; Starbucks's coffee academy points to cocoa and citrus. Coffee Review has praised the deep, quiet richness of the classic Blue Mountain cup.
cup.why: One estate owner credits the cloud cover: it cools the slopes and slows ripening, which he says gives a more complex cup.
cup.prized: Mildness, sweetness and balance, with little or no bitterness.
cup.watch: Mustiness. In a 2010 tasting Coffee Review found a mild musty note in all three Blue Mountain samples and blamed slow or uneven drying after the long truck trip from the wet mills. Fakes are the other risk: a cheap 'Blue Mountain' is almost certainly not real, a producer told PDG.

story.text: Governor Sir Nicholas Lawes brings coffee to Jamaica, near Castleton; World Coffee Research dates the arrival of Typica from Martinique to 1730.
The Coffee Industry Regulations draw the Blue Mountain area's boundary and name the coffee works allowed to process it, among them Mavis Bank and Wallenford.
On January 9, 60% of that year's harvest leaves Kingston for Japan; since 2019 Japan has marked the date as Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee Day.
New JACRA regulations restate the boundary and raise the Blue Mountain share required in a 'Blue Mountain blend' to at least 30% (the 1953 rules said 20%).
Hurricane Melissa damages about 35% of the coffee industry, by early estimates; in December JACRA starts handing out fertiliser and replacement seedlings.

sections.title: What the name means
body: JACRA's 2018 regulations define Jamaica Blue Mountain coffee as coffee grown in the Blue Mountain area, and they define that area by a boundary line run between named places such as Skibo, Chelsea and the western slope of the John Crow Mountains. The text sets no altitude and names no parishes. The rules often quoted, coffee from the parishes of St Andrew, St Thomas, Portland and St Mary grown at 3,000–5,500 ft (about 915–1,675 m), come from summaries such as WIPO's, not from the regulations.

Jamaica High Mountain Supreme is the premium grade of Jamaican coffee grown outside that area. Blue Mountain itself is sorted into No. 1, 2 and 3, No. 1 being the largest beans with the fewest defects, plus peaberry: smaller, rounder beans shaped like a rugby ball.

sections.title: From cherry to bag
body: Cherries are picked by hand on steep slopes and pulped at stations in the region, because Blue Mountain is a washed coffee. By WIPO's account, the wet beans reach a government-authorised processing works within 24 hours, are dried in the sun, and then rest in wooden silos or jute sacks for at least eight weeks before being sorted by hand.

sections.title: Right now
body: Early estimates put Hurricane Melissa's damage at about 35% of the coffee industry. In December 2025 JACRA began handing out fertiliser and about 15,000 seedlings for the Blue Mountain region, with about 10,000 more for High Mountain farms.
High Mountain was shrinking before the storm: 5,321 boxes in 2024/25, down from 12,231 in 2020/21. In July 2026 JACRA was training farmers to revive it.

JACRA's acting director general said in April 2026 that 145,000 boxes of Blue Mountain coffee were produced in 2025, above a projection of 127,000; the 2022 crop was 248,151 boxes. About J$132 million (Jamaican dollars) had gone on seedlings, fertiliser and other inputs since the storm, mostly in St Thomas, Portland and St Andrew.

harvest.text: Picked over a long season, roughly September to April, says Starbucks's coffee academy. One Blue Mountain farm says its pickers work from mid-August to the end of May.

cup.text: Royal Coffee describes Kenya's signature as grapefruit-like citrus and bright acidity, sometimes with a savory, tomato-like note. Sweet Maria's names citrus, blackcurrant and berry, balanced at best by syrupy, cane-sugar sweetness and sometimes a winey edge.
cup.why: Ozone notes that SL28, one of Kenya's most important varieties, is famous for its acidity.
cup.watch: Sucafina notes that some think the classic Kenyan flavor has grown less distinct as farms switched from SL varieties to Ruiru 11, and Sweet Maria's warns that people who dislike acidity won't enjoy Kenyan coffee.
cup.prized: Intensity with balance: Sweet Maria's says the best Kenyas pair bright citrus and blackcurrant acidity with syrupy, cane-sugar sweetness.

facts.label: of coffee to be harvested in 2026/27 (USDA forecast)

story.text: Missionaries brought coffee from Réunion and planted it near Nairobi; 1893 is sometimes given as the date.
Scott Agricultural Laboratories selected SL28, SL34 and SL14, still Kenya's classic varieties.
A coffee berry disease epidemic led to Ruiru 11, a disease-resistant hybrid released in 1985.
Production reached 128,941 tonnes; by 2008/09 it had fallen to 32,460 tonnes.
Batian, resistant to leaf rust and coffee berry disease, was released.
A new Coffee Act revived the Coffee Board of Kenya and wrote a direct, digital payment system for farmers into law.

sections.title: The varieties: SL28 to Batian
body: SL28 is prized for its cup and drought tolerance but falls to the major diseases; SL34, once thought to be a Bourbon, is now known to be related to Typica (Royal Coffee). Ruiru 11, bred after the 1968 coffee berry disease epidemic, is compact and resistant but has a poor name among specialty tasters. Batian, released in 2010, resists both leaf rust and coffee berry disease.

Sucafina wrote in 2020 that most farms still have SL trees, most also have Ruiru 11 and, more and more, Batian, so many lots are blends of them. Royal Coffee now calls Batian the country's most-planted tree. No official shares are published, so the order of the list is a judgment.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: About 80% of Kenyan coffee is sold through farmer cooperatives; corporate and family estates handle the rest (USDA, 2026). Murang'a alone has up to 100,000 smallholders, says Royal Coffee.

The coffee area shrank from about 170,000 hectares in the early 1990s to about 119,000 in 2020, says the Kenya News Agency; USDA expects 106,000 hectares to be harvested in 2026/27. Farms near Nairobi, Thika, Kiambu and Nyeri were uprooted for housing, though that has slowed over the past two years.

records.name: Laos
records.summary: Bolaven Plateau coffee: mostly Robusta, with a growing washed Arabica side.
records.lede: About 95% of Laos's coffee grows on the Bolaven Plateau in the south, a cool upland of red basalt soil where French colonists planted coffee from around 1915. Most of it is Robusta, but for about 20 years the government has pushed growers toward Arabica, and washed Catimor, Typica and even Gesha lots now reach specialty roasters.

the Paksong coffee area (2,600–4,400 ft)

regions.name: Bolaven Plateau (Paksong)
regions.teaser: Nearly all Lao coffee, centered on Paksong in Champasak province; the Bolaven Coffee Cooperative also has members in Salavan and Sekong. Red basalt soil and rain from May to October

harvest.text: Arabica is picked from November through January, after a May-to-October rainy season.

grows.species: mostly Robusta, with about a quarter Arabica
grows.text: About three-quarters Robusta, which Sweet Maria's says is mainly used for everyday coffee, such as a local drink sweetened with condensed milk. For Arabica, Catimor spread from the 2000s, and specialty farms also grow Typica and a little Gesha. The Arabica that reaches specialty roasters is usually washed or semi-washed, and some Robusta is sold natural; no source gives national process shares.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's calls Paksong Arabica Brazil-like: low in acidity and mild, with raw sugar and walnut, a tea-like acidity and a faint cacao-nib and tobacco finish. Its 2025 washed Typica (87 points) showed caramel, brown sugar, berry tea and a hint of lemon. Cooperative Coffees' profiles of the Bolaven Plateau cooperative's coffee mention nutty and caramel notes with muted to mild acidity.
cup.watch: New-crop lots can taste greenish and slightly vegetal, Sweet Maria's warns.

story.text: French colonists plant the first coffee and, after trials in the north, settle on the south.
Early French plantings of Arabica, Robusta and Liberica largely fail, hit by leaf rust and two world wars.
After leaf rust destroys Arabica trees, farmers are encouraged to plant hardier Robusta.
Farmers widely adopt Catimor, a rust-resistant Arabica that promised high returns, often in place of Robusta.
The Bolaven Plateau Coffee Producers Cooperative is founded with French development aid.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Robusta in Laos grows unusually high, at about 1,300 m (4,300 ft). Growth is held back by chronic labor shortages, which can leave ripe cherries unpicked, and by unexploded ordnance left from the Vietnam War. "Bolaven Coffee" is a protected geographical indication, a legally registered origin name.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: Coffee is one of Laos's top three farm exports by value. The Bolaven Coffee Cooperative, founded in 2007 as the Bolaven Plateau Coffee Producers Association with French development aid, has 484 member households in Paksong, Laongam and Thateng districts, all certified organic and Fair Trade. Its members farm about 1,611 ha of Arabica and 371 ha of Robusta. In 2025 it exported 46 containers (40 of Arabica, 6 of Robusta), and it can sell directly to roasters in Laos and abroad.

records.name: Sri Lanka
records.summary: Once a coffee giant, until leaf rust turned Ceylon to tea.
records.lede: In the 1860s Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, was one of the world's three biggest coffee producers. Coffee leaf rust, a fungal disease that strips the leaves, struck around 1870 and wiped the industry out within about 20 years, and planters replaced it with tea. Coffee is now a small crop, mostly from smallholdings, of about 2,500 t a year, which growers are trying to rebuild around hill-country Arabica.

regions.teaser: Hill country near 1,900 m (6,200 ft). Mellow and earthy with black pepper, says the Export Development Board

regions.name: Kandy
regions.teaser: Mid-country hills that grow both Arabica and Robusta

regions.name: Matale
regions.teaser: Where the Dutch made the first systematic planting, in 1740. Arabica and Robusta

regions.name: Badulla
regions.teaser: Hill-country Arabica

regions.name: Kegalle and Kurunegala
regions.teaser: Lower country, grown to Robusta
regions.alt: Robusta zone: below about 600 m · 2,000 ft

grows.species: Arabica in the hill country, Robusta lower down; a little Liberica
grows.text: No source gives the split between Arabica and Robusta. The Department of Export Agriculture promotes its own Lak Parakum Arabica for the hills, and the Export Development Board also lists Catimor and other local Arabica and Robusta selections (such as IMY and S274), plus a little Liberica. Specialty lots are washed, honey or natural; no figures say which is most common.

cup.text: The Export Development Board describes well-processed Nuwara Eliya coffee as mellow and earthy with black pepper, and says Sri Lankan specialty lots cupped abroad have scored above 86 points, with chocolate, nut and berry notes.
cup.watch: Picking and processing. Unripe picking and poor processing get lots rejected by importers, and the Department of Export Agriculture estimates only about 20–30% of local coffee meets export standards.

story.text: The Dutch make the first systematic attempt to grow coffee, with trials in Matale.
After the 1833 Colebrooke–Cameron reforms, the British build coffee plantations worked by Tamil laborers recruited from South India.
Ceylon, Brazil and Indonesia are the world's three largest coffee producers.
The first recorded leaf rust epidemic hits; planters called the fungus "Devastating Emily", and over the next 20 years it spread across the island.
Only about 4,600 ha (11,400 acres) of coffee remain, and tea has taken its place.
The Department of Export Agriculture starts reviving coffee with free saplings, cash grants and technical help.
An Australian-funded program pilots a central processing center where farmers deliver ripe cherries, to make quality more consistent.

sections.title: How the rust ended it
body: Ceylon's planters had covered huge areas with a single crop, and there were no effective fungicides. Each rust pustule can release about 150,000 spores that survive drying and travel far, so the fungus stripped nearly every tree. Exports of about 100 million pounds a year in 1870 shrank to 5 million pounds of production by 1889.

The British government sent the botanist Harry Marshall Ward, who could not save the plantations. His lasting lessons were that fungicide has to be on the leaf before spores land, and that vast single-crop plantings invite epidemics. Most of the dead coffee was replanted with tea, which is why Sri Lanka is known for tea today.

sections.title: Growing it now
body: The Department of Export Agriculture recommends Arabica above about 400 m in the mid and up-country (Nuwara Eliya, Kandy, Matale, Badulla) and Robusta below about 600 m (Kegalle, Kurunegala, Kandy, Matale). Yields average only 450–500 kg per hectare, and in 2022 the country exported about 51 t. Other sources set the bar higher: the Export Development Board says Arabica grows above 800 m (2,600 ft), and a 2025 Climate Fact Checks report gives 1,000–2,200 m (3,300–7,200 ft).

Arabica traditionally flowered mainly in March–April, with a smaller flowering in October–December, a Department of Export Agriculture researcher told Climate Fact Checks; in 2023 flowering became irregular and spread through the year, and main-season yields fell.

sections.title: Rebuilding it
body: From the early 1990s, many Central Highlands smallholders, mostly tea farmers, kept a few old coffee trees and sold the green beans cheaply through Colombo trading houses, while high-end cafés and hotels imported their coffee. Since about 2017 the Australian-funded Market Development Facility has backed specialty coffee instead: a central processing center for ripe cherries from 2020, and drying houses designed for irregular rain. About 60% of coffee farmers are women, the program says.

Large tea companies are now diversifying into coffee, and the Department of Export Agriculture funds saplings, new planting and extension services. Exports are still tiny but rising: from 30.47 t in 2021 to 50.56 t in 2022.

records.name: Madagascar
records.summary: Mostly natural Robusta, on an island holding half the world's coffee species.
records.lede: Madagascar grows mainly Robusta along its east and northwest coasts and a little Arabica on the central highlands, and most of it is dried whole in the cherry. Much of the crop is drunk at home, where local prices have run above export prices, and exports have collapsed, from tens of thousands of tonnes a year in the late 1990s to 495 tonnes in 2020. The island is also home to about half of the world's known coffee species, most of them wild and found nowhere else.

regions.name: Southeast coast
regions.teaser: Robusta from Mananjary down to Farafangana; one French company had over half a million trees around Mananjary in the 1950s

regions.name: East and northeast coast
regions.teaser: Robusta around Toamasina (Tamatave), Antalaha and Sambava, the north end of an east-coast belt that runs south to Vangaindrano

regions.name: Sambirano

regions.name: Central highlands
regions.teaser: Smallholder Arabica, near Lake Alaotra and in Itasy, Amoron'i Mania and Haute Matsiatra, where one exporter buys from farms of 15–50 trees

harvest.text: Robusta picking starts in June and July (PDG). FAO's 2000 profile gave May or June to October, and one new exporter's first season ran June to August (Sprudge, 2025).

grows.species: About 90% Robusta and 10% Arabica
grows.text: Almost all natural: picked by hand and dried in the cherry, partly because water is scarce; washed coffee exists only in small, experimental lots (PDG, 2022). Robusta is about nine-tenths of the crop. Apart from Ratelo, a new Arabica on trial, no source names the Arabica varieties grown.

cup.text: Madagascar Coffee Company finds its Arabica fairly sweet, with citrus on lighter roasts, and says natural processing brings out acidity in its Robusta, with a chocolate-covered-cherry effect (Sprudge, 2025). PDG says Malagasy Robusta has long been known for a smooth mouthfeel and less of the classic Robusta taste.
cup.prized: Q graders (the industry's certified tasters) scored one farm's 2019/20 Arabica at 83 and 84 points; its grower calls it a clean cup with body (PDG).
cup.watch: The Robusta trees average about 70 years old, which lowers yields and invites disease, and one exporter says the island has no dry mill, the plant that hulls and sorts green coffee for export (PDG; Sprudge, 2025). Washed coffee exists only in small, experimental lots.

story.text: The Merina kingdom worked with planters from nearby Réunion to build a coffee industry around the highland capital; coastal plantations followed.
Coffee passed vanilla among the colony's exports, nearly all of it shipped duty-free to France.
Production peaked at an estimated 1.1 million bags; in 1988 the coffee trade was opened to private exporters.
Exports fell from about 43,600 tonnes in 1999 to 495 tonnes in 2020; 852 tonnes went out in the first quarter of 2026, a season L'Express called a historic collapse.
The government drew up a 2026–2036 revival program with an indicative budget of about $150 million; its first phase (2027–2031) targets 46,800 tonnes a year on 45,000 hectares.

sections.title: Wild coffee
body: About 65 of the world's roughly 130 known coffee species grow in Madagascar, against 48 in the rest of Africa, and Kew botanists Aaron Davis and Franck Rakotonasolo described six more from the north in 2021. These wild coffees, grouped as Mascarocoffea, mostly have little or no caffeine and taste too bitter to farm, a Malagasy researcher told Sprudge, but breeders cross them with farmed coffee; the researcher estimates 70% of the native species are endangered.
Ratelo, an Arabica now on trial, brings in genes from a cross of Coffea eugenioides and Robusta.

sections.title: Drunk at home
body: A large share of the crop never leaves the island. Bags of green coffee are sold in local markets for people to roast themselves, and much of it is drunk at street kiosks, often strong and with plenty of condensed milk (PDG, 2022). Small cafés called hotelys traditionally roast it in a pan over charcoal, grind it by hand and filter it through a woven basket (Sprudge, 2025).

Domestic demand is strong and local prices run above export quotes, a 2016 presentation for UNCTAD's green-export review of Madagascar noted, which helps explain why so little is exported. Exports are overseen by the National Coffee Marketing Committee (CNCC) and handled by a few firms, the largest of which sells blends rather than single-farm coffee (PDG).

records.regionsNote: Robusta covers about 95% of the coffee-growing areas (a 2004 farm-ministry figure): the east coast from Sambava to Vangaindrano, the Sambirano in the northwest, and the Diana and Sofia regions. Arabica runs along the highlands from Bealanana south to Ambalavao (PIK, 2024).

cup.text: Coffeeness describes Mexican coffee as smooth, balanced and silky, with a base of dark cocoa and milk chocolate and notes of nuts, caramel, spice and sometimes citrus or stone fruit. Sweet Maria's calls it typically light-bodied and mild, with subtle flavors, and Coffee Review describes the classic washed cup as sweet, balanced, chocolaty and nut-toned.
cup.why: Region matters: Sweet Maria's says the cup varies widely from region to region. Processing is starting to matter too: Coffee Review found a natural from Nayarit crisply sweet and fruit-driven, unlike the classic washed style.
cup.prized: High-grown lots: Sweet Maria's says the best come from farms at 1,800 m (5,900 ft) and up, often from old Typica plants with a clean, classic profile.
cup.watch: Bulk lots are often poorly picked and processed, with taints from under-ripe cherries, says Sweet Maria's.

story.text: Spanish settlers bring coffee from Cuba and the Dominican Republic, probably first to Veracruz.
Plantations start exporting larger volumes.
The Mexican Revolution leads to land redistribution, which shaped the communal land structure many coffee farms still have.
The national coffee institute, INMECAFÉ, is dismantled as the International Coffee Agreement's export quotas end, and farmers turn to cooperatives.
Leaf rust, a fungal disease, cuts production by about half; since 2015 national programs have replanted about 150,000 ha with rust-resistant seedlings.

sections.title: Who grows it
body: About 545,000 farmers grow coffee on about 711,000 ha in 14 states (SIAP figures for 2021), and SADER, the agriculture ministry, estimates that around 90% of them farm 2 hectares or less. Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla hold about 85% of the area and 90% of output. Coffee Review counted more than 600 cooperatives in 2022.

Arabica grows from about 400 to 2,200 m (1,300–7,200 ft), and Robusta lower, from about 100 to 1,300 m (330–4,300 ft), in Chiapas, Veracruz and Oaxaca. USDA forecasts Robusta at 560,000 of Mexico's 4.14 million bags in 2026/27, up from 340,000 in 2024/25.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Veracruz dominates Mexico's Cup of Excellence, the national competition and auction for top lots: it had 23 of the 33 winning lots in 2026, against 5 for Chiapas. Geishas filled the top places; the winner, an experimental natural Gesha from Finca Santa Cruz in Chiapas, scored 91.33 and sold for $94.70 a pound.

records.name: Myanmar
records.summary: Shan State smallholders and Mandalay estates, known for clean naturals.
records.lede: Myanmar's coffee comes mainly from Shan State, where smallholders grow Arabica on plots of a hectare or less, and from Mandalay Region, where larger estates around Pyin Oo Lwin wash much of their crop. A quality push that began in the mid-2010s taught farmers to sort and process for specialty buyers, and cup scores rose from the low 70s to the mid 80s within a few years. Buyers single out its clean, sun-dried naturals.

regions.teaser: Smallholders, often with 10–20 trees beside food crops. Cherries go to a central mill or are sun-dried on raised beds

regions.name: Mandalay (Pyin Oo Lwin)

regions.name: Kayin State

regions.name: Chin State
regions.teaser: Listed by the importer Sucafina among Myanmar's key coffee states

harvest.text: Picked from late November or December to March, in the dry season, which makes sun-drying easier; exports run from April to October.

grows.species: mostly Arabica in the highlands, with Robusta lower down
grows.text: Catuai and Catimor are the main varieties, and most smallholders grow Catuai, says the trading platform Algrano; there are smaller amounts of SL28, SL34, S795 and Gesha. Most coffee is natural, sun-dried in the dry harvest season, often on raised beds; Mandalay's estates wash most of theirs, and some estates now make honey lots. Arabica grows in the highlands and Robusta lower down, but no source gives the split.

story.text: Missionaries plant the first coffee at Myeik and Dawei; Robusta growing in Kayin State begins around the same time.
Catholic missionaries bring Arabica to Shan State.
The government, with the UN, promotes coffee to replace opium poppy, and in 1986 imports several tons of seed to build a national program.
A government program offering land, financing and technical support raises output.
A USAID-funded project run by Winrock International and the Coffee Quality Institute trains Ywangan farmers in farming, sorting and processing, and helps fund wet and dry mills.
After the military takeover, a Swiss-backed effort to register Ywangan as a geographical indication goes on hold.

cup.text: Processing is what sets Myanmar apart, says the trading platform Algrano: producers make very clean naturals that former Coffee Quality Institute staff compare to Panama's. Royal Coffee New York tasted grape, tangerine, caramel and red apple in a Ywangan lot of SL28 and Catuai.
cup.why: The harvest falls in the dry, sunny season, and Sucafina says that dry heat suits naturals, coffee dried in the whole cherry.
cup.watch: Logistics. Roads, processing plants and port capacity lag behind, and since 2021 military rule has stalled efforts such as registering Ywangan as a protected origin name.

sections.title: Before the quality push
body: Farmers used to hand-pulp their cherries and sell the beans unsorted at village "five-day markets", and traders often moved them on to China and Thailand. Local cherry prices rose from 300 kyat per viss (1.63 kg) in 2014 to 3,700 kyat in 2023.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: In Ywangan, growers now deliver cherry daily to a central collection point, where it is inspected, graded and sorted, then sent on to Pyin Oo Lwin for processing and export. The Myanmar Coffee Association estimates exports to neighboring markets at 3,000–4,000 t a year, with China the top buyer. It has signed memorandums of understanding with coffee schools, associations and chambers of commerce in Yunnan, and said in 2026 that it plans to sell more high-scoring specialty Arabica and fine Robusta to China.

records.name: Malawi
records.summary: A small, estate-led crop of washed Arabica, Geisha included.
records.lede: Malawi grows a small crop of washed Arabica and some Robusta, and unlike most origins, most of it comes from estates; a few thousand smallholders farm the northern and central hills. Catimor hybrids make up most of the northern smallholders' coffee, Geisha is also grown widely, and one roaster describes floral cups with stone fruit, sweet citrus and a milk-chocolate finish.

regions.name: Northern hills
regions.teaser: Smallholder co-ops in Misuku, Phoka, Viphya, South East Mzimba and the Nkhata Bay highlands, where shaded coffee is grown; Misuku's ridges sit at about 1,700–2,000 m

regions.name: Central hills
regions.teaser: Smallholders in Ntchisi, Dedza and Ntcheu; Ntchisi East holds the Mzuzu union's newest members

regions.name: Thyolo and Mulanje
regions.teaser: The south, where commercial estates began; most grow unshaded coffee

harvest.text: Picked from April to September (Cafe Imports) or into October (Sucafina); the Mzuzu union's smallholder lots come in from June to September. It usually reaches importing countries between November and February.

grows.species: Mostly Arabica, plus some Robusta
grows.text: Essentially all washed: pulped, fermented in tanks and dried, often on raised beds. Catimors, mainly Catimor 129 (sometimes called Nyika), are widely planted and make up most of the Mzuzu union's smallholder lots; Geisha is widespread but only a small share of those lots. No source ranks the estates' varieties.

cup.text: Achilles Coffee Roasters describes medium acidity and body with mild sweetness and, next to Kenyan coffee, florals, stone fruit and sweet citrus with a clean milk-chocolate finish. Importer InterAmerican tastes stone fruit, berries and citrus with juicy acidity in the Mzuzu union's lots.
cup.prized: Specialty growers are setting apart their Geisha, SL28 and Bourbon-type lots, says Cafe Imports.
cup.watch: Catimor, widely grown, is hardy but usually cups lower, and Cafe Imports says it has had to cancel contracts over scores and defects.
cup.why: People who know Malawi's local Geisha strain taste its Ethiopian heritage in a lean toward flowers, citrus and cacao, says Coffee Review, which suggests it may turn out to be "Geisha lite, or perhaps a more savory Geisha".

story.text: Missionaries brought the first coffee, which one roaster says came from Edinburgh's Royal Botanic Garden; sources date it from the 1880s (Sucafina) to 1891 (Achilles).
The larger estates were concentrated around Thyolo and Mulanje in the south.
Independence; land redistribution and cooperatives later made coffee more workable for small growers.
Coffee wilt disease nearly wiped out smallholder coffee.
Malawi began hosting a site of the world's largest Arabica variety trial; its first harvest, at Mzuzu in 2022, let local cuppers taste 29 varieties.

sections.title: An unusual mix of trees
body: After a wilt disease devastated the first Arabica, a researcher from Ethiopia brought in Geisha and Agaro, says Achilles. Catimor 129, selected in Malawi for release in 2006 and sometimes called Nyika there, is common here and in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

sections.title: How it's sold
body: There is no government control of coffee exports, says Achilles, and the Mzuzu union in the north helps smallholders export. Mzuzu Coffee, the northern brand, works with over 2,000 smallholders in six cooperatives in the north and centre, exports about 75% of its coffee green, and earned $700,000 from exports in 2023/24; it aimed for 300 tonnes of green coffee in 2024–25 (MBC, 2024).
Mzuzu's lots are blended and then sorted by grade at its dry mill, so its coffees are sold by grade, such as AB, rather than by farm or variety (InterAmerican).

records.name: Malaysia
records.summary: A small, mostly Liberica crop from Johor, Sabah and Sarawak.
records.lede: Malaysia grows only about 2,900 t of coffee a year, and most of it (87% in 2024) is Liberica, a species that makes up only about 1% of the world's coffee. Most comes from Johor, Sabah and Sarawak, and the country imports about two-thirds of the coffee it uses. Small producers are now trying specialty processing on Johor Liberica and growing highland Arabica in Sabah.

regions.name: Johor
regions.teaser: The long-time heart of Malaysian Liberica, grown in coastal Batu Pahat villages such as Bagan and Senggarang. About two-thirds of the 2018 crop

regions.name: Sabah
regions.teaser: Highland Arabica around Ranau, mostly Catimor, some of it sold under the Sabarica brand; Tenom once had about 1,000 ha of Robusta. More coffee land than Johor in 2018 (1,400 ha against 932 ha), but half the harvest

regions.name: Sarawak
regions.teaser: One of the three main coffee states in 2024; small plantings also grow in Kedah, Pahang and Selangor

grows.species: mostly Liberica (87% in 2024), with some Robusta (10%) and a little Arabica (3%)
grows.text: Mostly Liberica, much of it from Johor's coastal villages, and traditionally roasted dark with sugar and margarine for kopi kampung; Sabah's small Arabica crop is mostly Catimor. No source says which process is most common: Johor's House of Kendal uses natural, honey and anaerobic processing on Liberica, and Sabah's Arabica growers use washed, honey and natural.

cup.text: Johor roaster Adam Esham of House of Kendal describes his Liberica as candy-sweet with a round, silky mouthfeel: natural-process lots lean wine-like with strong jackfruit notes, and honey-process lots toward hazelnut and chocolate.
cup.watch: Liberica's reputation. Little high-quality Liberica reaches the market, so many drinkers think of it as poor coffee, and the same roaster says much of its flavor is lost if it is processed and roasted like Arabica or Robusta.
cup.why: Adam Esham of House of Kendal credits Batu Pahat's coastal clay soil for the beans' sweetness, and says Liberica has the highest sugar content of any coffee.
cup.prized: Carefully processed Johor Liberica. House of Kendal's anaerobic and nitrogen-maceration lots show rum, wine, raspberry, jackfruit, floral and bubblegum notes, and in milk drinks Liberica brings out sweetness and hazelnut.

story.text: Malaysia grows about 25,000 t of coffee a year on average.
Coffee area shrinks about 13% a year and output about 16% a year, as oil palm and other crops win out and labor costs rise.
Raw coffee imports grew from US$10 million to US$222 million a year.
Output is down to 3,369 t, mostly from Johor and Sabah.
Output is 2,861 t; replanting uses the government's Liberica clones MKL5, MKL6 and MKL7, with MKL-8 to MKL-10 in testing.

sections.title: About USDA's figure
body: USDA's world coffee tables list Malaysia at about 1.5 million 60-kg bags (about 90,000 t) for 2026/27, all as Robusta. That is roughly 30 times the 2,861 t that Malaysia's agriculture minister gave for 2024, of which 87% was Liberica. This page uses the ministry's figures. Malaysia also imported 126,062 t of coffee beans in 2024.

sections.title: How Malaysians drink it
body: Kopitiams, coffee shops (kopi is Malay for coffee, tiam is Hokkien or Hakka for shop), date from the colonial era, when they began as small stalls on plantations and in villages. Orders such as kopi-O, kopi-C and kopi-gau mix the coffee with sugar, condensed milk or evaporated milk. Modern kopitiam chains such as Old Town White Coffee spread from the 1990s.

Traditional kopi kampung is roasted until strong and bitter, the beans caramelised with sugar and margarine, and served with plenty of condensed milk; House of Kendal's 100% Liberica Kopi Bagan is made for fans of this style.

cup.text: Perfect Daily Grind's 2021 guide describes the typical Nicaraguan cup as having a bright, citric acidity and a smooth body, with floral, citrus or chocolate notes. Coffee Review describes the traditional washed style as sweet, balanced and rich, often full-bodied, with chocolate, stone fruit, aromatic wood like cedar, ripe orange and hints of sweet flowers.

feel.acidity: usually moderate (Coffee Review); bright and citric in a 2021 guide

cup.why: Altitude matters: producers quoted in the guide say higher farms give more complex cups, while lower ones struggle more with disease and drying. Coffee Review's profile is of the classic washed style, fermented and rinsed, which is how almost all Nicaraguan coffee is made.
cup.prized: High-grown lots of unusual varieties, often from Nueva Segovia. At the 2026 Cup of Excellence, the national competition for top lots, a natural Geisha from Finca Los Alpes in Dipilto scored 92.00 and sold for $140 a pound; Maracaturra, Pacamara and Maragogipe lots also place well. Coffee Review says these newer experiments range from pure and gently bright to lush, brandy-like and fruit-toned.
cup.watch: Drying. Sweet Maria's says parchment sold half-dried through middlemen can turn musty or moldy in the bag, and that drying on tarps at high temperatures, in a system built for speed rather than quality, hurts the cup.

story.text: Coffee starts to be grown on a large scale.
Coffee is the country's largest export crop, and stays that way for about a hundred years.
A US trade embargo runs through these years, during the Cold War conflict with the Sandinista government; in 1990 the country moves to an elected government.
A collapse in world coffee prices brings severe hardship and makes Nicaragua a leading example in the campaign for fair trade coffee.
Leaf rust, a fungal disease, hits hard and Robusta is legalized for lower elevations; by 2026 growers had replanted about 20,000 ha of Arabica, about 14% of the coffee area.

sections.title: How it's grown
body: Almost all of it is Arabica from the north-central highlands. USDA counted 87% of plantations there in 2021, mainly in Jinotega, Matagalpa and Nueva Segovia, and an AFP report in 2019 put Jinotega and Matagalpa alone at 78% of the crop. Planted area is about 143,000 hectares (2026).

Farms are small: in 2021 USDA said more than 97% of producers were smallholders, and Cafe Imports counts about 44,000 producers. Caturra made up about 72% of plantings in that 2021 count. Robusta, legal since 2013, grows in the southern Caribbean lowlands near Nueva Guinea and is forecast at 140,000 of the 2.44 million bags in 2026/27.

sections.title: In competitions
body: Nueva Segovia, on the Honduran border, dominates Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence: it had 23 of the 32 winning lots in 2025, when washed and natural or honey lots were judged separately. Geishas took the top spots, alongside Maracaturra, Maragogipe and Pacamara.

records.name: Nepal
records.summary: A tiny, mostly washed mid-hills crop, grown since 1938.
records.lede: Nepal grows only about 640 t of green coffee a year (2024/25), spread across some 45 districts, mostly in Bagmati, Koshi and Gandaki provinces. Most of it is washed Bourbon, Typica and Caturra from largely organic farms. The planted area has more than doubled in a decade, but yields per hectare have fallen.

a hermit, Hira Giri, plants the first seeds in Gulmi

regions.name: Bagmati (Kavre, Nuwakot)
regions.teaser: The biggest producing province in 2024/25, about 290 t. Kavre (121 t) and Nuwakot (about 90 t) are the top two districts

regions.name: Koshi (Ilam)
regions.teaser: The east, with the most coffee area (about 1,700 ha); Ilam grew 83 t in 2024/25, near tea country

regions.name: Gandaki (Syangja)

regions.name: Lumbini (Gulmi, Arghakhanchi, Palpa)

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: Bourbon and Typica are the most common, with Caturra (brought from Papua New Guinea around 1990) and some Catimor and Pacamara. Mostly washed, often at pulping centers that buy fresh cherry (about 70% was wet-processed in a 2010 study); natural, honey and anaerobic lots are a small, growing share.

cup.text: Nepali coffees tend toward bright acidity and a medium body, with notes from floral and citrus to chocolate and spice depending on region and process, says exporter Himalaya Coffee Company in a sponsored Perfect Daily Grind article.
cup.watch: Roast level. Beans roasted darker, as they are for export, turn strong, bitter and burnt-tasting, The Kathmandu Post noted in 2019; the home market asks for lighter roasts.

sections.title: How high it grows
body: Sources disagree. A 2016 suitability model, cited in a 2026 research review, puts Nepal's suitable coffee land at about 600–1,350 m (2,000–4,400 ft) in the mid-hills, and a plot study sampled farms at 525–1,275 m. Sweet Maria's and a 2010 Kavre study call 800–1,600 m (2,600–5,250 ft) good for coffee, while a 2025 Perfect Daily Grind article sponsored by the exporter Himalaya Coffee Company says most farms sit at 1,000–2,100 m (3,300–6,900 ft).

sections.title: Growing problems
body: In 2016 white stem borer, an insect pest, broke out in Gulmi, and some farmers reported losing up to 60% of their yield a year. Growers also cite unpredictable rain and frost that damage blossoms and cherries, low pay for farm work, and fading interest in farming; one study suggests up to 72% of Nepal's coffee land could become unsuitable by 2050.
Nepal also drinks more than it grows: Sweet Maria's notes that local demand exceeds supply, so the country imports instant and branded coffee.

sections.title: About these figures
body: Production numbers come from Nepal's agriculture ministry, as compiled in a 2026 preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. The taste notes come from Himalaya Coffee Company, an exporter that sponsored the article they appeared in, so treat them as company-reported.

harvest.text: Picked from about November to March, farmers in Kavre told a 2010 study (its literature review says October to March); the Kathmandu Post says ripe red cherries are picked in November.

story.text: Hira Giri, a hermit from Burma, brings coffee seeds to Aapchaur in Gulmi district.
More coffee seed is brought in from India.
Commercial growing takes off: a commercial nursery opens in 1981, the first processing mill in 1983, and Gulmi's Coffee Development Centre in 1984.
Nepal makes its first recorded green-coffee export, dry-processed beans to Japan.
Donor programs push washed processing and organic certification, and a National Coffee Policy follows in 2004.
Nepal ratifies membership of the International Coffee Organization.

cup.text: Panama's fame rests on Gesha, which World Coffee Research describes as having delicate floral, jasmine and peach-like aromas; Ozone Coffee adds bergamot and a tea-like texture in Boquete lots. Coffeeness describes its other regions more softly: caramel, chocolate and nut in Volcán, and milk chocolate and brown sugar in Renacimiento.

feel.acidity: bright in Gesha; mellow in Renacimiento

cup.why: Sucafina credits bajareque, a fine mist blown over the mountains, which cools the farms and slows ripening so the cherries build more sugar and aromatic oils.
cup.prized: Gesha's floral clarity, which first set an auction record at Best of Panama in 2004.
cup.watch: Gesha needs altitude: Sucafina reports that at lower elevations it gave very poor-tasting coffee.

story.text: Commercial coffee growing begins; immigrants from Europe, including Sweden, Norway and Germany, set up farms around Boquete in Chiriquí.
CATIE, the Central American research center in Costa Rica, distributes Gesha, then called T2722, across Panama.
The Specialty Coffee Association of Panama starts the Best of Panama competition and auction.
Hacienda La Esmeralda's Gesha wins Best of Panama and sells for $20.10 a pound, then an unheard-of price.
Lamastus Family Estates' natural Elida Geisha sets a Best of Panama record at US$10,013 a kilo; in 2025 a Hacienda La Esmeralda washed Gesha goes higher, to US$30,204.

sections.title: A small producer
body: Panama grows little coffee: Coffeeness puts it at 100,000–120,000 60-kg bags a year and Sucafina at about 150,000, around 27th in the world. Almost all of the specialty coffee comes from Chiriquí province, from Boquete, Volcán and Renacimiento; Robusta grows in the lowlands of Bocas del Toro and Darién, mostly for drinking at home.

sections.title: Process experiments
body: Panama's auction farms are known for trying new methods. Lamastus Family Estates, growing coffee since 1918, makes washed, natural and honey lots plus anaerobic ferments and anaerobic slow-dried coffee. Carbonic maceration, a sealed ferment that uses carbon dioxide to push out the oxygen, is closely tied to Jamison Savage of Finca Deborah: Saša Šestić, who won the 2015 Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated coffee, shared the method with him that year, Savage began trying it in 2016, and he says he was the first to make it work with a Geisha.
Other farms work on drying and temperature: Hartmann dries coffee in dark rooms rather than on beds or in machines, and Carmen Estate keeps its fermentations cool, at about 15–20 °C (59–68 °F).

cup.text: Sweet Maria's describes good Peruvian lots as clean washed coffees led by brightness, with moderate fruit or floral hints and good sweetness: Central American brightness in a South American flavor package. German retailer Roastmarket says Peruvian coffee mostly tastes low in acid, with a flat profile, a simple but strong body and subtle cocoa and nut notes, and US roaster Colipse calls it clean and citrus-accented.

feel.acidity: bright in top lots, often low in everyday ones

cup.why: Sweet Maria's credits the growing conditions, from altitude to soils and climate: the best Peruvian coffees grow very high, often above 1,800 m (5,900 ft), mostly on old Typica plants.
cup.prized: Clean, bright, sweet washed coffees from very high farms. In the Cup of Excellence, every top-three lot from 2023 to 2025 came from Cajamarca or Cusco and was washed, most of them Geisha.
cup.watch: Sweet Maria's warns that poor picking and processing, hot coastal processing plants and the long trip overland can ruin a coffee, that sweetness and fruit can fade a few months after arrival, and that some lots have a blunted acidity.

story.text: Coffee reaches Peru, though it isn't grown for export until close to the 20th century, says Cafe Imports.
Britain takes about 2 million hectares as payment on a defaulted loan, and much of it becomes British-owned coffee plantations, later sold off or split into small farms.
A leaf-rust epidemic infects half of Peru's coffee fields; Catimor, a rust-tolerant group, is planted en masse afterwards and now makes up most trees.
Peru holds its first Cup of Excellence, with five lots scoring 90 or more.
The national coffee board, JNC, counts 380,000 hectares and 200,000 producers, and says 70–75% of the coffee area needs replanting because its trees are past 15 years.

sections.title: Organic and cooperatives
body: Peru is the world's leading exporter of organic coffee, with about 90,000 certified organic hectares, USDA reported in 2026. Coffee Review ties that, and Fair Trade certification, to the cooperative model, which it credits with raising quality and returning premiums to small growers.

More than 90% of the coffee is grown on farms under 5 hectares (12 acres). Cafe Imports says about 30% of smallholders belong to cooperatives; the JNC counts 260 coffee cooperatives, 60 of them with well-equipped cupping labs.

sections.title: Replanting after the rust
body: World Coffee Research says Peru has no national coffee breeding program, that Catimor spread en masse and informally after the 2012–13 epidemic, and that many farmers lack good seed. Since 2015 it has trialed 31 varieties in Peru; IPR 107 and Parainema stood out for yield and rust resistance, and seed lots of both are being planted in Amazonas, Cajamarca and San Martín.

Rust is still a problem: USDA said in 2026 that it now affects nearly 40% of the crop, and that the coffee berry borer, a beetle that bores into the cherries, is a problem especially below 1,500 m (4,900 ft).

records.name: Philippines
records.summary: Four coffee species, from Mindanao Robusta to Batangas barako.
records.lede: The Philippines is one of the few countries that grows all four commercial coffee species: Robusta, Arabica, Liberica (sold locally as barako) and Excelsa. Robusta is most of the crop, much of it from Mindanao, while small Arabica farms on Mt Apo and in the Cordillera mountains are building a specialty name. The country grows far less than it drinks and imports most of its coffee.

facts.label: 60-kg bags forecast for 2026/27 (about 28,500 t)
of output was Robusta in 2020; Arabica was 16.7%
of the coffee Filipinos drink is imported (2024)
Mt Apo's Arabica farms (4,600–5,600 ft)

regions.name: Sultan Kudarat
regions.teaser: The top coffee province: in 2021 it grew about 86% of SOCCSKSARGEN's crop, and that region grew about 36% of the country's

regions.name: Mt Apo (Davao del Sur)
regions.teaser: Smallholder Arabica on steep slopes around Bansalan. Its farms took the top three Arabica places in the 2021 national competition

regions.name: Bukidnon
regions.teaser: Part of the Mindanao coffee belt with the Davao Region and Sultan Kudarat; it has land but little capital, says the magkape zine

regions.name: Benguet and the Cordillera
regions.teaser: Shade-grown Arabica in the northern mountains, such as Agnep Heritage Farms in Benguet at 1,620 m (5,300 ft); Sagada also places in competitions

regions.name: Ilocos Sur
regions.teaser: Robusta: its farmers took the top five Robusta places in the 2021 national competition

regions.name: Batangas and Cavite
regions.teaser: Home of barako (Liberica), where most of the country's Liberica grows. Lipa is where coffee was first planted, in the 1740s

harvest.text: The general harvest runs from October to March.

grows.species: mostly Robusta (76.5% in 2020), then Arabica (16.7%), with Liberica and Excelsa making up the remaining 7% or so
grows.text: Mostly Robusta, much of it from Mindanao, then Arabica from Mt Apo and the Cordillera; no published source splits Liberica from Excelsa or ranks the Arabica varieties. Processing isn't documented either: the 2021 national Arabica winner was a natural Catimor, and young farmers are trying fermentation-based methods.

cup.text: Davao baristas describe Mt Apo Arabica as bright, fruity and nutty, with lemon, cacao and nut notes, says the magkape coffee zine (2025). The winning Arabica in the 2021 Philippine Coffee Quality Competition, a natural Catimor from Bansalan at 1,560 m, scored 85.86 with peach, guava, chocolate, apricot and almond.
cup.prized: Mountain Arabica from Mt Apo and the Cordillera; Ilocos Sur Robusta, whose 2021 winner showed cherry, almond, caramel, dark chocolate, dates and prunes; and barako, whose flavor the Philippine Coffee Board calls strong and bold.
cup.watch: Scale and consistency: in 2020 farms averaged only about 0.54 t of dried cherry per hectare, and most farmers work 1–2 ha.

story.text: A Spanish Franciscan friar is said to plant the Philippines' first coffee tree at Lipa, Batangas. Barako (Liberica) came later: it reached Southeast Asia in the 1800s.
The Philippines becomes one of the world's biggest coffee exporters, shipping from Batangas and Cavite; PCAARRD ranks it fourth in 1880.
Coffee leaf rust, a fungal leaf disease, reaches the islands in 1889, and with pests and Brazil's oversupply the boom collapses in the 1890s.
Robusta, now most of the crop, was introduced under American rule.

A 1960s law, Republic Act 2712, banned coffee imports and fixed farm prices under the International Coffee Agreement's quota system; after the agreement collapsed in 1989, the country joined GATT and the WTO and import controls went.
Farms at the foot of Mt Apo take the top three Arabica places in the national Philippine Coffee Quality Competition.

sections.title: Barako
body: Barako is the Philippine name for Liberica, grown mainly in Batangas and Cavite. Its fragrance is often compared to aniseed, and many Filipino coffee drinkers prefer it to Arabica. Low production has put it on Slow Food's Ark of Taste, a catalogue of endangered heritage foods.

The Philippine Coffee Board says drinkers describe barako as smoky and chocolatey with floral and spicy undertones, strong enough that some find it too dense, and that the beans smell like durian while roasting. It is usually dark-roasted, finely ground and drunk black or with a little muscovado sugar.

sections.title: About the numbers
body: Philippine figures vary by source and by unit. The 2022 industry roadmap counted about 60,600 t of dried cherry from about 113,000 ha in 2020; USDA counts green coffee in 60-kg bags. Either way, the country grows only about 15–30% of the coffee it drinks, depending on whose figures you use.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: Most farms are 1–2 ha, and in Bansalan on Mt Apo often under 1 ha. Multinationals such as Nestlé hold over 80% of the domestic market, says the magkape zine. Since import controls ended, imports grew from US$69 million in 2005 to over US$262 million in 2014, while exports fell from US$6.2 million to US$2.6 million.

records.name: Papua New Guinea
records.summary: Highland smallholder coffee descended from Blue Mountain seed.
records.lede: Smallholders grow at least 85% of Papua New Guinea's coffee, most of them growing Arabica above 1,500 m (4,900 ft). The main regions are in the highlands, and most highland plants trace back to the 1930s Blue Mountain plantation at Wau, spread over many years from a station in the Aiyua Valley.

facts.label: 60-kg bags forecast for 2026/27 (980,000 in 2023/24)
grown by smallholders
where most smallholders grow Arabica (4,900 ft+)
for whom coffee is a major source of income, mostly in farm households (2024)

regions.name: Western Highlands
regions.teaser: A key region around the provincial capital, Mount Hagen, and the Waghi Valley, home of Sigri Estate. With Eastern Highlands, more than 80% of the crop in 2012

regions.name: Eastern Highlands
regions.teaser: Capital Goroka; Kainantu grows coffee too. Over many years, the Aiyua Valley station here spread Blue Mountain stock through the highlands

regions.name: Jiwaka
regions.teaser: A key highland region on the importer Sucafina's list; coffee berry borer was first found here, at Banz, in 2017

regions.name: Simbu (Chimbu)
regions.teaser: The fourth of the central highland provinces where Coffee Review says most of the crop grows

regions.name: Morobe
regions.teaser: Home of Wau, where the colonial government planted Arabica in 1928, on the farm later named Blue Mountain Coffee. Still one of the key regions on the importer Sucafina's list

harvest.text: Main crop from May to September, with a small fly crop (a second, lighter picking) in January and February.

grows.species: Arabica, grown mostly by highland smallholders; a little Robusta on the coast
grows.text: Washed is the standard method: pulped, fermented about 36 hours, washed, then dried on raised beds, tarps or in mechanical dryers. Importers list Arusha and Typica as the main varieties, with some Blue Mountain, and Robusta grows in coastal areas.

story.text: A colonial government report gives the first official record of coffee.
The Variarata plantation, which had 20,000 Arabica trees by 1897, began exporting to Australia.
The colonial government planted Arabica at a Department of Agriculture station in Wau; its 1931 buyer, Carl Wilde, renamed it Blue Mountain Coffee.
Most highland plants today are genetically linked to the Blue Mountain plantation's trees of this decade, later spread across the highlands through the Aiyua Valley station.

Australians pioneered the modern industry and brought in conventional fermenting and washing. Coffee land grew from 147 hectares in 1951 to 4,800 in 1965, mostly through highland smallholders, Sucafina says.
Coffee berry borer, a beetle that bores into the cherry, was found at Banz in Jiwaka in February, and soon in Eastern Highlands.

sections.title: How it's processed
body: Many smallholders pulp their cherry with small drum pulpers or by hand, ferment it for about 36 hours, then wash off the mucilage (the sticky fruit layer left on the seed). The parchment is dried to about 10.5% moisture on raised beds or tarps, or in mechanical dryers, of which the Asaro dryer is the most popular. Some farmers sell cherry instead of parchment.

sections.title: How coffee is sold here
body: Estate coffee from wet mills near the main highway was traditionally graded A or B, and smallholder coffee was bulked together as grade Y. Coffee Review says the lines have blurred: careful smallholders now sell their coffee separately, and some old plantations now run as central mills buying from smallholders, or are owned by tribal associations or local people. Only a small share comes from large outside-owned estates, chiefly Sigri.

sections.title: Right now
body: Yields are low: about 417–560 kg of dry parchment per hectare in a 2024 study of Simbu and Eastern Highlands, against about 1,080 kg in Colombia. Over three-quarters of the communities in that study said they had lost more than half of the previous harvest to berry borer, and in the March–June 2023 season farmers were paid 3.5–7.0 kina (US$0.90–1.81) per kilogram of dry coffee.

cup.text: Coffee Review finds the better estate and mill lots bright but balanced and sweet, with fruit, floral and often chocolate notes, and sometimes a grapefruit-like tang. The importer Mercon prizes a crisp, apple-like acidity with floral, candy-like flavors, and a washed Typica from Sigri Estate scored 94 at Coffee Review in 2022 for clove, cinnamon, green apple and cocoa nib.

feel.body: can be very full and syrupy

cup.why: Conventional fermenting and washing, brought in by Australians in the 1950s, give a cleaner, more familiar cup than Indonesia's wet-hulled coffee, says Coffee Review.
cup.prized: Clean, carefully processed lots, usually from mills near the main highway, and the best village coffees, which reach specialty lists, often as organic or fair trade.
cup.watch: Smallholder lots bulked as grade Y are often inconsistent: rustic, mildly fermenty and a little earthy, though Coffee Review finds some charming.

records.name: Puerto Rico
records.summary: Sixth-largest producer in 1896; now grows under a tenth of its coffee.
records.lede: In the 1800s Puerto Rico was one of the world's leading coffee origins, sixth-largest in 1896, says Coffee Review. Mountain towns such as Adjuntas, Yauco and Lares still grow it, about 32,000 quintales in 2024/25, but that was under 8% of what the island used; the rest was imported. Since Hurricane María in 2017, groups including World Coffee Research have set out to help rebuild the industry, while a shortage of pickers leaves coffee on the trees.

regions.name: Yauco
regions.teaser: One of the oldest coffee areas, and home of Yauco Selecto, which Coffee Review in 1998 called often a splendid coffee

regions.name: Adjuntas
regions.teaser: Still the island's main coffee-producing town

regions.name: Jayuya
regions.teaser: Farms in the Jayuya valley sit at 1,100–1,200 m, and Jayuya Valley has its own origin seal

regions.name: Utuado
regions.teaser: The leading coffee area before 1898, and the island's third-largest producer in 2002

regions.name: Lares
regions.teaser: One of the main coffee municipalities, with Yauco, Adjuntas, San Sebastián and Las Marías

regions.name: Maricao
regions.teaser: With Indiera, among the oldest coffee areas; it boomed with coffee in the 1800s

harvest.text: Picked from August on the lower farms to January in the highest, says the University of Puerto Rico's extension service.

grows.text: Mostly the rust-resistant Limaní and Frontón, which World Coffee Research found predominate (2019), with older Typica, Bourbon and Pacas. Washed and machine-dried is the norm; anaerobic naturals are a new, experimental niche.

cup.text: Coffee Review says the best Puerto Rican lots show the Caribbean style: soft but powerful, with a fragrant, fruit-toned sweetness. In 1998 its tasters called Caribbean coffees at best full, rounded and balanced, adding that neither boldness nor intense acidity is their virtue. A light-roasted Adjuntas coffee reviewed in 2007 showed flowers, orange and honey; an anaerobic natural from Adjuntas scored 92 in 2023 with pomegranate, vanilla and rum-barrel notes.
cup.watch: Processing and drying faults. Many lesser lots have carried a faint mustiness, and in a 2010 tasting all three Puerto Rico samples had mild drying taints and scored 85–87.
cup.why: A University of Puerto Rico guide says higher-grown coffee has bigger beans and more body, aroma and acidity, though well-processed low-grown coffee can still reach specialty grade.

story.text: Coffee is first planted in Puerto Rico.
Puerto Rico ranks sixth among the world's coffee producers.
The island passes from Spain to the United States; sugar cane becomes the focus and coffee declines.
The island's Agricultural Experiment Station releases Limaní, a rust-resistant variety selected from a Brazilian population.
Hurricane María hits; World Coffee Research, TechnoServe and others begin helping rebuild the industry.

sections.title: Right now
body: Farmers are paid a minimum of $18 an almud (a measure of about 28 pounds of coffee cherry), a price set in 2017. In August 2026 the Secretary of Agriculture backed a review, with proposals of $20 to $23. He says the island averages about 34,000 quintales but could pick about 100,000 if there were enough hands, because unpicked coffee falls to the ground and is lost.
The Department of Agriculture estimated in 2021 that the island was about 7,000 pickers short.

sections.title: Where the rest comes from
body: Most coffee drunk on the island is imported, and much of the local crop is blended with it, the Secretary of Agriculture says. In 2023, 52% of the Dominican Republic's coffee exports went to Puerto Rico.

sections.title: Rebuilding after María
body: Hurricanes Irma and María destroyed millions of coffee trees in 2017, along with nurseries and seed lots. World Coffee Research and partners planned to give more than 2 million trees directly to farmers and trained nurseries to grow healthy, true-to-type plants. WCR found two varieties predominate on the island's farms, Limaní and Frontón, both bred on the island to resist leaf rust, but its 2017 DNA tests showed that seed of both was no longer pure. Limaní is a Timor Hybrid × Villa Sarchí cross (a Sarchimor); Frontón is a Catimor line with similar traits, the University of Puerto Rico says.

cup.text: Visit Rwanda, the national tourism board, describes a silky, creamy body with lemon, orange blossom and a caramel aftertaste, and Sweet Maria's often finds black tea and lemon in its Rwandan lots. Melbourne Coffee Merchants tastes floral, bright coffees in the north and jammy, syrupy ones in the south.
cup.watch: The potato taste defect, a raw-potato smell that swamps the cup, turns up in coffees from the Great Lakes, Rwanda's among them; it is linked to bacteria spread by the Antestia bug.

facts.label: where its Arabica grows (3,950–7,200 ft)

story.text: Bourbon Mayaguez reached Rwanda, after arriving in Congo's Mulungu collection in the 1930s; selections from its trees became Bourbon Mayaguez 71 and 139.
The Rwanda Agriculture Board released RAB C15, which resists leaf rust and coffee berry disease.
Rwanda dropped its zoning rule, which had made farmers sell cherry within set areas; Sucafina says cherry then travelled farther and 2024 quality dipped.
The base price for cherry rose to Rwf 750 a kilo, 25% above 2025's Rwf 600.

sections.title: Washed, and what else
body: Most Rwandan coffee is fully washed at its stations: about 80%, by a January 2026 KT Press report, or about 62% of exports by World Coffee Research's count. Naturals, honeys and anaerobic lots make up roughly 5% of exports.
Stations pay for ripe cherry and much less for floaters, the light cherries that float in water: in 2023 cherry for fully washed coffee fetched Rwf 410 a kilo and floaters Rwf 100, says KT Press.

sections.title: The trees
body: Nearly all Rwandan coffee is Arabica, mainly traditional Bourbon and Typica types, says World Coffee Research. Bourbon Mayaguez 139 and 71, Bourbon selections made in East Africa, are common in Rwanda and Burundi; WCR rates BM139's cup very good at high altitude but notes it is susceptible to leaf rust and coffee berry disease.
RAB C15, released in 2015, resists both diseases but isn't widely planted yet, and an estimated 39% of Rwanda's coffee trees are over 30 years old.

records.name: Saudi Arabia
records.summary: Terraced Jazan mountain farms growing Khawlani coffee for centuries.
records.lede: Saudi Arabia grows a small amount of Arabica on terraced farms in its southwestern mountains, mostly in Jazan Province. Khawlani tribes there have grown it for more than 300 years, and in 2022 UNESCO added their growing and processing know-how to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. The government is now investing to grow far more of it.

facts.label: where coffee suits the southern highlands (2,600–6,550 ft)
coffee trees in the southwest in 2022
of 43 Jazan farm samples graded specialty (80+ points) in an FAO study; top score 86
UNESCO lists Khawlani coffee know-how as intangible heritage

regions.name: Jazan
regions.teaser: The heart of it: about 1,985 of the country's 2,535 coffee farms (2022), in mountain districts such as Al-Dayer, Fayfa and Al-Aridah
regions.alt: The largest farm, at Al Qateel: about 1,500 m · 4,900 ft

regions.name: Asir
regions.teaser: The second-biggest area: about 300 farms (2022)

regions.name: Al Baha
regions.teaser: The third: about 250 farms (2022), plus a planned Coffee Development City for about 300,000 more trees

harvest.text: Picked mostly from October to January; FAO researchers found December 2021 to be the main picking season in Jazan. Trees flower from late March and the cherries take about six months to ripen. Saudipedia, by contrast, says picking usually begins in spring.

grows.species: Arabica
grows.text: Khawlani is the best-known type, and Saudipedia names Khawlani and Harari as the two main types; Perfect Daily Grind adds Berri and Bahri, though no source gives shares. Coffee is traditionally dried in the whole cherry (natural), as were all 43 farm samples in FAO's 2022 study; washed and honey methods are also used, and some farmers are trying anaerobic fermentation.

cup.text: Arabian Coffee Institute co-founder Almohanad Almarwai lists raisins, dates, dried fruit, dark chocolate, cardamom and cinnamon among Saudi coffee's flavor notes, and in a 2022 Jeddah cupping (the industry's standard tasting) of coffees from seven countries that he led, Saudi Khawlani stood out for dried fruit, dates, chocolate and caramel. The retailer Bateel describes its natural Jazan coffee as dark chocolate and caramel with a touch of grapefruit.
cup.watch: Water and old trees. Rain is unpredictable and steep slopes are hard to irrigate, old trees yield little and show defects, and in 2022 a single small mill served Jazan and was often swamped with unhulled coffee.

story.text: Khawlani tribes were growing coffee in these mountains: UNESCO and Saudipedia both put it at about 300 years or more, and some local accounts claim far longer.
As the economy turned to oil, many families gave up farming coffee.
After the government launched coffee festivals in Jazan, about half a dozen local landowners began growing coffee commercially.
The Saudi Heritage Preservation Society applied to UNESCO to protect Khawlani growing methods.

The Year of Saudi Coffee: the Public Investment Fund launched the Saudi Coffee Company, planning $320 million over 10 years and 900,000 more Arabica trees, and UNESCO inscribed the Khawlani tradition.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Seeds are sown in soil-filled mesh bags and kept in shade for three to four months, then planted out on terraces that hold water and soil. Trees first fruit after two to three years. Cherries are picked by hand and dried, then hulled by rolling a stone cylinder over the dried fruit on a large flat stone, which frees the bean while limiting cracks.

sections.title: About the numbers
body: Published figures disagree widely. Saudipedia, a government-run encyclopedia, put output at about 2,400 t a year from 398,000 trees on 2,535 farms (2022). The same year, the Christian Science Monitor reported about 300 t from about 400,000 trees, and Perfect Daily Grind estimated about 300 t for 2020, with about 400,000 trees on 600 farms by the end of 2021 able to give about 800 t. Targets differ too: 2,500 t by 2032 in one report, about 5,000 t a year in another. Treat any single production number with care.

sections.title: Drinking it at home
body: Saudi Arabia drinks far more coffee than it grows: in 2022 it imported about 80,000 t a year, worth about $320 million. Saudi drinkers tend to like a very light roast, stopped just before first crack (the popping sound when beans start to open in the roaster), and home-grown Khawlani sells for a premium: one Jazan farmer got $32 a kilo from wholesalers, while shoppers in Riyadh and Jeddah paid $80–110.

records.name: South Sudan
records.summary: A wild home of Arabica, and the source of Rume Sudan.
records.lede: South Sudan's Boma Plateau holds wild Arabica that a 2021 genetic study found distinct from Ethiopia's, confirming the country as one of the species' centers of origin. Seed collected there in 1941 is the likely ancestor of the Rume Sudan variety. Farmed coffee is a recent restart: washed Robusta from Yei became the country's first coffee export in 2015.

facts.label: where Boma's wild Arabica mostly grows (3,950–7,200 ft)
seed gathered at Rume, likely parent of Rume Sudan
wild Arabica here by IUCN criteria; Critically Endangered once climate change is counted
first coffee export: washed Robusta from Yei

regions.name: Boma Plateau
regions.teaser: Wild Arabica in the Rumit and Ngelecho forests of Upper Boma, Jonglei; villagers plant it too

regions.name: Yei
regions.teaser: Smallholder Robusta, washed at wet mills the farmers set up, and first sold by Nespresso in 2015

grows.species: Wild and village-grown Arabica on the Boma Plateau; farmed Robusta around Yei
grows.text: The only coffee grown for sale in the sources is Robusta around Yei, washed at wet mills the farmers set up. On the Boma Plateau, the country's only known Arabica, coffee grows wild in the forests and is planted around villages, but researchers saw no commercial harvest in 2012.

story.text: Botanist A. Chevalier made the first record of Arabica on the Boma Plateau in 1929; J. G. Myers confirmed wild trees in its forests in 1938.
A. S. Thomas collected seed and sent it to East African research stations; it is the likely source of the Rume Sudan and Barbuk Sudan varieties.
A team including Kew's Aaron Davis and WCR founder Tim Schilling found wild Arabica again, in poor health; they collected only leaves, not seed.
Robusta from Yei, sold by Nespresso as Suluja ti South Sudan ("beginning of South Sudan" in Kakwa), became the country's first coffee export.
Genetic tests on the 2012 samples confirmed Boma as a center of origin for Arabica; fighting since 2013 has kept researchers from going back.

sections.title: Where Rume Sudan comes from
body: Rume is a spot on the Boma Plateau about 2–3 miles south of Barbuk, at about 1,250 m (4,100 ft), and it was already largely cleared for maize when Thomas visited in 1941. His seed went to breeding stations in Kenya and Tanganyika, and the CATIE genebank received Rume Sudan and Barbuk Sudan from Kenya in 1953.

In the 2021 tests, only one of the Rume Sudan samples from CATIE carried a genetic marker found only in South Sudan's wild coffee. The authors think it unlikely any Arabica still grows at Rume itself; the variety lives on at a few specialty farms, such as in Colombia.

sections.title: Under threat
body: The wild trees grow about 88 km from the nearest wild Arabica in Ethiopia. The region has lost forest for about 70 years, and the civil war that began in 2013 displaced up to 4 million people; in 2021 WCR warned that the few plants seen in 2012 may already be gone.

Satellite maps show the forest suited to wild coffee shrank from 16.2 km² in 2000 to 15.3 km² in 2020, and the authors estimate that 84.2% of the plateau's potential forest cover is already gone; clearing of the undergrowth has made much of what remains unsuitable.

sections.title: How Boma's coffee is used
body: The 2012 team saw no coffee harvested for sale. Villagers near Barbuk collect the leaves to make coffee-leaf tea. The trees planted in Rumit village mix genotypes from both wild forests, which suggests villagers carried home fruit gathered in the wild. Trees at Bayen look like introduced material, perhaps from British planting attempts in the late 1940s.

sections.title: Yei's Robusta
body: TechnoServe and Nespresso began working with Yei smallholders in 2011. By January 2016 the farmers had set up six wet mills, more than 700 attended monthly training, and cooperatives had raised over 20,000 seedlings; USAID joined that year, and the project aimed for nine cooperative-owned wet mills and 1,500 trained farmers by 2019. Nespresso had put in more than CHF 700,000 by 2015 and planned CHF 2.5 million.

TechnoServe's project page stops at early 2016. Since then, fighting and displacement have left many Yei farmers unable to tend their coffee, and in 2025 Radio Yei reported overgrown farms at risk from dry-season wildfires.

cup.text: The only farmed coffee described is the 2015 Yei Robusta, which Nespresso said had a bold, silky texture with intense dried-cereal aromas and subtle woody notes (New Food, 2015). No tasting notes have been published for Boma's wild Arabica, though its 1941 collector remarked on the bold beans of Barbuk coffee, and its likely descendant Rume Sudan is grown for specialty coffee in Colombia.
cup.watch: Supply is tiny: the first Robusta was sold only in extremely limited volumes, to Nespresso club members in France.

records.name: Sierra Leone
records.summary: Natural Robusta country, where wild stenophylla was found again in 2018.
records.lede: Sierra Leone grows mostly Robusta on small farms in the east and south, and most of it is dried whole in the cherry. Coffee was a bigger export than cocoa before the 1991–2002 civil war, when most farms were abandoned, and output has never recovered. The country is also home to stenophylla, a wild coffee once exported from Freetown, which Kew scientists found again in 2018.

regions.teaser: Kenema, Kailahun and Kono, where most of the coffee grows

regions.name: The south and other districts
regions.teaser: Bo, Pujehun and Moyamba, plus Koinadugu and Tonkolili; wild stenophylla survives in Moyamba's Kasewe Hills

harvest.text: Picked by hand from December to March and dried on patios. Cherries picked once the rains build in late March often can't dry down to the 10–12% moisture that export needs (PDG).

grows.species: Mostly Robusta, with pockets of Liberica and a little stenophylla
grows.text: Almost all Robusta, dried whole in the cherry on patios; attempts at washing stations have mostly failed (PDG, 2023). Liberica, grown alongside stenophylla in the late 1800s, survives in pockets in Robusta plantations and abandoned farmland (Lahai et al., 2023); stenophylla is still grown on a few farms in negligible volumes, and in new trial plots.

story.text: Stenophylla, known locally as Highland coffee, was exported from Freetown; French buyers reportedly rated it with top Arabica.
The British introduced Robusta, which became a bigger export than cocoa before the civil war.
Output ran at about 20,000 tonnes a year.
Civil war; most coffee farms were abandoned, and most trees standing today were planted before it.
An EU-funded program pruned and fertilized abandoned farms, with some success, though volumes stayed low.
In December, Kew's Aaron Davis and NRI's Jeremy Haggar found wild stenophylla again: first a single plant, then a healthy population in a forest farther east.

sections.title: The lost coffee
body: Stenophylla grows wild in hot lowlands at about 400 m (1,300 ft) and tolerates more heat than Arabica. A sample from partners in Sierra Leone, cupped in London in 2020, scored 80.25, a specialty score on the Arabica scale, and seedlings were to be planted in Sierra Leone and on Réunion from 2021 to test it as a crop (CIRAD). It yields poorly, one reason it never became a world crop (Lahai et al., 2023).

By the end of 2023 about 5,600 seedlings grown from 300 wild plants were in eight trial plots. An early-2024 heatwave brought 59 days at 40°C (104°F) or more, and about 80% of the plants survived, with shaded plots doing far better than unshaded ones; the first harvest was expected in 2025 (Sucafina). Exporting seeds or seedlings needs the government's approval.

sections.title: Selling it
body: Up to 80% of the crop is exported, Walid Bahsoon told PDG in 2023, and some goes unofficially across the borders to Liberia and Guinea. Coffee is not known for quality here, partly because of drying problems.

The government no longer sets farmgate prices, as the old Produce Marketing Board once did. Exporters sometimes send buying agents to farms three or four months before harvest, and the agents may lend growers money; in 2020 coffee exports earned $4.79 million against cocoa's $47.3 million. At home coffee is a luxury for most people, boiled in big pots and sold at kiosks (PDG, 2023).

cup.text: Little is published about the cup of Sierra Leone's everyday Robusta, and PDG says the country is not known for quality. Its wild stenophylla is the exception: a Sierra Leone sample cupped in London in 2020 scored 80.25, a specialty score, and cuppers often compare stenophylla to high-grown Bourbon Arabica (Sucafina, 2025).
cup.prized: Stenophylla, which French buyers reportedly ranked with top Arabica when it was exported from Freetown in the 1890s–1920.
cup.watch: Drying. Cherries picked once the rains build in late March often can't dry to export moisture, and buying agents bulk coffee from many farms, which makes quality control hard (PDG, 2023).

records.name: El Salvador
records.summary: Bourbon, Pacas and Pacamara from the land of volcanoes.
records.lede: El Salvador is Central America's smallest country, and its coffee grows in volcanic soil across six regions; the western Apaneca-Ilamatepec range alone gave 53% of the 2022–23 crop. Bourbon is the main variety, followed by two born here: Pacas, a natural Bourbon mutation, and Pacamara, a very large-beaned cross of Pacas and Maragogipe.
