where most coffee grows (4,250–5,250 ft)

regions.name: The north
regions.teaser: Kasama, Mbala, Nakonde and Isoka along the Muchinga escarpment: nearly all the crop, and the big Kasama estates; the best lots grow above 1,500 m

regions.name: Lusaka and the south
regions.teaser: A few estates near Lusaka, Serenje and Mazabuka

harvest.text: Picked from May to August (PDG) or into September (Algrano), in the long dry season, which makes sun-drying easier.

grows.species: Arabica only
grows.text: Most coffee is fully washed at the estates' own wet mills; naturals, pulped naturals (a honey style) and anaerobic lots are a small, experimental share. Catimors are widely planted on the Kasama estates for disease resistance, alongside Kenya's SL28 and SL34, but no source gives shares; Starmaya and Marsellesa are newer plantings.

cup.text: The African Fine Coffees Association calls Zambian coffee full-bodied with sweet, mild acidity, and importer Covoya describes its lots as mostly citrus with berry and melon. Algrano hears clean, balanced washed cups that range from citrus and fruit to chocolate and caramel, and Sweet Maria's found a washed Kateshi Estate Catimor heavy-bodied, with brown sugar and malted chocolate.
cup.prized: Pulped naturals (skin removed, the sticky fruit layer left on to dry) add sweetness to the acidity and tend to be the best Zambian coffee, says ZCGA chair Teija Lublinkhof; a few experimental SL28 micro-lots have scored as high as 89.
cup.watch: Zambia has no flavor identity buyers recognize, the way they do Kenya's or Ethiopia's, says Algrano.
cup.why: Coffee comes from large farms with careful central wet mills, which earned Zambia its name, Coffee Review says, as a dependable source of cleanly washed, high-grown coffee with at least a hint of Kenya-like intrigue.

story.text: Settler farmers were already growing coffee around Mbala.
The World Bank funded coffee projects, the Kasama estates among them, to move the economy beyond copper.
Zambia began exporting coffee commercially.
Exports peaked at 6,654 tonnes; after funding dried up and a 2005/06 drought, many smallholders pulled out their trees and exports fell to 180 tonnes by 2015.
Olam bought the assets of the Kasama Coffee Company, in receivership since 2008, and renamed it Northern Coffee Corporation.

sections.title: Estates and outgrowers
body: Olam's Northern Coffee Corporation runs five estates (Kateshi, Ngoli, Luombe, Isanya and Nsunzu) in Kasama, Mbala and Mungwi districts, with about 2,171 ha under coffee, and buys from more than 3,000 small outgrowers (ZANIS, 2022). PDG put its share of exportable coffee at about 97% in 2021.
Exports recovered to almost 2,000 tonnes in 2019. Zambia is landlocked, so northern coffee travels overland to Dar es Salaam in Tanzania to be shipped.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Zambia borrowed Kenya's grading system when its industry was set up with World Bank and FAO help, so bags carry Kenyan-style screen grades such as AA and AAA; Sweet Maria's notes that Catimor's large beans make the AAA grade possible. The lots Sweet Maria's has bought carry an estate name, Kateshi near Kasama, alongside the grade.

records.name: Zimbabwe
records.summary: Eastern Highlands Arabica, slowly rebuilding after the farm seizures.
records.lede: Zimbabwe grows Arabica in the Eastern Highlands along the Mozambique border, mainly in Manicaland's Chipinge, Chimanimani and Mutasa districts. In the early 1990s it produced more than 15,000 tonnes a year; after farm seizures began in 2000, output fell to a few hundred tonnes, and smallholders are now slowly bringing it back.

facts.label: a year in the early 1990s, from more than 20,000 farmers
a year by 2023, from two estates and about 450 small farms
of the crop lost by the early 2000s
Honde Valley to Chipinge (2,800–4,500 ft)

regions.name: Chipinge
regions.teaser: Most of the crop and the most suitable land; Catimor is popular here for rust resistance and yield

regions.name: Chimanimani
regions.teaser: Second to Chipinge in land suited to Arabica

regions.name: Honde Valley
regions.teaser: Rain all year, tea and coffee estates, and the base of Nespresso's revival program

regions.name: Mutare and the Vumba
regions.teaser: Mutare district, Vumba Mountains included; the smallest suitable area of the three

harvest.text: PDG gives May to September and Sweet Maria's June to November; both cover June to September. Most rain falls from November to March.

grows.species: Arabica only
grows.text: Mostly washed and sun-dried, the traditional way, with some honey lots (Sweet Maria's). Catimor is popular, especially in Chipinge, for its rust resistance and good yields, and SL14, SL28, SL34 and Caturra are also popular (PDG, 2021); no source gives shares.

cup.text: Sweet Maria's calls Zimbabwe a balanced "drinking coffee" with body, chocolate-like flavors and moderate acidity, and finds Chipinge lots aromatic and slightly spicy. PDG adds bright, berry-like or citric acidity, with chocolate and wine notes.
cup.prized: At its best, says Sweet Maria's, fine acidity set against complex roasty, almost savory notes.
cup.watch: Some lots have tasted wild or unclean, or earthy and a little leathery, says Sweet Maria's, which partly blames the Catimors and other Robusta-interbred Arabicas that replaced older varieties.

story.text: Travellers brought coffee in, but plant disease destroyed most of the small plantations in the 1920s.
After a resurgence from 1958, a commercial industry took hold.
More than 20,000 farmers grew over 15,000 tonnes a year.
Forced evictions of commercial farmers began; with low prices and bad weather, about 97% of the crop was lost.
Nespresso and the NGO TechnoServe began training Honde Valley smallholders, and Nespresso pays them premium prices.

sections.title: Rebuilding
body: In 2023 the Nespresso program paid about $8 a kilo, close to double what local buyers paid, to some 450 Honde Valley smallholders. A 2018 government plan aimed for 10,000 tonnes by 2024; in 2023 the head of the Coffee Research Institute in Chipinge said it was still too early to tell whether that would be met.
On bags, Zimbabwe's top AA grade is often marked "Code 53", says Sweet Maria's.

sections.title: Right now (2026)
body: Most coffee farms today are tiny. A 2025–26 survey for the EU's new deforestation rules recorded 948 coffee farms in Manicaland with a median size of a quarter of a hectare, and found that over 99% had not cleared forest since the 2020 cutoff, so nearly all can keep selling to Europe.

Smallholder output reached about 60 tonnes in 2023, up from 39.2 tonnes in 2021, on about 164 hectares, most of it in Chipinge and Mutasa districts. Nespresso paid smallholders an average of $6.50 a kilo, 98% of the coffee grown is for export, and World Coffee Research has brought in 31 varieties for local trials (Manica Post, 2024).

records.name: Anaerobic

cup.common: Turned-up fruit, often tropical, with a winey or tangy, yogurt-like edge and a fuller, sweeter feel.
cup.text: Reviewers report intensity above all: a fuller mouthfeel, often more sweetness, fruit like passion fruit and mango, and a tangy, lactic note like yogurt or fresh cheese. Anaerobic washed lots came out leaner and brighter than anaerobic naturals.
cup.why: With air shut out, yeasts, which tend to make fruity, boozy notes, are partly held back, lactic acid bacteria do more of the work, and everything slows down, so ferments run for days. The longer the coffee stays sealed, the stronger the effect, though variety, ripeness and drying still shape the cup. What grows inside varies: one Brazilian study of a sealed tank found lactic bacteria and yeasts scarce, with other bacteria (Enterobacteriaceae) and a mold family (Nectriaceae) dominating, while another found lactic acid mainly in the sealed-ferment coffees.
cup.prized: Intensity, sweetness and a full mouthfeel with the fruit still clean. In one review site's 2021 tasting of 43 anaerobic coffees, 19 scored 93 or higher.
cup.watch: A runaway ferment tastes sharp, vinegary, solvent-like or savory; a big temperature rise in the tank is the warning sign. Even when it works, too much intensity can hide the coffee's own character, one roaster warns.

byCoffee.text: In Coffee Review's 2021 tasting, anaerobic natural Wush Wush lots were silky and floral with a yogurt-like lactic tang, some with a savory or cedar-like edge.

Producers here took up sealed tanks in the late 2010s. In the same tasting, a Castillo given a sealed phase went tart and tropical (passion fruit, mango), and an anaerobic natural Pink Bourbon was light and tropical (lychee, jasmine).
Mills ferment sealed for several days, aiming at the fruit-forward style buyers in North America and Europe want; one 2019 Costa Rican anaerobic tasted of raw chocolate and cinnamon.
In a trial on Conilon (a Brazilian Robusta type), five days sealed with a chosen yeast raised the cup score by more than 3 points.

The Lamastus family's anaerobic slow-dry naturals ferment sealed for five to six days, then dry for about 60 days; Coffee Review found one Catuaí full of chocolate, with a huge mouthfeel and a tart, goat-cheese-like lactic acidity.

steps.title: Seal it in
steps.text: Whole cherries or pulped coffee go into tanks or bags; valves let carbon dioxide out without letting air back in.

steps.title: Ferment sealed
steps.text: Microbes use up the oxygen and work slowly. Some producers track sugar (Brix), pH or temperature and stop at a set point: one Costa Rican mill starts at 22–25 °Brix and stops at 16. There's no single recipe.
steps.hours: about 1–6 days; about 96 h at one Costa Rican farm

steps.title: Finish and dry
steps.text: It's then dried as a natural, honey or washed coffee.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: the whole cherry for anaerobic naturals, mucilage and parchment for anaerobic honeys, and parchment only once an anaerobic washed coffee is washed.

story.text: Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a Colombian coffee described as carbonic macerated, drawing wide attention to sealed-tank ferments.
A Costa Rican anaerobic won bronze at the Golden Bean North America competition, and Coffee Review's editor wrote that, judged by standards of ten years earlier, many such coffees might seem flawed.
In Coffee Review's tasting of 43 anaerobic coffees, 19 scored 93 or higher.
A Brazilian study of sealed, nothing-added tanks found that 48–72 hours built up more aroma compounds, such as esters, and gave more varied cups than 24 hours.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup barred anaerobic coffees from its Traditional Washed category.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source counts anaerobic lots by country. Producers in Colombia and Costa Rica began experimenting with sealed tanks around 2015, and Panamanian estates use them as well: of the 12 anaerobic coffees Coffee Review wrote up in 2021, all rated 93 or higher, five were Colombian, four Ethiopian (three of them anaerobic naturals of the Wush Wush variety), two Panamanian and one Peruvian.
Named producers include Costa Rica's La Chumeca mill and the CoopeTarrazú cooperative, the Lamastus family's Elida Estate in Panama, and Luiz Paulo Pereira in Brazil, who has added small batches.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Most bags pair the word with the base method: anaerobic natural, anaerobic washed or anaerobic honey, double anaerobic, or ASD (anaerobic slow dry). Cafe Imports calls it AEF, anaerobic-environment fermentation, and uses “anaerobic impregnation” when spices, molasses or fruit are added, which makes it a co-ferment.
The label isn't always exact: one coffee Coffee Review first took for an anaerobic natural had been fermented in a covered vessel that wasn't sealed.

sections.title: In research
body: Brazilian researchers call the plain version self-induced anaerobic fermentation (SIAF): the fruit's own microbes use up the oxygen in a closed tank. In a 2022 study, 48 and 72 hours built up more aroma compounds such as ethyl acetate than 24 hours, and made the cups more varied.

A 2023 study added yeasts to sealed ferments of natural and pulped coffee: all scored above 80, the best reported at 86.5, with citrus, caramel, honey and chocolate notes, though the seeds' viability, their ability to sprout, fell.

records.name: Carbonic maceration

cup.common: Big, juicy fruit and intense sweetness, with a syrupy texture and wine-like acidity, roasters say.
cup.text: Roasters describe explosive fruit, a syrupy texture, intense sweetness and wine-like acidity. In one review site's tasting, carbonic lots were more restrained: bright and layered, with only a soft hint of fruity funk.
cup.why: Added carbon dioxide pushes out more oxygen than a plain sealed tank, and with the cherries left whole, one roaster says the fruit breaks down from the inside out. The method comes from Beaujolais winemaking. In Brazilian trials, lactic bacteria (Leuconostoc and Lactobacillus) dominated carbonic ferments, and warmer, longer ferments scored better.
cup.prized: Big, clean fruit and sweetness. A carbonic Sudan Rume from Colombia won the 2015 World Barista Championship.
cup.watch: Pushed too far, it becomes overwhelming or unstable. Labels are loose too: one roaster says the 2015 winner was depulped first, unlike wine's whole-fruit method.

byCoffee.text: The 2015 world title came with a carbonic Sudan Rume from Colombia. In a 2021 tasting, a carbonic lot from Nariño showed quiet chocolate, citrus and flowers with only a soft hint of fruity funk.
In the same tasting, a Colombian Gesha fermented under pressurized CO2 and dried in the whole fruit stayed bright, layered and complex, with a very subtle funk.

Jamison Savage of Finca Deborah says he was the first to carbonic-macerate a Geisha successfully; his carbonic coffees are described as bright and winey, layered, with high acidity and more aromatics.
One roaster's carbonic Kenyan, sealed with added CO2 and then slow-dried 25–35 days in thick layers, showed blackberry, lime-like acidity and hibiscus rather than herbal or savory notes.
In a Brazilian trial on Conilon (a Robusta type) grown at 208 m (680 ft), 120 hours of carbonic maceration at 38 °C (100 °F) scored 83.25, against 78.64 for 24 hours at 18 °C (64 °F).

steps.title: Load whole cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries, usually whole, go into a sealed tank.

steps.title: Flush with CO2
steps.text: Carbon dioxide is added to push the oxygen out, and temperature and yeast activity are watched as it ferments.
steps.hours: days; sealed ferments generally run about 1–6, and Brazilian trials ran 24–120 h

steps.title: Dry slowly
steps.text: The cherries usually dry whole, in thick layers in one example; times vary.

records.layers: Usually everything: whole cherries (skin, fruit flesh, mucilage and parchment) go through the CO2 tank and dry that way. Some versions depulp first.

story.text: Fermenting whole fruit in CO2-filled tanks became a staple of Beaujolais winemaking for Gamay grapes.
Specialty coffee producers began experimenting with sealed tanks and controlled fermentation.
Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume from Colombia.
In Panama, Jamison Savage began carbonic-macerating Geisha at Finca Deborah, crediting Šestić's work.
Producers in Colombia, Costa Rica and elsewhere took up sealed tanks and extended ferments.
Šestić wrote that his team had run more than 1,500 fermentation experiments on over 50 farms in ten countries.
Brazilian studies found carbonic ferments scored higher when warmer and longer (in a Conilon trial), and that lactic bacteria dominated them.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source counts carbonic lots by country. Colombia produced the 2015 world-title coffee, and Coffee Review's 2021 tasting included a carbonic lot from Nariño and a carbonic Geisha from elsewhere in Colombia; producers in Colombia and Costa Rica began experimenting with sealed tanks around the same time. In Panama, Jamison Savage makes washed and natural carbonic lots at Finca Deborah.

Šestić's own team tests it at Finca El Arbol in Nicaragua, at about 1,100 m (3,600 ft), and says two carbonic lots from neighboring farms placed in Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence top ten. One roaster has sold a Kenyan SL28/SL34 sealed with added CO2, and Brazilian researchers have trialled it on Conilon.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Pushed too far it becomes overwhelming or unstable, and it doesn't guarantee a better cup: in the Brazilian Conilon trial, short, cool carbonic ferments scored lowest.

The name has also covered for flavoring. In 2019 a coffee disqualified from a competition in Ecuador had been carbonic-macerated and then given added tropical fruit flavoring, and a competitor who later won the Italian Brewers Cup with it didn't know.

sections.title: In research
body: A 2022 Brazilian trial vacuum-sealed Conilon cherries, injected pure CO2 and fermented them for 24 to 120 hours at 18, 28 or 38 °C (64, 82 or 100 °F); scores generally rose with temperature. A 2023 Brazilian study found Leuconostoc bacteria led early and at cooler temperatures, and that at 38 °C more Lactobacillus went with better scores.

records.name: Co-fermented

cup.common: The cup can taste noticeably of what went in, such as pineapple or ginger, on top of the coffee.
cup.text: It can taste clearly of the addition: a coffee co-fermented with pineapple would taste noticeably of pineapple, says one trade article, and one Colombian Gesha made with mossto and hops tasted of fresh ginger, lime and hops, says an importer.
cup.why: Part of the flavor comes from the added ingredient itself, though one project's data suggest only about 3% of the added fruit ends up in the cup. Some additions mostly steer the ferment instead: mossto (juice and microbes from an earlier batch) is used to speed it up and control it, and cinnamon is sometimes added to regulate its pace more than for flavor.
cup.prized: Results that still taste distinctly like coffee, with its own flavors turned up. At best they score very high: Coffee Review named a Kona coffee fermented with oranges its top coffee of 2024, at 98 points.
cup.watch: Critics call it adulteration that masks the coffee and can taste synthetic, and artificially flavored imitations tend to taste one-dimensional. In the US, labels don't have to list what went in, which matters for allergies.

byCoffee.text: In Quindío, one producer's lots use mossto, hops, ginger or chili, and an importer says they taste of the additions while still tasting like coffee.

Jairo Arcila's Pink Bourbons, fermented sealed with fruit and wine yeast, were sold with notes of peach cordial and honey blossom (a peach lot) and of strawberry, nougat, caramel and rose (a strawberry lot).
A washed lychee co-ferment of Castillo from the Arcila family's Finca La Pradera was sold with notes of lychee, rose water and apricot.
Hula Daddy's Orange Kahiko, fermented in the whole fruit with oranges grown on the same farm, was Coffee Review's top coffee of 2024 at 98.
Best of Panama excluded infused coffees in 2024 and disqualified four lots it said were altered with additives, citing the need to protect Panama coffee's identity.

steps.title: Sort the cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries are floated in water to remove unripe or light ones and debris, as with any careful lot.

steps.title: Add the extras
steps.text: Fruit (fresh, cut or dried), spices, hops or mossto go in with the whole cherries or the pulped coffee, sometimes with a wine yeast to help the ferment along.

steps.title: Ferment together
steps.text: They ferment along with the coffee, often sealed away from air in bags or tanks; in one Colombian exporter's lots the whole cherries sit with the fruit and their pulp on.
steps.hours: 48–72 h in Cofinet's lots; 96 h in one Quindío lot, after 72 h in whole fruit

steps.title: Pulp and dry
steps.text: The cherries are pulped, sometimes washed clean, and dried on raised beds or in dryers down to about 9.5–11% moisture; in some lots mashed fruit is spread on the coffee as it dries.
steps.hours: 22 days on raised beds in one Quindío lot

steps.title: Finish before green
steps.text: Everything has to go in before the coffee is dry-milled into green beans; adding anything later is barred at the World Barista Championship.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: the additions go in with pulped coffee or with whole fruit. In Cofinet's lots in Colombia, whole cherries ferment with the fruit and are then pulped; one lot was washed clean before drying, while for others mashed fruit was added to the parchment as it dried.

story.text: Rumors of an 'infusion' method began to circulate, and at the World Barista Championship in Amsterdam Saša Šestić tasted an espresso with a strong cinnamon flavor that its competitor put down to a special yeast.
A coffee with intense added tropical fruit flavoring was disqualified from a competition in Ecuador, while a Colombian exporter sold cinnamon co-ferments and disclosed what it had done.
The SCA changed World Barista Championship rules to allow additives as long as they go in before the green-coffee stage.
Best of Panama excluded infused coffees, while Coffee Review named an orange co-fermented Kona its top coffee of the year.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup allowed co-ferments only in its Experimental category, and an Amsterdam roaster told a trade site they had only really started to sell in the past three years.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source gives volumes, but most named producers are in Colombia, where the practice is generally thought to have begun; Perfect Daily Grind names Diego Bermúdez, Edwin Noreña and Rodrigo Sánchez as pioneers, and training programs have spread it across the country's growing regions. In Quindío, the Arcila family's company Cofinet runs fruit co-ferments at its La Pradera mill, and Noreña makes mossto, hop and chili lots at Finca Campo Hermoso.

Elsewhere it's scattered: Hula Daddy co-ferments with oranges in Kona, Hawaii, and a pineapple co-ferment from Ethiopia has been sold. Some competitions push back: Best of Panama excluded them in 2024. Roasters selling them include ones in the US, Japan, South Korea, the UAE and parts of Europe.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Bags say “co-fermented” or “co-ferment”, “infused”, “fruit maceration” or “macerated” (one roaster's packaging read “espresso blend with peach maceration”), and the importer Royal Coffee uses “additive fermentation”. Many lots are simply named after what went in, such as Peach, Lychee or Strawberry, or get playful names, such as one Amsterdam roaster's “Candy Crush”. “Mossto” on a bag means juice from an earlier batch was added.
Coffee Review's 2026 award draws the line by timing: co-fermented means added during fermentation, infused means after drying, flavored means after roasting. Bags don't always follow it.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: The biggest risk is not knowing what's in the bag. Coffees presented as fermented have turned out to carry flavorings: Saša Šestić wrote in 2021 that a Colombian Cup of Excellence entry with rose-water and red-fruit aromas, described as fermented and thermal-shocked, was tested in Europe and found to have been infused with essential oils. Allergens are an open question, since US rules don't require additives to be listed.

In the cup, one roaster says two batches of the same co-ferment can taste noticeably different, and espresso can make them overwhelming. Saša Šestić suggests a check for undeclared infusion: steep 20 g of coarsely ground green coffee in 40 °C (104 °F) water for 10–15 minutes; strong jasmine, rose or cinnamon from green coffee is a strong sign of added flavor.

records.name: Cold fermentation
records.summary: A ferment kept cool to slow it down and stretch it out.
records.lede: The coffee ferments in chilled or temperature-controlled tanks, so the microbes work more slowly and the ferment can run longer before it goes wrong. Coffee Review described a Colombian Gesha whose whole cherries spent three days in refrigerated tanks. There's no agreed temperature or recipe; it's a choice producers make inside other methods.

facts.label: a Colombian Gesha's refrigerated whole-cherry ferment
how long one agronomist says he can ferment below 20 °C (68 °F)
a Panama estate's tank target (59–68 °F)
one champion's range for complex acidity (39–46 °F)

steps.title: Chill the tank
steps.text: Whole cherries or pulped coffee go into refrigerated or temperature-controlled tanks.

steps.title: Ferment slowly
steps.text: Kept cool, the ferment runs longer than it would in a warm open tank.

steps.title: Keep it even
steps.text: Producers hold the temperature steady, since uneven temperature inside a tank can cause off-flavors.

records.layers: Whatever the base method leaves on: the whole fruit when cherries are chilled whole, or just the sticky mucilage on the parchment when the coffee is pulped first.

cup.common: Producers and reviewers link it to cleaner, sweeter cups with more complex acidity, but the evidence is a handful of farm trials and tastings.
cup.text: Coffee Review found that three refrigerated days brought out the deeply sweet yet brisk, savory side of a Colombian Gesha. A Panamanian estate says its 15–20 °C tanks give a sweeter lactic ferment and a cleaner washed coffee.
cup.why: Temperature sets the speed of fermentation. In one champion barista's trials, a 24-hour dry ferment at 16 °C (61 °F) tasted balanced while 26 °C (79 °F) gave an alcoholic acidity, and another producer says lower temperatures hold back fungi that can cause unwanted flavors. A 2024 research review notes that low temperatures can slow microbes so much that a ferment takes several days to reach its end point.
cup.prized: A slower, steadier ferment that can be stopped at the right moment instead of racing ahead in warm weather.
cup.watch: It takes chilled or adapted tanks (one Panama estate brought in beer tanks), and the taste claims come from producers' own trials; a champion barista who recommended cold ferments for acidity said in 2017 that coffee had little fermentation research. Cooler isn't always better: in a Brazilian carbonic trial on Conilon, the 18 °C (64 °F) ferments scored lowest and the 38 °C (100 °F) ones highest.

byCoffee.text: In Coffee Review's tasting, three days of refrigerated whole-cherry fermentation emphasized the sweet, brisk and savory side of a Colombian Gesha from Finca Monteblanco.
Carmen Estate says holding its tanks at 15–20 °C gives cleaner washed coffees with more sweetness and complexity.

spectrum.label: Alcoholic acidity if it runs warm

story.text: Saša Šestić told Perfect Daily Grind that fermenting at 4–8 °C favors complex acidity and 18–20 °C favors sweetness.
Coffee Review rated the Old Soul Co. Colombia Monteblanco Gesha Cold Fermentation, from producer Rodrigo Sánchez, 93 points.
Carmen Estate in Panama adapted beer tanks to hold its ferments at 15–20 °C.
A Brazilian trial on Conilon found carbonic ferments scored higher as temperature rose from 18 to 38 °C (64 to 100 °F).

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source gives figures; it's a choice producers make inside other methods. Named examples: in Colombia, Rodrigo Sánchez's Monteblanco Gesha, chilled three days in refrigerated tanks, and El Paraíso in Cauca, whose sealed ferments run at about 18–19 °C (64–66 °F); in Panama, Carmen Estate in Volcán, Chiriquí, which holds its tanks at 15–20 °C (59–68 °F).

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Cold fermentation” or “cold ferment”, as in the Monteblanco Gesha Cold Fermentation that Coffee Review rated in 2019. Carmen Estate calls its version temperature-controlled, or slow, fermentation.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Uneven temperature causes off-flavors, and the edge and center of a tank can differ, Carmen Estate warns. Go too cold and the ferment can drag on for days; in one study a fermenter held near 2 °C (36 °F) was used to loosen mucilage so a machine could strip it, not to build flavor. And cool doesn't guarantee better: the Brazilian Conilon trial's coolest carbonic ferments scored lowest.

records.name: Extended fermentation

cup.common: A stronger version of whatever the ferment brings: more pronounced fruit, tang or funk than the same coffee fermented briefly.
cup.text: It doesn't add one particular flavor. In sealed tanks, one review site notes, the longer the coffee stays in, the stronger the effect; a Colombian Gesha chilled for three days came across deeply sweet, brisk and savory.
cup.why: Microbes keep turning the fruit's sugars and acids into other acids, alcohol and aroma compounds for as long as they have fuel and moisture, so more time means more of what they make. Sealing or chilling the tank slows them down, which is what lets a ferment run for days.
cup.prized: More sweetness and depth with the coffee still clean; one leading Colombian lactic producer says its best lots ferment past 80 hours.
cup.watch: Pushed too far it turns vinegary or overwhelming, and too much intensity can mask the coffee's own character.

byCoffee.text: Kenyan mills already ferment long by washed standards (overnight, then up to 36 more hours) before a 12–48 hour soak. The soak holds the coffee safely until drying space opens and may make batches more consistent.
A Colombian Gesha (Monteblanco) fermented whole for three days in refrigerated tanks scored 93 with Coffee Review in 2019, which found it deeply sweet, brisk and savory.
One slow-dried natural from Elida Estate, six days sealed and 60 days on the patio, showed lots of chocolate, a huge mouthfeel and a tart, lactic acidity reviewers likened to fresh goat cheese.

In Brazilian trials on Conilon (a Robusta type), longer was often better: 120 hours of carbonic maceration at 38 °C (100 °F) scored highest in a 24–120 hour trial, and a chosen yeast in a 120-hour sealed ferment raised scores by over 3 points.

spectrum.label: Ferment that drowns out the coffee

steps.title: Slow it down
steps.text: Sealing out air or chilling the tank slows the microbes so the ferment can run longer.

steps.title: Ferment for days
steps.text: The ferment runs well past the usual 12–72 hours of a washed coffee; there's no standard length.
steps.hours: examples: about 72 h chilled, 80+ h lactic, 96 h sealed, up to about 6 days

steps.title: Stop and dry
steps.text: The producer ends it, sometimes when the sugar level (Brix) falls to a target, then washes or dries the coffee.

records.layers: Depends on the base method it's added to: the whole cherry, the mucilage and parchment, or parchment only.

story.text: A Colombian Gesha fermented whole for three days in refrigerated tanks scored 93 with Coffee Review.
A Brazilian study of sealed tanks found that 48–72 hours built up more aroma compounds and gave more varied cups than 24 hours.
La Palma y El Tucán, a leading Colombian lactic producer, reported its best results from ferments beyond 80 hours.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup kept extended or deliberately flavor-changing ferments out of its Traditional Washed category.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: There are no figures; long ferments run through most experimental processing. Examples: La Palma y El Tucán in Colombia (lactic lots past 80 hours), Edwin Noreña in Quindío (72 hours in the whole fruit, then 96 more), Costa Rica's La Chumeca mill (about 96 hours sealed) and Panama's Elida Estate (120 hours sealed for its slow-dried naturals).
Kenya is the traditional case of a long washed ferment: its mills ferment in two stages, overnight and then for up to 36 more hours, before a soak in clean water.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “extended” or “prolonged” fermentation, as in one roaster's “prolonged 88-hour cherry fermentation”, or just the hours in the name, as in another's “FES Anaeróbico 120h”. The founder of the roaster WatchHouse argues that printing exact hours and temperatures only adds to the confusion.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Longer isn't automatically better. A Brazilian farm says an over-extended ferment can cost a lot of quality, with acidity, body and sweetness much diminished. Over-fermentation can produce black or “stinker” beans, and in one study ferments stopped at a lower pH (3.9 rather than 4.3–4.6) cupped worse. In a sealed tank, a sharp rise in temperature warns that the ferment is running away toward vinegar.

sections.title: In research
body: Brazilian studies have tested long ferments directly. In sealed, nothing-added tanks, 48–72 hours gave more aroma compounds and more varied cups than 24 hours. In another trial, yeast-started ferments at 28 °C (82 °F) ran from 36 to 288 hours (12 days), and the fermented coffees outscored unfermented ones.

records.name: Fermented
records.summary: Microbes eating the fruit's sugars, from picking until it dries.
records.lede: Fermentation is microbes, mostly yeasts and bacteria, breaking the coffee fruit's sugars down into acids and alcohols. It starts soon after picking and happens in washed, honey and natural coffees alike, so the word “fermented” on its own doesn't say what the producer did. Producers steer it with time, temperature, oxygen and sometimes added microbes, and that's where most new process names come from.

facts.label: typical tank ferment for a washed coffee
sealed ferments in experimental lots
where one Brazilian farm stops its ferments
that fermentation has raised, or lowered, a coffee's score in one champion's work

steps.title: Pick the fruit
steps.text: Fermentation begins once the cherry is picked, because the fruit holds both sugar and water for microbes to use.

steps.title: Ferment in tank or fruit
steps.text: In a washed coffee the pulped seeds ferment in tanks; in a natural the whole fruit ferments during the first days of drying.
steps.hours: 12–72 h in tanks · first days of drying

steps.title: Watch and stop it
steps.text: Careful producers track temperature, pH (acidity) and Brix (sugar) and end the ferment when it reaches their target.

steps.title: Dry it down
steps.text: Drying continues until the beans are down to about 11–12% moisture.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: in a washed coffee only the sticky mucilage on the parchment ferments; in a natural the whole fruit ferments around the seed while it dries.

cup.common: In traditional washed coffee its effect on taste was long ignored; in today's experimental lots reviewers often find extra sweetness and fruit, with a sour, yogurt- or sour-beer-like edge.
cup.text: A well-run ferment can lift sweetness, acidity and body and add fruit, caramel or chocolate notes, says one Brazilian farm. One long-running review site finds experimental ferments usually sweet but often sour, like plain yogurt or sour beer.
cup.why: Yeasts such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae and bacteria such as Lactobacillus turn the fruit's sugars into acids, alcohols and aroma compounds, and some of these show up in the green beans. Temperature sets how fast it all happens.
cup.prized: Control: a ferment that's tracked and stopped on time. One producer warns that good fermentation draws out what the coffee already has, but can't add quality that wasn't grown in the field.
cup.watch: Gone too far, it tastes of vinegar, rotten fruit, sour milk or wine gone bad, and over-fermented beans can look reddish and smell of rotting fruit. It can also leave black or “stinker” beans, and one study found that stopping a ferment at a lower pH went with lower cupping scores. One champion barista says fermentation has raised, and also lowered, a coffee's score by as much as eight cupping points (cupping is the industry's standard tasting).

byCoffee.text: In Colombia, Central America and Hawaii, washed coffees ferment in tanks for roughly 24–48 hours to break down the mucilage before washing.
In Brazil, Ethiopia and most Robusta, the fermenting happens inside the fruit as it dries in layers about 10 cm (4 in) deep for 10–25 days.

In a 2024 study of a 24-hour wet ferment in Santa Catarina, yeasts and lactic bacteria were scarce; the cup scored 80.83, with butter, caramel, cocoa and malt but low acidity and a lack of cleanliness.
Cenicafé found different microbes leading spontaneous ferments of Tabi (acetic bacteria) and of Castillo and Variedad Colombia (lactic and mixed-acid bacteria); Tabi cupped highest, 82.7–83.2.
Kenyan mills ferment in two stages, overnight and then for up to 36 more hours, before a soak of about 12 hours in clean water (up to 48 when the drying beds are full).

story.text: A Brazilian study found lactic acid bacteria made up over 97% of the bacterial DNA sequenced by the end of an ordinary coffee ferment.
Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship with a carbonic-macerated Sudan Rume, a coffee fermented in tanks flushed with carbon dioxide.
Šestić told Perfect Daily Grind that most processing inconsistencies come from fermentation, and that the coffee industry had done little research on it.
Coffee Review's editor wrote that, judged by the standards of ten years earlier, many of the new fermented coffees might seem flawed.
A trade article noted there were still no industry standards for naming processing methods and little agreement on what the names mean.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Fermented” alone is vague. Words like “anoxic” or “acetic” have appeared on bags as producers look for new ways to shape flavor and raise cup scores, and one roaster, the head of WatchHouse, argues that printing exact hours and temperatures only adds to the confusion.

sections.title: How producers steer it
body: Temperature and time are the big two: one agronomist says that below 20 °C (68 °F) he can let a ferment run up to 36 hours, while at higher temperatures problems can show up in the cup after 24. Others seal the tank to cut oxygen or add a chosen yeast or bacterium.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Everywhere coffee is processed; what changes is how. Washed coffee, the norm in Colombia, Central America, Kenya and Hawaii, ferments in tanks after pulping; Kenya's mills do it in two stages before a soak. In the natural coffees of Brazil and Ethiopia, and in most Robusta, it happens in the fruit as it dries.

The deliberately steered ferments sold under new names (anaerobic, carbonic, lactic, yeast-inoculated) appear mostly in specialty lots; reviewed and imported examples come from Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ethiopia, Peru and Brazil.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Under-fermented, the mucilage isn't fully broken down and unwanted microbes can grow; over-fermented, it can leave black or “stinker” beans and, a Brazilian farm says, much less acidity, body and sweetness. Ferments stopped at too low a pH have cupped worse, and molds growing on the coffee give the drink negative flavors.

sections.title: In research
body: Studies find the microbes can differ a lot between farms and methods. Lactic acid bacteria dominated one Brazilian ferment, while in another, in Santa Catarina, yeasts and lactic bacteria were scarce and the cup lacked cleanliness. In a 2023 trial with an added yeast at 28 °C (82 °F), ferments of 36 to 288 hours all outscored unfermented coffee.

records.name: Honey

cup.common: More sweetness and body than washed, with rounder acidity, but less fruit and ferment than a natural.
cup.text: One long-running review site found honeys rounder in acidity than washed coffees, with less citrus and more chocolate and sweetness. An importer adds caramel, nutty and sometimes jammy, stewed-fruit notes.
cup.why: The mucilage stays on while the beans dry, so microbes keep fermenting it until the seed is down to about 11% moisture; in lab tests, pulped naturals' sugar levels fall between washed and natural beans. Drying matters too: one veteran reviewer suspects most of the differences between the honey lots he tasted came from how they were dried.
cup.prized: Sweetness and a syrupy body with more clarity than a natural: well-made honeys taste less powerful than naturals but clearer and more defined.
cup.watch: The sticky beans can mold or spoil if they aren't turned often, and drying too slowly invites over-fermentation. The green beans often look uneven, which puts some roasters off.

byCoffee.text: Honey is usually said to have started here. Small private micro-mills (over 150 since 2000) have led the country's processing experiments, and strict wastewater rules make full washing costly. Mills use the color names differently.
Brazil's pulped natural keeps nearly all the fruit flesh on; one roaster describes it as nutty and chocolatey with low acidity.
Like natural, honey tends to add fruit, sweetness and ferment to Gesha, where washing leans floral and citrus, one roaster says.

steps.title: Pulp off the skin
steps.text: The skin and fruit flesh come off, leaving some or all of the sticky mucilage on the parchment.

steps.title: Choose how much stays
steps.text: Some mills scrub part of the mucilage off by machine; others leave it all on and change the drying to get the different colors.

steps.title: Dry, turning often
steps.text: The sticky beans are raked several times an hour at first, then turned daily, and keep fermenting until about 11% moisture. Darker honeys dry longer; times vary by mill and weather.
steps.hours: about 1–3 weeks: one roaster lists 6–8 days for white honey up to 15–20+ for black; one importer says 18–25 days on average

records.layers: Mucilage (some or all of it) and parchment. The skin and fruit flesh are removed before drying.

story.text: Limited commercial volumes of honey-processed coffee first appeared, according to a Brazil-based exporter; one roaster dates Brazil's related pulped natural to the 1970s.
Costa Rica's micro-mill wave began with La Candelilla; more than 150 small mills followed.
An earthquake damaged Costa Rica's water infrastructure; one roaster says modern honey is often traced to it and credits the Chacón family's Las Lajas mill.
Coffee Review still called honey relatively new, tasting lots from El Salvador, Costa Rica and Nicaragua.
