sections.title: Where it's done
body: Costa Rica is where honey first became popular, led by small micro-mills (La Candelilla in 2000, more than 150 since) that invest in honey, natural and anaerobic lots. It's made elsewhere in Central America too: all the honey samples Coffee Review tasted in 2012 came from El Salvador, Costa Rica and Nicaragua.

Brazil's version, pulped natural, was pioneered there “about fifteen or twenty years” before 2012, Coffee Review said, which puts it in the 1990s; one roaster dates it to the 1970s. In a 2019 survey of Brazilian growers, 14% pulped the skin off before drying (cereja descascado), against 85% making naturals. No published figure gives honey's share of any country's output.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: The sticky beans have to be raked several times an hour at first and turned at least daily after that, or they can mold. The longer they take to dry, the more likely they are to ferment and develop defects, and black honeys dry longest. The green beans often look uneven, which puts some roasters off.

records.name: Kenyan double ferment
records.summary: Ferment, wash, then soak under clean water before drying.
records.lede: Kenya's factories (its washing stations) pulp the cherries, ferment the sticky coffee in tanks, wash it down channels, and then hold the clean parchment under fresh water before it goes onto raised drying beds. The whole ferment-and-wash cycle can run past 72 hours. It's credited with Kenya's very clean, bright cups, though a Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine thinks the country's varieties likely contribute significantly.

facts.label: the second ferment in lower tanks, after a night in the first tank
the soak in clean water
how long the whole ferment-and-wash cycle can run
drying on raised beds

steps.title: Sort, pulp and grade
steps.text: Cherries are sorted for unripe or insect-bitten fruit, pulped, and the parchment is graded into separate tanks.

steps.title: Ferment in tanks
steps.text: The pulped coffee ferments overnight and often longer, sometimes in two stages with a stir or a move between tanks. An FAO report put it at 1–4 days depending on the weather, checked by feeling for a gritty texture after washing a sample.

steps.title: Wash in channels
steps.text: The coffee is pushed down a channel, which scrubs off the last of the sticky fruit.

steps.title: Soak under clean water
steps.text: The clean parchment sits fully under fresh water, changed so that little or no fermentation happens; an FAO report gives about 12 hours, and it stays longer when the drying beds are full.

steps.title: Dry on raised beds
steps.text: It then dries on raised mesh tables to about 11–12% moisture, normally in about two weeks.

records.layers: Only the parchment: skin and fruit come off at the pulper, and the sticky mucilage is fermented and washed away before the soak.

cup.common: A bright, very clean cup with citrus and blackcurrant-like acidity.
cup.text: Sweet Maria's calls Kenya one of the brightest, cleanest cups in the world, with citrus, blackcurrant and berry acidity balanced by syrupy, sometimes wine-like sweetness. Another importer adds grapefruit-like citrus and occasional savory, tomato-like notes, and one grinder maker's guide mentions black tea and florals.
cup.why: Nobody has fully explained it. An FAO report on Kenya says local studies found that a soak of about 12 hours after fermentation improves the coffee's colour and taste. A Cafe Imports researcher suggests the soak might even out temperature and microbes, trigger reactions in the still-living seed or leach compounds out of it, but presents these only as possibilities. One roaster claims the soak builds amino acids behind the citrus acidity; no published study has tested that.
cup.prized: Cleanliness and consistency. The many handling steps also give extra chances to find and remove defects.
cup.watch: The soak is partly a way to store wet coffee in busy weeks, so its length depends on bed space, and copying the method elsewhere won't necessarily make a coffee taste Kenyan.

byCoffee.text: Bright, clean citrus-and-blackcurrant cups, though a Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine thinks Kenya's varieties likely contribute significantly to that profile.

It's hard to predict how the Kenyan process would taste on other coffees, says Cafe Imports' Taya Brown; in Guatemala, a whole-cherry pre-ferment followed by a normal tank ferment could also be called “double fermented”, though it's a different process.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Kenya first: it grows almost only Arabica and processes it by the wet method, and the soak after fermentation is part of the usual sequence at its cooperative “factories” (washing stations). Burundi's fully washed coffees, made at washing stations, also get a second soak after fermentation.
Elsewhere, “double fermented” on a bag may mean something different, such as Guatemala's whole-cherry pre-ferment followed by a normal tank ferment.

sections.title: Why the soak
body: It helps when the drying beds are full: washed parchment can wait under water, kept cool and away from insects, until there's space. It adds another point to pick out defects, and may make batches more consistent.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Bags may say “double fermentation”, “Kenyan process” or “double washed”. A Cafe Imports researcher quoted in Barista Magazine calls “double fermentation” a bit misleading, since the second wet step is mostly a soak, and the term can mean different processes.

story.text: An FAO report on Kenya described fermenting for 1–4 days, then about 12 hours fully under water, which studies in Kenya had found improves the coffee's colour and taste, before about two weeks on mesh tables.
Perfect Daily Grind reported that Burundi's fully washed coffees also get a second soak after fermentation, a step also called Kenyan processing or double fermentation.
Barista Magazine traced the soak to Kenya as a way to hold washed coffee until drying space freed up, and a Cafe Imports researcher called the “double fermentation” name a bit misleading.

records.name: Koji
records.summary: Cherries dusted with the mold behind sake and miso.
records.lede: Koji is Aspergillus oryzae, a mold used for centuries in Asian food and drink; in Japan it's used to make sake and miso. Producers spread its spores on coffee cherries and let it grow in open air for a day or more, and its enzymes break starches down into sugars that later fermentation can use. It started at one Colombian farm, El Vergel, in 2020, had been tried on farms in about eight countries by 2022, and most claims about what it does still come from the people who developed it.

facts.label: spores per kilo of cherries
price of spores, in 2022
score gain one producer claims
a koji coffee at the World Barista Championship

steps.title: Prepare the starter
steps.text: Producers use bought spores, or a cheaper “rice koji”: steamed rice dusted with spores and left until it's covered in white fuzz, then dried, ground and sifted.

steps.title: Sort and spread
steps.text: Ripe cherries are floated and sorted, then spread thin, no more than about 5 cm (2 in) deep in one recipe, in containers or on raised beds.

steps.title: Dust the cherries
steps.text: About 2 grams of spores go evenly onto each kilo of cherries and are mixed in gently; early trials on green coffee instead gave strong umami flavors most drinkers disliked.

steps.title: Let the mold grow
steps.text: In the shade and open to air, the mold spreads over the cherries as a white fur; one recipe keeps them at 25–30 °C (77–86 °F), or the koji dies.
steps.hours: 24–72 h (36 h and about 2 days in two lots)

steps.title: Dry it gently
steps.text: The cherries dry whole, as a natural: in one El Vergel lot about 10 days in the sun, then 2–4 days in dryers at no more than 38 °C (100 °F); another recipe keeps drying below 34 °C (93 °F).

records.layers: The whole cherry in the usual koji natural: the mold grows on the skin and the seed dries inside the fruit. Colombian producer Wilton Benítez does it differently, pulping the coffee after a koji ferment in a bioreactor and fermenting it again, so it dries without the skin and fruit.

cup.common: More body and a creamier, rounder mouthfeel, with more sweetness and a long aftertaste, say the people who make it.
cup.text: In a blind comparison run in Japan, the US, the Netherlands and Finland, the koji sample scored higher, with more body, a longer aftertaste and more refined acidity, according to one of its developers. Coffee Review rated three koji lots from Colombia's Cauca 94–95 in 2023 and 2024, finding them tropical and floral with a creamy or syrupy feel, though those coffees went through several other steps too.
cup.why: Koji's enzymes break big starches into sugars that microbes can ferment, and it makes amino acids and glutamates (the savory, umami kind); one developer says it also produces esters and aldehydes that boost fruity aromas. El Vergel thinks it enhances what's already there more than it creates new flavors. In a lab study that grew it on Robusta beans from India, the roasted coffee had more pyrazines, a group of aroma compounds.
cup.prized: Extra body and aftertaste, and perhaps a point or two on a coffee that's already good; a koji Papayo from Cauca scored 95 with Coffee Review in 2023.
cup.watch: Applied to green coffee it tasted strongly of umami, and even on cherries the savory side can show: one roaster lists “balsamic-like umami” among an El Vergel koji Java's notes and says the aftertaste keeps building. One developer says farms making 82–83 point coffee will gain more from selective picking, sorting and clean tanks, and in 2022 the safety and choice of strains for wider use were still being confirmed.

byCoffee.text: El Vergel has used koji on Geisha, Bourbon, Caturra and Java, and says Java responded especially well; one roaster's El Vergel koji Java listed red cherry, redcurrant, pink grapefruit and tamarind, with a savory, balsamic-like finish.
Wilton Benítez's koji Papayo from Granja Paraíso 92 scored 95 with Coffee Review in 2023: lychee, passion fruit, bergamot and jasmine, with a very rich, creamy mouthfeel.

Benítez's koji Geshas scored 94 (2023) and 95 (2024) with Coffee Review, with bergamot, lychee and flowers and a full, syrupy mouthfeel. In Panama, TNT Lab's koji natural Gesha was sold with notes of magnolia, blood orange and blueberry.

story.text: Koji has been used in Asian food and drink; in Japan it makes sake, amazake and miso.
El Vergel in Colombia produced the first koji-processed coffee, with consultant Christopher Feran, who called the method the Koji Supernatural Protocol.
Kaapo Paavolainen, Finland's 2021 barista champion, used a koji coffee at the World Barista Championship in Milan.

Its developers had published the process open-source in English and Spanish, and Bloomberg reported koji trials on farms in Colombia, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Brazil, Thailand, China, Vietnam and Indonesia.
Coffee Review rated Wilton Benítez's koji Papayo from Cauca 95 points.

sections.title: Who's behind it
body: Coffee consultant Christopher Feran; Kaapo Paavolainen of One Day Coffee in Finland; Elias Bayter of El Vergel Estate in Colombia; and Koichi Higuchi of Higuchi Matsunosuke Shoten, an Osaka maker of koji starters whose expertise was sought for the early trials. Bloomberg also names Mason Salisbury of Luminous Coffee and chef Jeremy Umansky among the collaborators.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Most named producers are in Colombia. El Vergel, the Bayter family's farm in Fresno, Tolima, at about 1,500 m (4,900 ft), made the first lots and sells them through the Forest Coffee platform. Wilton Benítez's Granja Paraíso 92 in Piendamó, Cauca, runs its own version in a bioreactor.

Outside Colombia it's rarer: TNT Lab at Finca Santamaria in Paso Ancho, Panama, sells a koji natural Gesha, and in 2022 Bloomberg reported trials on farms in Guatemala, Costa Rica, Brazil, Thailand, China, Vietnam and Indonesia.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “koji” or “kōji”, “koji natural”, or “Koji Supernatural”, the name its developers gave the method; one trade article also lists “oryzae coffee”, after the mold's species name. In 2022 Bloomberg reported koji coffee cost about twice as much per pound as regular coffee, or $5 to $7 a cup in most shops.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Mold on coffee is normally a fault: a 2024 research review says unwanted molds give the drink negative flavors, so koji is a deliberate exception that depends on growing the right food strain under control. It needs air and steady warmth, about 25–30 °C (77–86 °F) in one recipe, or it dies.

Done on green coffee it gave strong umami flavors most drinkers disliked. In 2022 its developers said they were still making sure it was a fully safe process and choosing strains for commercial use, and that cost, at about US$17 for 30 g of spores, was the biggest hurdle.

records.name: Lactic

cup.common: A creamier cup with a yogurt-like tang and more sweetness.
cup.text: Producers describe a creamier, velvety body, more sweetness, and chocolate and butter notes; reviewers often find the lactic tang fused with fruit.

feel.acidity: tangy; brighter in some pulped lots

cup.why: Sealed away from air, lactic acid bacteria (the yogurt kind) gain ground over yeasts and turn the mucilage's sugars into lactic acid; a salt brine of about 2–3% helps because these bacteria tolerate salt better than most competitors. They often take over ordinary ferments too: in one Brazilian study they accounted for over 97% of the bacterial DNA sequenced by the end of a spontaneous ferment. One producer says the falling pH also sets off enzyme reactions that shape flavor, and that up to 90% of the glucose and fructose is gone compared with a natural.
cup.prized: Body and sweetness with chocolate. One consultant calls it a cleaner, lower-risk route than other experimental ferments, though one that sets a coffee apart more than it improves it.
cup.watch: It takes skill and trial and error; fungi can cause off-flavors, one reason producers keep tanks cool. One producer warns it may not suit drinkers of traditional coffee.

byCoffee.text: La Palma y El Tucán, in Cundinamarca, has championed the style; its producer reports more sweetness, chocolate and butter, with the best results from ferments past 80 hours. The 2019 World Barista Champion used a Sidra from the farm.
One La Palma lactic Sidra, after an 88-hour cherry ferment, was sold with blueberry and passion fruit, hints of caramel and sweet spice, a creamy texture and a juicy lactic acidity.

Finca La Bandida's lactic natural, whole cherries fermented 65 hours with lactobacilli, scored 93 with Coffee Review in 2021: cherry, chocolate fudge and toffee, vibrant citrus acidity and a satiny mouthfeel.

Adding the lactic bacterium Leuconostoc mesenteroides to sealed-tank Conilon (a Brazilian Robusta) gave a cup with caramel, fruit and spice notes. In Ecuador, a Robusta “lactic natural”, made by adding lactic acid itself to a sealed whole-fruit ferment, scored 92 with Coffee Review in 2023, crisply creamy with a gently fermenty finish.

steps.title: Pulp, or keep whole
steps.text: Many lactic lots are pulped first, though some start from whole or even dried cherries.

steps.title: Seal and add a starter
steps.text: The coffee is sealed away from air, either letting the bacteria already on the fruit take over or adding a lactic starter culture or a salt brine of about 2–3% (2% is usually enough, one consultant says).

steps.title: Ferment, watching pH and heat
steps.text: Producers track pH and temperature. La Palma y El Tucán's co-founder says lowering the temperature holds back fungi that cause off-flavors, though one roaster describes the same farm's method as keeping the temperature high, so there's no agreed setting; lengths vary by producer.
steps.hours: 65 h (a Huila lot) to 80+ h (La Palma's best lots)

steps.title: Ferment the mucilage
steps.text: In one La Palma lot, the cherry ferment was followed by a shorter ferment of the sticky mucilage.

steps.title: Dry slowly
steps.text: Lots are sun-dried, often on raised beds; one La Palma Sidra dried for 31 days and was finished in a mechanical dryer.

records.layers: Often the mucilage and parchment, when the coffee is pulped before the sealed ferment. Whole-cherry lactic naturals, such as one Huila Pink Bourbon, ferment and dry in the whole fruit.

story.text: A Brazilian study found lactic acid bacteria, mainly Leuconostoc and Lactococcus, made up over 97% of the bacteria by the end of an ordinary coffee ferment.
Coffee Review described oxygen-limited ferments that hold back yeasts and favor lactic acid bacteria, sometimes called lactic acid fermentation.
Jooyeon Jeon won the World Barista Championship using a Sidra from La Palma y El Tucán, a farm that champions lactic fermentation.
Coffee Review rated a lactic natural Pink Bourbon from Huila's Finca La Bandida 93 points.
A coffee consultant called lactic fermentation a cleaner, safer alternative for producers using other methods, though one that sets a coffee apart more than it improves it.
A research review reported that adding Leuconostoc mesenteroides to sealed Conilon ferments gave caramel, fruit and spice notes.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source counts lactic lots by country, but the best-known producer and most lots on the market are Colombian. La Palma y El Tucán, in Zipacón, Cundinamarca, at about 1,750 m (5,750 ft), is the best-known name, which Perfect Daily Grind calls a pioneering specialty farm; another Cundinamarca grower, Gladys Cruz, has sold lactic lots made with La Palma's method, and Huila's Finca La Bandida sells them too.

Ecuador has them as well, from a washed lactic Typica grown in Pichincha to a Robusta lactic natural from Santa Elena. In Brazil, researchers have tested lactic bacteria on Conilon, the country's Robusta.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Look for “lactic”, “lactic natural”, “lactic washed” or “washed, lactic fermentation”, or Spanish “láctico”. The word covers different methods: bacteria added to whole cherries, a salt brine, sealing so native bacteria take over, or, in one Ecuadorian Robusta, lactic acid itself added to the ferment. One roaster sells a La Palma “Lactic Sidra” that the farm made with its “Bioinnovation” method, fermenting cherries 107 hours with compost in clay pots buried in the forest floor.
“Lactic” is also a tasting word: reviewers use it for a yogurt-like tang in coffees that weren't lactic-processed, such as a Costa Rican double anaerobic natural with “subtle lactic notes”.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Getting it right takes in-depth knowledge and trial and error, and avoiding defects is hard. Fungi growing in the tank can cause unwanted flavors, which is why La Palma lowers the temperature. Coffee Review's editor wrote in 2019 that some oxygen-limited coffees taste sour, like plain yogurt or sour beer, and that by older standards many would seem flawed.
La Palma's co-founder expects it to stay niche because of the control it takes, and warns it may not suit drinkers of traditional coffee.

records.name: Mechanical drying
records.summary: Warm, moving air in a machine dries the coffee faster and evenly.
records.lede: Instead of the sun, a machine moves warm air through the coffee; a guardiola, for example, is a horizontal rotating drum. Temperature and humidity are easier to control, so drying is faster and more uniform, and it stops the spontaneous fermentation that sun-dried coffee goes through. Often the coffee is partly dried in the sun first and the machine finishes it.

facts.label: suggested top temperature for parchment (104 °F)
suggested top temperature for naturals (113 °F)
machine drying of some Colombian experimental lots
target moisture

steps.title: Pre-dry (often)
steps.text: Coffee is often partly dried in the sun first, or pre-dried in an overhead silo.

steps.title: Load the dryer
steps.text: It goes into a guardiola or another rotary dryer with a perforated drum, which turns the coffee in a steady flow of warm air.

steps.title: Hold the heat steady
steps.text: Producers are advised to hold the temperature steady through parts of the drying and keep it below about 40 °C (104 °F) for parchment or 45 °C (113 °F) for naturals.

steps.title: Stop at target
steps.text: Drying ends at about 11–12% moisture.
steps.hours: about a day for El Paraíso's lots

records.layers: Any: washed parchment, parchment with its mucilage, or whole cherries can go through dryers, a 2024 review says, though one importer says naturals can't be machine-dried the way washed coffees are.

cup.common: When gentle, a clean, consistent finish; too hot or rushed, it costs quality.
cup.text: A 2024 review credits machines with faster, more uniform drying. Finca El Paraíso says its low-temperature, dehumidifying dryers protect aromatic compounds and help the coffee store without defects, while one importer calls flash-drying coffee to cut its moisture terrible for the cup.
cup.why: Controlled heat and humidity dry the coffee more evenly, and fast drying halts the fermentation that would otherwise carry on in the fruit or mucilage.
cup.prized: Consistency, and drying on schedule in wet weather or when patios and beds are full; at the peak of harvest, some Central American mills fire their dryers with wood.
cup.watch: Too much heat costs quality (one guide's limits are 40 °C for parchment and 45 °C for naturals), and rotary dryers were long linked with commodity-grade coffee. Dryers also cost money many small producers don't have, so some sell their coffee wet instead.

byCoffee.text: Finca El Paraíso machine-dries its thermal-shock lots for about a day at 34–42 °C (93–108 °F); another lot had 12 hours in a dryer and then about 15 days in a parabolic (covered) dryer.
With rain likely during harvest, coffee often starts in the sun and is finished in a Guardiola.
Mechanical drying prevents the spontaneous fermentation that whole fruit goes through while it sun-dries, a 2024 review notes.

spectrum.label: Heat damage from drying too hot or too fast

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Colombia: machine drying, mostly in silo dryers since the 1970s, is used on about 27,650 farms with more than 5 ha of coffee, which produce 31% of the crop (Cenicafé, 2017), while sun drying is used mainly on farms making under about 3,500 kg of dry coffee a year; an ICO guide says about half the farms in the Caldas region use silo dryers. Brazil: 34% of growers in a 2019 survey used mechanical dryers, and fixed-bed dryers are widely used in Zona da Mata, Minas Gerais.

Central America: rotary dryers are still called Guardiolas, and Costa Rica's protected-name rules allow Guardiolas, vertical and static dryers, or a mix of sun and machine. Kenya: estates have used dryers for years, but few cooperative factories have them. Overall, an ICO guide says machine drying has become much more common, at least on larger farms.

sections.title: Drying in the dark
body: Finca Hartmann in Panama dries coffee in drawers in a dark room, using a large dehumidifier and fans rather than sun or high heat. Its owner sees it as an option for small producers who lack space for traditional drying or money for rotary dryers.

sections.title: Types and temperatures
body: The common types are rotary drums (Guardiolas), static-bed or silo dryers, and vertical counter-flow dryers. An ICO guide gives typical drying times of 12–24 hours; Cenicafé gives 18–32 hours to take parchment from 52–55% to 10–12% moisture. Most set-ups need the coffee partly sun-dried first, from about 60% to about 30% moisture.

Temperature advice differs by source and by what is measured. A Perfect Daily Grind guide says parchment shouldn't be dried above 40 °C (104 °F) or naturals above 45 °C (113 °F); the ICO guide says bean temperatures above 45 °C can damage quality and keeps silo air below 50 °C (122 °F); Cenicafé caps the drying air at 50 °C; and Colombia's protected-name rules allow air up to 55 °C (131 °F). Furnace smoke getting into the drying air can taint the coffee.

story.text: Engineer José Guardiola designed a rotating drum dryer in Guatemala; Barista Hustle calls Guardiolas the first large-scale coffee drying machines, and rotary dryers in Central America still carry the name.
Cenicafé developed its silo dryer, and Colombia's coffee federation moved from Guardiolas to it.
Silva and Lacerda Filho built a fixed-bed dryer at Brazil's Federal University of Viçosa that was widely taken up by small and medium farms.
Cenicafé estimated that 27,650 Colombian farms with more than 5 ha of coffee machine-dry, and that they produce 31% of the country's coffee.
In a survey of Brazilian growers, 34% used mechanical dryers.

records.name: Monsooned
records.summary: Indian natural coffee aged for months in the monsoon wind.
records.lede: Natural (dry-processed) Indian coffee is spread out in well-ventilated warehouses on the Malabar Coast through the June–September monsoon, soaking up the moist sea wind for 12 to 16 weeks. The beans swell to nearly double their size, turn pale straw-yellow and lose much of their acidity. It recreates the taste coffee used to pick up on six-month voyages by sail to Europe, and both the Arabica and Robusta versions are protected names in India.

facts.label: in the monsoon wind
the southwest monsoon season
bean size after monsooning
registered as a Geographical Indication in India

steps.title: Start with a natural
steps.text: Only top-grade, dry-processed coffee, dried on the estate to about 11% moisture and then hulled and graded, is used.

steps.title: Spread on warehouse floors
steps.text: The beans are spread 10–15 cm (4–6 in) deep on the cement floors of well-ventilated warehouses and raked about every 3 hours.

steps.title: Bag loosely and stack
steps.text: They're packed half-full into unstitched jute bags, stacked so the wind can pass, and emptied and rebagged once a week.

steps.title: Wait out the monsoon
steps.text: The coffee is done when the beans have swollen and turned pale yellow, the color of straw.

steps.title: Sort and fumigate
steps.text: Beans that didn't monsoon, black beans and broken ones are picked out, and the coffee is fumigated, graded and packed for export.

records.layers: None of the fruit: monsooning starts after the dried cherry has been hulled and graded, so it's the bare green bean that meets the wind.

cup.common: Heavy, mellow and low in acidity, with an earthy, aged character.
cup.text: India's Coffee Board describes good body, mild acidity, sweetness and a mellow taste with a distinctive aged, musty flavor. One importer finds it spicy, earthy and smoky with sweet tobacco and a creamy body; another writer notes spice and almonds.
cup.why: The beans soak up water, from about 9% to 13–15% moisture, and get much lighter for their size (density drops from about 1.24 to 0.86–1.00 g/ml in the Arabica). Microbe counts rise several-fold, sugars fall slightly and soluble solids rise slightly.
cup.prized: Body and low acidity: it's a sought-after part of espresso blends, especially Scandinavian and German ones, and one importer says it adds a rich crema. The Coffee Board says it's mainly used in blends to mellow rougher, more acidic coffees and give them richness.
cup.watch: Above about 14% moisture, mold grows fast, and the coffee is prone to weevils, which is why warehouses rake, rebag and sort constantly. The Coffee Board notes that attempts elsewhere on the mainland didn't produce the flavor.

byCoffee.text: On the Coffee Board's sensory scale, monsooned Arabica scores 3.5–4.0 for acidity and 6.0–7.0 for body.
Monsooned Robusta scores lower still for acidity (1.5–2.5) and a little higher for body (6.5–7.5).

spectrum.label: Musty, aged flavor that fans seek out

story.text: Indian coffee went to Europe on wooden sailing ships around the Cape of Good Hope, about six months at sea, and arrived pale, swollen and musty-tasting, a character European buyers came to like.
Steamships and the Suez Canal cut the trip to about a month, the flavor disappeared, and Malabar Coast exporters devised monsooning to bring it back.
Cecil Gifford wrote about monsooning Robusta in the journal Indian Coffee, the earliest of the records the Coffee Board cites.
A Coffee Board member reported on bringing monsooned coffee back after the war.
Monsooned Malabar Arabica and Monsooned Malabar Robusta were registered as Geographical Indications, with certificates dated 28 March 2008 and the Coffee Board as applicant.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: In India only: the Coffee Board says monsooned coffee is prepared at curing works on the west coast of southern India, from June to September. The protected name covers monsooning on the Malabar Coast, from Mangalore in Karnataka to Kozhikode (Calicut) in Kerala. The Arabica comes from estates in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and the Araku Valley, and the monsooned beans are graded by size as AAA, AA, A and Triage; the Coffee Board calls Monsooned Malabar AA the best grade.

sections.title: Who buys it
body: One big exporter, Aspinwall, processed more than 3,500 tonnes in 2018, and buyers have included Nespresso, Benecke and Grecof.

records.name: Mossto
records.summary: Juice from fermenting cherries, reused to start the next batch.
records.lede: Mosto is Spanish for fresh fruit juice, the “must” of winemaking. In coffee it's the liquid that collects as cherries ferment, full of yeasts, bacteria, sugars and acids, which is saved and added to a new batch as a starter, a trick known as backslopping. Recipes vary a lot: some use only the coffee's own juice, while others add yeast, sugar or other fruit.

facts.label: of the cherry weight comes off as mosto
when the mosto is often collected
ferment time in the Bolivian washed method
batches before the mosto needs refreshing

steps.title: Ferment a first batch
steps.text: Coffee ferments in a closed tank and releases liquid, the mosto, whose pH and microbes are watched.

steps.title: Collect the mosto
steps.text: The liquid is drawn off, often around the 72-hour mark, when microbial activity is strongest.

steps.title: Start the next batch
steps.text: Freshly pulped coffee goes into a new tank with the mosto added, so the yeasts and bacteria go straight to work on the mucilage.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.text: In the washed version, the coffee is rinsed and dried like any washed coffee.

records.layers: In the washed method, only the sticky mucilage on the parchment ferments with the mosto before it's rinsed off. Mossto naturals keep the whole cherry on through fermentation and drying.

cup.common: Riper, juicier fruit than a plain washed coffee while keeping the washed coffee's clarity, say roasters who sell it.
cup.text: One roaster describes stone fruit, fruit cordial and grape-like sweetness with bright, complex acidity, and gives one lot's notes as cherry cordial, white grape and tangerine. A Sumatran mossto natural was sold with berry and citrus notes and a juicy body.
cup.why: The mosto carries a ready-made crowd of the yeasts and bacteria that thrived in the last batch, so the new ferment gets going quickly. Colombian producer Edwin Noreña calls it a catalyst that speeds up, controls and enhances fermentation.
cup.prized: Complexity without bringing in anything from outside, when the starter is made only from the coffee's own fruit.
cup.watch: Reused liquid can carry unwanted microbes into the next batch, and the leftover liquid can harm streams if it isn't treated. Some “mossto” lots are also fermented with added yeast, sugar or other fruit, so read the details.

byCoffee.text: Edwin Noreña's mossto Caturra, whose starter also had added yeast, glucose and other juices and which fermented with fruit pulp and nuts, was sold with notes of peach candy, rosewater and passion fruit.

Noreña's Lychee Hermoso spent 72 hours in a carbonic ferment in the whole fruit, then 96 hours after pulping in coffee must mixed with dried lychee, and 22 days drying on raised beds; Coffee Review scored it 95 in 2026, with red currant, pink grapefruit, rose and dark chocolate and a full, syrupy mouthfeel.
A cooperative's experimental mossto natural scored 86 points, with berry and citrus fruit and a silky mouthfeel.

The Lamastus family adds red juice from its sealed-tank naturals to fresh tanks of washed, natural and honey coffees, lots it labels “Dose”; Wilford Lamastus says it adds a subtle sweetness without changing the flavor much.

spectrum.label: Juicy, ripe fruit with washed clarity
Spoilage carried over in reused liquid

story.text: In Panama, Wilford Lamastus was using a similar idea, pouring the red juice from the bottom of his fermentation tanks into tanks of fresh coffee, lots he labels “Dose”.
An importer's review of co-fermentation quoted Edwin Noreña calling mossto a catalyst for fermentation.
Mossto lots were reaching beyond Latin America, such as a Sumatran cooperative's mossto natural.
Coffee Review rated Noreña's Lychee Hermoso, fermented in coffee must with dried lychee, 95 points.

sections.title: Who started it
body: No single inventor is named. One roaster says the washed mosto method is widely credited to the Rodríguez family's Agricafe in Caranavi, Bolivia, which uses it on small single-day microlots, and that Costa Rican micro-mills helped spread the technique.

sections.title: Is it a co-ferment?
body: Made only from the same coffee's fruit, it adds nothing from outside, which is how one roaster frames it. But some producers build the starter with added yeast, glucose or other juices and ferment alongside fruit pulp, which moves it toward a co-ferment.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: No source gives volumes. Beyond Bolivia, where the washed method is credited to Agricafe, Costa Rica, with its independent micro-mills, has been at the forefront of experimenting with it. In Colombia, Edwin Noreña's Finca Campo Hermoso in Quindío uses mossto with fruit, hops or chili, and Cauca's thermal-shock producers save the juice from a first ferment, feed it more yeast and ferment the pulped coffee in it. Panama's Lamastus family adds tank juice to its “Dose” lots.
It has spread to Asia too: Sirinya Coffee in Doi Chaang, Thailand, makes a mosto natural, and a cooperative in Gayo, Sumatra, sold one in 2026.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Spelled “mosto” (Spanish for fresh juice, English “must”) or “mossto”, the spelling in Royal Coffee's interview with Noreña and on some importers' listings; Coffee Review writes “coffee must”. Mosto naturals are sometimes sold as “Candy Natural”, and the Lamastus family's lots carry “Dose” in the name.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: Whatever grows in the starter goes into the next batch, good or bad, and a batch of mosto keeps its vigor for only a couple of ferments. Temperature and microbes vary, so results can be unpredictable unless conditions are kept steady, and the leftover liquid is strong enough to harm streams if it isn't treated. Some “mossto” lots also add yeast, sugar or other fruit, so the name alone doesn't tell you what went in.

records.name: Natural

cup.common: Ripe or dried fruit (berries, stone fruit, prune-like notes) and a heavier body than the same coffee washed.
cup.text: Berry, stone-fruit or dried-fruit notes and a heavier body than the same coffee washed. It can turn wine-like or brandy-like; when the fruit rots, the cup goes bad.
cup.why: Yeasts and bacteria ferment the fruit around the seed during the first days of drying, and some of what they make, especially fruity-smelling esters, seems to get into the seed and survive roasting. Studies don't support the idea that fruit sugar soaks into the bean: naturals keep more of their own simple sugars because the pulp holds back germination, while sucrose, over 90% of the bean's sugar, hardly changes. Drying speed matters too: long drying pushes toward wine or whisky notes, and drying that's too short can leave the flavors muted.
cup.prized: Clean, distinct fruit with little or no ferment. Coffee Review found the ferment virtually undetectable in the cleanest Ethiopian naturals, and at the 2019 Best of Panama auction the winning naturals sold for much more than the washed winners.
cup.watch: With the whole fruit on, it can over-ferment, mold or rot, especially when it dries too slowly or the cherries are under- or overripe. Then a bitter, rotten edge appears, most of all as the cup cools.

byCoffee.text: Well-made ones are known for sweet berry fruit (blueberry and strawberry in fine lots), sometimes floral with a honey-like sweetness; some carry a mild brandy- or whiskey-like edge.

Brazil has long dried most of its Arabica this way (90% in a 1987 estimate), mostly on patios. One importer describes pulpy, coffee-cherry fruit rather than Ethiopian blueberry, with dark chocolate, toasted nuts and caramel, lower acidity and a heavy body.
Natural and honey Geshas tend to bring more fruit, sweetness and ferment into the cup, while washed ones lean floral and citrus, one roaster says.

Practically all of the world's Robusta is dried in the fruit. In a trial cited by a 2024 review of Robusta-type fermentation, adding a chosen yeast to naturals raised the cup score by about 1.5 points and cut mold by about 90%.

steps.title: Ferment in the fruit
steps.text: Ripe whole cherries are spread on patios or raised beds, and yeasts and bacteria feed on the fruit, mostly in the first days. Ripe fruit matters most here.

steps.title: Dry slowly
steps.text: The cherries are turned until the seed is down to about 11–12% water. Weather sets the pace, so times vary widely.
steps.hours: about 10–30 days; 60+ days for deliberately slow-dried lots

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: The dried cherries rest before milling.
steps.hours: 30 days or more at one Panama estate

steps.title: Hull
steps.text: A dry mill removes the dried skin, fruit and parchment.

records.layers: Everything: skin, fruit flesh, mucilage and parchment all stay on the seed until it's dry.

story.text: Southern Ethiopia dried all of its coffee in the whole fruit, a very old practice, until washing arrived.
Starbucks first brought the cleaner 'new natural' style to North American retail; Coffee Review calls the style more an update and revival of the old method than an innovation.
Coffee Review's report 'Brandy and Surprises' covered the new naturals: careful small-batch versions of drying in the whole fruit.
At the Best of Panama auction, the winning naturals sold for much higher prices than the washed winners.
The USDA's Ethiopia report put the country's coffee at 70–80% unwashed (natural) and 20–30% washed.

facts.label: of the world's coffee is dry-processed, and practically all Robusta
of Ethiopia's coffee is natural (2021)

drying in the sun; 60+ for deliberately slow-dried lots

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Most of the world's coffee, and practically all Robusta, is dry-processed. Brazil has long made most of its Arabica this way: 90% in a 1987 estimate, and 85% of growers in a 2019 survey, mostly dried on patios. Ethiopia is the other big natural producer: about 70–80% of its coffee was unwashed in 2021, and washed coffee averaged around 30% of exports in 2006–2013. The ICO's coffee groups call Brazil, Ethiopia and Paraguay the “Brazilian Naturals”.

Yemen's traditional coffees are dried in the fruit, much as they were centuries ago. FAO's country profiles from 2000 listed Robusta countries such as Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Angola and DR Congo as dry-method producers.

In washed-coffee countries, naturals are a smaller, growing specialty line: Costa Rica's micro-mills are investing in them and the style is rising there partly because it can command higher prices; about 30% of the Colombian single-farm coffees Coffee Review tasted in 2021 were naturals; and at Panama's 2019 auction, naturals sold for far more than washed coffees.

sections.title: On the bag
body: Natural, dry-processed, sun-dried and unwashed all name this method; the ICO's glossary treats “unwashed” and “natural” coffee as the same thing. Ethiopian bags often pair a grade with the process, as in “Gr1 Natural”. “Sun-dried” alone doesn't settle it, because washed coffees are often dried in the sun too.

records.name: Patio-dried
records.summary: Spread out on concrete or asphalt in the sun, and turned.
records.lede: The coffee is spread thinly in the sun on a large open floor, often concrete or asphalt, and turned so it dries evenly. How well it goes depends on the weather: rain, heat, humidity and sunshine all shape the result. In rainy regions producers often start on the patio and finish in a mechanical dryer.

facts.label: average patio drying at one Panama farm
sun drying a washed coffee
sun drying a natural or honey
layer of whole cherries for a sun-dried natural; guides differ (2–4 in)

steps.title: Spread it out
steps.text: Cherries or parchment are spread thinly across a concrete or asphalt patio.

steps.title: Turn it often
steps.text: It's turned regularly; coffee that isn't turned dries unevenly and can overheat in strong sun.

steps.title: Mind the weather
steps.text: Coffee doesn't dry at night or in the early morning and rain can harm it, so some mills build covered patios.

steps.title: Finish
steps.text: Drying ends at about 11–12% moisture, sometimes in a mechanical dryer when rain threatens.

records.layers: Any: parchment for washed and honey coffees, the whole cherry for naturals, and in Indonesia the bare wet-hulled bean.

cup.common: No signature taste; the result depends on the weather and on how clean and well run the patio is.
cup.text: A 2024 review notes that the quality of sun-dried coffee depends on rainfall, temperature, humidity and sunshine, and one importer singles out very clean patios as a mark of the best mills.
cup.why: The fruit keeps fermenting in the first days of drying, so coffee that dries too slowly in damp weather can ferment out of control, while coffee left unturned in hot sun dries unevenly and can overheat.
cup.prized: Clean, well-turned patios; one importer's partner mills in Indonesia are building covered patios to lengthen drying.
cup.watch: Rain can delay drying or harm quality, and on open floors birds and animals can damage or contaminate the coffee.

byCoffee.text: Bare beans dry fast on tarps or patios, which one importer warns can be harsh and uneven without the parchment's protection.
Because rain can fall unexpectedly during harvest, coffee often starts in the sun and is finished in a Guardiola dryer.

spectrum.label: Clean, evenly dried coffee from clean, well-turned patios
Over-fermented when it dries too slowly
Poor taste and mold risk on plastic tarps or bare soil

story.text: An early Brazilian alternative to the open patio, mesh trays running on rails under a fixed roof, was patented by Corrêia de Silva.
Costa Rica's protected-name rules listed concrete patios and African beds among the accepted ways to sun-dry, alongside machine and mixed drying.
In a survey of Brazilian growers, 42% dried on concrete or asphalt patios and 9% on earth, more than used mechanical dryers (34%) or raised beds (10%).
A Perfect Daily Grind guide quoted Pinhalense's Bruno Ribeiro on the patio's exposure to “rollercoaster” weather, and put sun drying at 6–9 days for washed coffee and 10–14 for naturals and honeys.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: In Brazil, concrete or asphalt patios were the most common drying method in a 2019 survey of growers, and most Brazil naturals are dried on patios rather than raised beds. An ICO hygiene guide notes that cement or brick is widely used for Arabica, while bare earth is common for Robusta.

Colombia's protected-name rules allow sun drying on cement platforms or machine drying; sun drying is used mainly on farms making under about 3,500 kg of dry coffee a year. Cenicafé describes covered parabolic and tunnel solar dryers, and an ICO guide describes Colombia's movable wooden “carros” and “elbas”, cement floors under a movable roof. Costa Rica's rules list concrete patios beside African beds; in Guatemala's San Marcos, where rain can fall without warning at harvest, producers typically start drying in the sun and finish in a Guardiola dryer. In Indonesia, wet-hulled beans dry on tarps or patios.

sections.title: Doing it well
body: Keep the layers thin and turn them. An ICO hygiene guide puts near-optimum loads at about 4 cm for parchment and 5–6 cm for cherries; Barista Hustle's course says no more than 5 cm (2 in) for cherries and about 2.5 cm (1 in) for wet parchment, with naturals taking about three weeks and parchment about 14 days. Layers that are too thick dry too slowly.

Millers rake the coffee into piles at midday, since too much sun can crack the parchment, and cover it at the end of the day, because rain and night dew rewet it. Plastic tarps have given poor taste results and, in some tests, a build-up of ochratoxin (a mold toxin) as water pools beneath them, and drying straight on soil is strongly discouraged.

records.name: Raised beds
records.summary: Mesh tables off the ground, so air moves around the coffee.
records.lede: The coffee dries on mesh-topped tables raised off the ground. Air circulates around it, it stays clear of dirt and contamination from the ground, and workers can spread it thin and turn it. Raised beds are used at Kenyan and Ethiopian washing stations and for many specialty lots elsewhere; one Panama farm uses them mostly for slow-dried lots.

facts.label: washed Kenyan parchment
honeys to naturals at one mill
slow-dried lots at one Panama farm
moisture when it's done

steps.title: Spread it thin
steps.text: Parchment or whole cherries are spread thinly across the mesh.

steps.title: Turn it often
steps.text: Workers turn it regularly so it dries evenly.

steps.title: Sun, shade or cover
steps.text: Beds can stand in full sun, under shade, in polytunnels or in greenhouses.

steps.title: Dry to target
steps.text: Drying ends at about 10–12% moisture.

records.layers: Depends on the base method: clean parchment for washed coffees, parchment with its sticky mucilage for honeys, the whole cherry for naturals.

cup.common: No flavor of its own; beds are chosen for clean, even drying.
cup.text: Esmeralda says raised beds let air circulate for clean, evenly dried coffee, and one importer pictures small, covered raised beds as ideal for higher cup quality.
cup.why: Air moves more easily around coffee on a bed, the coffee stays away from contamination on the ground, and thin, well-turned layers dry evenly. Coffee that isn't turned properly is left unevenly exposed to heat and airflow.
cup.prized: Clean, even drying; one Panama farm uses its beds mostly for slow-dried lots.
cup.watch: Bed space runs short at the peak of harvest: Kenyan mills keep washed coffee soaking until beds free up, and many small producers can't afford beds or dryers and sell their coffee wet.

byCoffee.text: Washed parchment moves from the soak to raised drying screens and dries in about 7–15 days.
Cherries go onto raised beds straight from the tree, and drying in the fruit strongly shapes their flavor, says Sweet Maria's.
The Lamastus family's anaerobic slow-dry (ASD) lots, from estates such as Elida, dry on raised, shaded beds.

spectrum.label: Clean, even drying with air all around
Uneven drying where the mesh sags
Poor cups from thick layers and drawn-out drying

story.text: A paper titled “A new type of coffee drying table” (Sonke) is the source a Kenyan Coffee Research Foundation scientist later cited for the table design, built to stay absolutely flat so the coffee can be stirred and dried evenly.
An FAO report on Kenya described washed parchment spread on wire mesh tables, no deeper than 0.5 in at first, drying for normally about 14 days.
Raised beds, thought to have started in Ethiopia, spread worldwide, particularly in Central America, Barista Hustle's processing course says.
In a survey of Brazilian growers, 10% dried on raised beds, against 42% on concrete or asphalt patios.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Raised beds, often called African or Ethiopian beds, are thought to have started in Ethiopia, where naturals go onto them straight from the tree. In Kenya, mesh drying tables are still the usual drying technology, and few cooperative factories have mechanical dryers.

They have spread worldwide, particularly in Central America, and they suit steep land, where level patios take a lot of labour and money to build; Costa Rica's protected-name rules list “camas africanas” among accepted sun-drying methods. In Brazil they're a minority (10% of growers in a 2019 survey). In Panama, Hacienda La Esmeralda uses them mostly for slow-dried lots, and the Lamastus family's anaerobic slow-dry lots dry on shaded beds.

sections.title: Building and using them
body: Most are simple timber or bamboo frames topped with food-safe mesh, galvanized chicken wire or palm leaves. The surface has to breathe and smell of nothing, so plastic sheeting won't do, though covers are needed when dew, rain or storms are expected.

The table must stay flat: sagging mesh leaves uneven layers that dry at different speeds. A Coffee Research Foundation scientist in Kenya advises shading parchment from strong sun between 10:30 am and 2:30 pm, and wrapping it in hessian or sisal cloth before putting plastic covers over it at night.

records.name: Slow dry
records.summary: Drying stretched over weeks, often on shaded beds, for even drying.
records.lede: Drying is slowed on purpose, using raised beds, shade, covers or even dark, dehumidified rooms, so the coffee loses water over weeks instead of days. Hacienda La Esmeralda in Panama uses raised beds for slow-dried lots that average 29 days, against 7–9 days on its patios. One importer says coffee dried slowly and evenly lasts longer, but too slow brings its own trouble.

facts.label: slow-dried lots on raised beds at one Panama farm
drying for an anaerobic slow-dry (ASD) natural
ordinary sun drying for a washed coffee, for comparison
past this, slow parchment drying hurts the cup, one importer says

steps.title: Ferment first (often)
steps.text: Many slow-dry lots start with a sealed ferment; Elida Estate's ASD naturals spend about five or six days sealed in tanks or bags.

steps.title: Spread thin, in shade
steps.text: The coffee goes onto raised beds, often shaded, or onto covered patios, spread thinly and turned.

steps.title: Lose water slowly
steps.text: Drying runs for weeks rather than days, down to about 10–12% moisture.

steps.title: Rest before milling
steps.text: Esmeralda then bags its dried coffee for at least 30 days to let it stabilize.

records.layers: Any, but the best-known slow-dried coffees are naturals and anaerobic naturals, dried with the whole fruit still on.

cup.common: No single flavor of its own; producers use it for clean, even drying, and one importer says slow, even drying helps coffee keep its quality longer.
cup.text: Esmeralda says its raised beds let air circulate for clean, evenly dried coffee. Coffee Review scored two of Elida Estate's anaerobic slow-dry naturals 93 and 94.
cup.why: The parchment shell and a gentle pace buffer the bean against harsh, uneven drying, and very fast drying is bad for coffee. In a lab study, beans dried with nightly pauses, like sun drying, took about eight days instead of five but ended with much the same sugars, so the authors concluded sugars can't explain quality differences between the two. Pace matters differently at each stage: a Coffee Research Foundation scientist in Kenya says drying must be fast at first, while the parchment is soaking wet and microbes can taint it, then slow and cool in the middle (“white”) stage so the parchment doesn't crack.
cup.prized: Even drying and a coffee that holds its quality. A Geisha natural dried in a dark room won best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.
cup.watch: Too slow is a problem too: coffee that doesn't dry quickly enough can ferment out of control or grow mold, and one importer says parchment drying for more than 30 days shows problems in the cup. In Kenyan trials where drying stretched to 12–20 days in thick 4–8 cm layers, all the coffee came out poor, possibly because of the long drying and thick layers.

byCoffee.text: Elida Estate's ASD Catuaí natural spent six days sealed and 60 days drying, and scored 94 at Coffee Review.
Finca Hartmann's dark-room drying produced the Black Jaguar natural Geisha from Guarumo farm, best natural Geisha at Best of Panama 2020.

spectrum.label: Over-fermented or moldy if it stays wet too long

story.text: Ratibor Hartmann of Finca Hartmann in Panama began drying coffee in drawers in a dark room with a dehumidifier and fans; by 2021 he'd been experimenting for almost ten years.
A dark-room-dried natural Geisha won best natural Geisha at the Best of Panama competition.
Coffee Review described anaerobic slow-dry naturals as drying 60 days or more and credited Wilford Lamastus of Elida Estate with popularizing them.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: In published sources, deliberate slow drying is mainly a Panamanian specialty practice: Hacienda La Esmeralda's raised-bed lots (about 29 days) and Elida Estate's anaerobic slow-dry naturals (60 days or more, popularized by Wilford Lamastus). Ratibor Hartmann of Finca Hartmann dries coffee in a dark room with a dehumidifier and fans, away from sun and heat, though no drying time is given. No published figure says how much coffee is dried this way.

Research is more cautious about long drying: trials reported by Kenya's Coffee Research Foundation found poor quality when drying ran to 12–20 days in thick layers, and one importer says parchment that takes more than 30 days to dry shows problems in the cup.

sections.title: A balancing act
body: Dry too slowly and the coffee can ferment out of control or mold; dry too fast and it suffers too: coffee left unturned in hot sun can overheat, and one importer calls very fast drying of bare beans harsh and uneven. The parchment shell itself slows drying and shields the bean from strong sun and day–night temperature swings.

records.name: Thermal shock
records.summary: A warm rinse, then a cold one, after a long ferment.
records.lede: After a long, controlled fermentation, the coffee is rinsed in warm water and then straight away in cold water. Perfect Daily Grind credits it to Diego Bermúdez of Finca El Paraíso in Cauca, Colombia. Producers say the swing “opens” the beans to take in aroma and then “seals” it in, but the roaster that explains this theory says research is still needed.

facts.label: the warm rinse (104 °F)
the cold rinse (54 °F)
El Paraíso's altitude (6,330–6,430 ft)
El Paraíso's Cup of Excellence top-10 finish

steps.title: Sanitize the cherries
steps.text: Ripe cherries are washed in ozonated water, sometimes with UV light, to cut down wild microbes.

steps.title: Sealed ferment
steps.text: Whole cherries ferment in sealed steel tanks, in some lots flushed with CO2 and seeded with yeasts selected from wild samples.

steps.title: Pulp and ferment again
steps.text: The cherries are pulped and the coffee ferments again with its mucilage.

steps.title: Warm rinse
steps.text: The coffee is rinsed in, or heated in its juices to, about 40–50 °C (104–122 °F).

steps.title: Cold rinse
steps.text: It then goes straight into cold water at about 10–12 °C (50–54 °F), which producers say stops the fermentation.

steps.title: Controlled drying
steps.text: El Paraíso lots then dry in machines at gentle heat, about 34–42 °C (93–108 °F), down to 10–11% moisture.

records.layers: It varies. In El Paraíso's double-ferment lots the shock comes after pulping, on parchment still coated in mucilage; other lots shock the whole cherries, before pulping or before a sealed ferment.

cup.common: Very intense, perfumed fruit, sometimes so intense that people suspect something was added.
cup.text: Roasters list notes like freeze-dried strawberry, cotton candy and violet, or citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit and lychee. One roaster's education director says the processing has an intensive impact on flavor.
cup.why: Unproven. The producers' working theory is that heat opens the beans' pores so they take in esters (fruity aroma compounds) from the fermentation juice, and cold closes them again; the quick swing may also halt enzymes, as blanching does to vegetables. The roaster that explains this says scientific research is still needed.
cup.prized: Big, clear aromatics, and roasters credit the step with a clean, consistent cup and with stopping fermentation before it goes too far.
cup.watch: The intensity led many to suspect that one El Paraíso release was infused with additives; the roaster selling it says the flavor came only from processing. Because the shock is one step among sanitizing, added yeast, sealed ferments and machine drying, it's hard to know how much of the flavor it causes.

byCoffee.text: Diego Bermúdez's double-washed thermal-shock Castillo was sold with notes of citrus, orange blossom, peach, mango, passion fruit, honey, lychee, strawberry, raspberry and plum; a neighboring Bermúdez farm's Castillo, processed by Diego, with freeze-dried strawberry, cotton candy and violet.

Wilton Benítez's lots, which follow a koji ferment with a bean-sealing step using hot and cold water, scored 94–95 with Coffee Review in 2023 and 2024, with lychee, bergamot and jasmine and a creamy or syrupy mouthfeel.

story.text: The Bermúdez family started Finca El Paraíso in Piendamó, Cauca.
El Paraíso won a regional competition, its way into specialty coffee.
Diego Samuel Bermúdez placed 10th in Colombia's Cup of Excellence with a washed Bourbon that scored 89.76.
He placed 24th with an anaerobic washed Castillo, and won the body and exotic categories of the coffee federation's Colombia, Land of Diversity contest.
Trade writers were describing thermal shock as his creation: a rinse at about 40 °C, then one at about 12 °C.

After disqualifying four lots, Best of Panama's organizers called “co-fermented” and “thermal shock” deceptive terms; Coffee Review's editor said they needed to explain how the alteration was confirmed.

sections.title: Who invented it
body: Perfect Daily Grind credits Diego Bermúdez. One roaster's education director credits him together with Wilton Benítez, and describes both sanitizing cherries and adding yeast strains selected from wild samples. Bermúdez co-founded a processing company, INDESTEC, with his brother and cousin, and the family now runs several more farms.

sections.title: Recipes differ
body: Lots sold as thermal shock don't follow one recipe. One roaster's listing describes washing whole cherries in 50 °C (122 °F) water, sealing them for 80 hours at 35 °C (95 °F) and spraying on a Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast; another producer shocks before pulping in a washed process.

sections.title: Where it's done
body: Most thermal-shock lots on the market come from Cauca, Colombia, where it started: Diego Bermúdez's El Paraíso, in the village of Los Arados at about 1,930 m (6,330 ft), and a neighboring farm run by a relative, Finca El Paraíso Villa Esperanza, whose coffee he processes. Wilton Benítez's Granja Paraíso 92 in Piendamó, Cauca, uses hot and cold water in its koji lots, and other producers, such as Paola Trujillo with an SL28, have made their own versions.

sections.title: On the bag
body: “Thermal shock”, “thermo shock” or “heat shock” (one listing reads “double anaerobic fermentation, heat shock, washing”). Lots are often named after a fruit, such as Bermúdez's Red Plum and Lychee releases, and Coffee Review describes Benítez's step as sealing the beans through “impacts of hot and cold water”.

sections.title: Risks and faults
body: The main risk is to trust. The flavors are intense enough that many drinkers suspected Bermúdez's Red Plum of being infused, and in 2024 Best of Panama's organizers called “thermal shock” a deceptive term, without saying how they confirmed that the lots they disqualified had been altered.

Because the shock is one step among sanitizing, added yeast, sealed ferments and machine drying, no one has shown how much of the flavor it causes, and the roaster that explains the theory says research is still needed.

records.name: Washed

cup.common: A clean, bright cup with clear acidity, where the coffee's origin and variety come through plainly.
cup.text: Importers describe washed coffees as clean and crisp, with caramel-like sweetness and pronounced acidity. A 2015 research review found wet-processed coffees more aromatic and acidic, and less bitter, burnt or woody, than dry-processed ones.
cup.why: The fruit comes off first, so microbes work on the sticky mucilage for 12–72 hours in a tank instead of for weeks around the seed, and the parchment dries in roughly one to two weeks. The seed changes too: lab studies find washed beans start germination-like activity within about a day of pulping, using up simple sugars (they end with roughly 5–10 times less glucose and fructose than naturals) and building amino acids, raw material for flavor in the roast.
cup.prized: Clarity: a cup in which place and variety are easy to taste. Kenya's best washed lots, for example, are prized for bright acidity with citrus, blackcurrant and berry.
cup.watch: A ferment left too long turns sour and alcoholic and can leave over-fermented 'stinker' beans. Separately, washed coffees left underdeveloped in the roast can taste sour or thin.

byCoffee.text: Kenyan mills ferment overnight, then up to 36 more hours, wash, and soak the parchment in clean water for 12–48 hours before drying. The best lots are known for bright citrus, blackcurrant and berry acidity, sometimes leaning winey.
Washed Ethiopians can have sparkling, citrusy acidity, with florals and sweet spice in the aroma, says one importer; the same coffees dried in the fruit lean toward berry and dried fruit.
Washing can bring out the variety's floral and citrus side, one roaster says; natural and honey Geshas can carry more fruit, sweetness and ferment.

Washing stations (the first private one opened in 2001, and over 200 since) are credited with greatly improving Rwanda's coffee. One importer's washed lots run floral and clear, with bright lemon acidity.

spectrum.label: Tangy, lactic from a long or sealed ferment

steps.title: Sort and pulp
steps.text: Cherries are floated to skim off unripe and overripe fruit, then a machine strips the skin and fruit flesh.

steps.title: Ferment in tanks
steps.text: The sticky mucilage left on the parchment ferments as microbes break it down. Dry tanks are usually done within a day; tanks under water can take longer, and Colombia's protected-name rules give about 14–18 hours in water-filled tanks. It varies with climate, water and microbes.

steps.title: Wash (and soak)
steps.text: The loosened mucilage is rinsed off. In Kenya the clean parchment then soaks under fresh water before drying.

steps.title: Dry the parchment
steps.text: Parchment dries on patios, raised beds or in machines until the seed is about 11–12% water. Weather and method change the time a lot.
steps.hours: about 6–15 days in the sun; about 29 on one estate's slow-drying raised beds; 18–36 h in a mechanical dryer

steps.title: Rest, then hull
steps.text: The dry parchment rests before a dry mill strips it off.
steps.hours: 30 days or more at one Panama estate

records.layers: Parchment only. The skin, fruit flesh and mucilage are all off before drying, so the seed dries in its papery parchment shell.

story.text: Washed processing reached southern Ethiopia, which until then had dried all its coffee in the fruit.
Rwanda's first private washing station opened in Huye, run by the Maraba cooperative; more than 200 followed.
Colombia's coffee research centre, Cenicafé, presented Ecomill, a washing system using 0.3–0.5 litres of water per kilo of dry parchment instead of 4–20 litres.
Colombia relaxed export rules that had long favored standard, clean-profiled wet-processed coffees, opening the door to naturals and experimental lots.
Coffee Review's new Kenneth Davids Cup set up a Traditional Washed category that excludes anaerobic, carbonic, inoculated, extended and co-fermented coffees.

facts.label: typical tank ferment, often about a day
ferment in water-filled tanks under Colombia's protected-name rules
share of Ethiopia's coffee that is washed (2021)
