sections.title: Growing it
body: Studies in Honduras and Costa Rica found no significant yield difference between Catuaí and Caturra. It needs plenty of fertiliser and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms) and coffee berry disease, though that disease isn't present in Central America. Mexico developed a similar variety, Garnica, around 1960–61.
Brazilian breeders have kept using it: Arara is a cross of Obatã and Yellow Catuaí, and Catucaí is a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí.

cup.text: The 2017 Cup of Excellence jury in Nicaragua called its prize lot balanced, with cinnamon, peach, cherry and hazelnut. Ozone Coffee says the variety can make clean, sweet cups with bright acidity.
cup.why: In Nicaraguan trials it out-scored Caturra on the SCA scale (the industry's 100-point cupping score), 80.4 to 76.3, and WCR says it shows exceptional cup potential when grown high and managed well.
cup.prized: WCR says it has exceptional cup potential when well managed at high altitude, on top of very high yields and strong rust resistance.
cup.watch: It needs very heavy feeding, can struggle to root in its first two years, and is susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms).

story.text: CATIE, CIRAD and PROMECAFE, a network of Central America's national coffee institutes, start the breeding program behind the region's F1 hybrids.
Centroamericano is released to Central American farmers; about 1,000 hectares were planted by 2017.
Gonzalo Castillo's lot from Las Promesas de San Blas in Nueva Segovia places second at Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence with 90.50 points.
CATIE begins supplying Centroamericano, Milenio and Esperanza plants to about 200 coffee-growing families in the Trifinio region of Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR describes a compact plant with large beans and very high yields that bears its first crop in year two. It is highly resistant to leaf rust and tolerates coffee berry disease, but nematodes can harm it, and it should not get too much nitrogen.
In a Nicaraguan trial of nine F1 hybrids, it showed no rust lesions and was among the two most promising for yield and stability.

records.lede: Gesha 1931 is a name Gesha Village, a farm in southwestern Ethiopia's Bench Maji zone, uses for one of its own Gesha selections. The farm picked it out of the varied wild coffee from around the Gori Gesha forest, keeping the plants whose shape, beans and cup came closest to Panama's Geisha. Roasters say the number is the year a British expedition first collected Gesha there.

La Cabra found jasmine, stone fruit and a black-tea finish in a natural from the Oma plot; Sey called a washed Oma lot intensely floral and tea-like in clarity; and Coffee Review's top-rated 2024 natural showed wisteria, bergamot, dried mango and cocoa nib.

Adam Overton and Rachel Samuel lease 471 ha in Bench Maji; seed they gathered with Willem Boot from the Gori Gesha forest's wild trees is planted there.

sections.title: Reading the bag
body: Gesha Village sells by plot and by selection. Roasters list three selections from the farm: Gesha 1931, Gori Gesha, and Illubabor Forest 1974, a disease-resistant selection named for the 1974 expedition that collected it. Plot names such as Oma, Surma and Gaylee are among the farm's eight blocks, named after nearby villages and sites.

sections.title: Gesha 1931 or Gori Gesha?
body: Both come from the same wild population. Sey says research and genetic testing point to the Gori Gesha forest as where Panama's Gesha was first collected, and that two groups were identified there: Gori Gesha and Gesha 1931, the plants most like Panama's Geisha. Roasters disagree on how Gesha 1931 relates to the Panama line: Intelligentsia calls it the original Gesha and the Panama line's forebear, while Rosso calls it a descendant of the Panamanian strain. No published genetic test comparing them was found.

Gesha Village, an estate about 20 km away in the Bench Maji zone, gathered seed there with Gesha specialist Willem Boot and planted it on the farm it leased in 2011.

World Coffee Research found that line distinct and uniform, and notes that several genetically different coffees have been called Gesha.
Gesha Village's Gori Gesha is a separate selection, taken straight from wild trees in the forest.

records.name: Icatu
records.summary: Brazil's tall Arabica with Robusta genes, bred at IAC from 1950.
records.lede: A tall, productive Brazilian variety from the Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC) that carries genes from Robusta. Breeders crossed a Robusta with doubled chromosomes (which made a fertile cross with Arabica possible) with Bourbon, then crossed the offspring back to Mundo Novo over several generations; Daily Coffee News calls it the world's first artificial, commercial Arabica × Robusta hybrid. So its Robusta genes came from a deliberate cross, not from the Timor Hybrid, the natural Arabica × Robusta hybrid widely used in Arabica breeding.

facts.label: when IAC began the Robusta × Bourbon cross
released by IAC (sources give 1992 or 1993)
and vigorous, with lots of side branches
leaf-rust resistance in its main lines

family.parentsText: Robusta (chromosome-doubled) × Bourbon, then backcrossed to Mundo Novo
family.line: IAC used a Robusta with doubled chromosomes, which allowed a fertile cross with Bourbon, then backcrossed to Mundo Novo for generations, selecting for disease resistance and Arabica traits.

grownIn.text: Widely grown in Brazil (Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Paraná, Espírito Santo); Ozone also cites a farm in El Salvador.

cup.text: Ozone Coffee describes Icatu as often sweet and rounded, with chocolate, caramel, nuts and dried fruit, and says it works well as espresso.
cup.why: Ozone finds that naturals lean further into dried fruit and sweetness, while washed lots show more clarity and structure.

story.text: IAC began crossing a chromosome-doubled Robusta with Bourbon.
IAC released Red and Yellow Icatu, by Ozone's dates (other sources say 1993).
Icatu Precoce, selected to ripen earlier, followed.

sections.title: Its children
body: Icatu is a parent of later Brazilian varieties: Catucaí came from a natural cross of Icatu and Catuaí, and EPAMIG's MGS Aranãs crosses a Catimor with Icatu IAC H3851-2.

sections.title: Growing it
body: In a 1995–2004 Embrapa trial in Acre state, the Icatu lines showed no rust while Mundo Novo did. A 2008 paper on the trial notes, citing earlier Brazilian work, that Icatu doesn't handle dry spells the way Robusta does, even with a good root system.

records.name: IHCAFE 90
records.summary: A Honduran Catimor for low farms; WCR rates its cup very low.
records.lede: A Caturra × Timor Hybrid variety from IHCAFE, Honduras's coffee institute, made for high yields at low altitudes with heavy fertilizing. World Coffee Research rates its cup potential very low and says it's now susceptible to rust in Honduras, yet IHCAFE 90 lots have placed in the country's Cup of Excellence, in 2017 and again in 2026.

facts.label: WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
first harvest
score of a washed IHCAFE 90 that placed 6th (Traditional) in Honduras's 2026 Cup of Excellence

sections.title: Its reputation
body: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude very low. Competitions cut the other way: IHCAFE 90 was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, and in 2026 a washed IHCAFE 90 from El Cutal, in Lempira, placed sixth in the Traditional category at 87.96 points and sold for $23.60 a pound.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR says it needs very high fertilization, suits the lowest altitudes and is planted at 4,000–5,000 plants per hectare. It's highly susceptible to ojo de gallo, a leaf-spot disease, and is now confirmed susceptible to leaf rust in Honduras. Coffeeness lists it in Copán, Comayagua, Agalta and El Paraíso.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra
family.line: Bred by IHCAFE in Honduras; WCR calls it highly similar to the line T5175.

grownIn.text: Honduras: Copán, Comayagua, Agalta, El Paraíso and Lempira.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: IPR 107
records.summary: Paraná's dwarf, rust-resistant Sarchimor bred for dense, machine-picked farms.
records.lede: A dwarf Brazilian variety bred in Paraná by IAPAR (now IDR-Paraná) from IAPAR 59 and Mundo Novo, and released in 2010. It was made to pair strong leaf-rust resistance with a small tree that suits tightly packed rows and harvesting machines. In World Coffee Research's trial across 23 sites in 15 countries, it was one of three varieties singled out for fairly strong, stable rust resistance.

facts.label: released, from crossing work begun in 1982
about the size of Catuaí, for dense planting
to leaf rust, in WCR's rating
its first crop after planting

family.parentsText: IAPAR 59 × Mundo Novo IAC 376-4
family.line: Crossed at IAPAR in Paraná and selected over generations (F3 progenies planted in 1998, F5 in 2006) for complete rust resistance.

grownIn.text: Bred for and recommended in Paraná, Brazil; also tested at 23 sites in 15 countries in WCR's international trial.

plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator; above 900 m (2,950 ft) at 5–15° latitude; above 700 m (2,300 ft) beyond 15°

story.text: IAPAR began the crossing program that led to IPR 107.
The selected third-generation (F3) progenies were planted out for testing.
Released to Brazilian farmers.
A WCR study of 29 varieties at 23 sites named it among the top performers for stable rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Its breeders recommend it for semi-dense to super-dense plantings in Paraná, with plants 0.5–0.7 m apart in rows 2.5–3 m apart. Over four harvests in Paraná it out-yielded both IAPAR 59 and Catuaí Vermelho IAC 81.

World Coffee Research lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer and as susceptible to nematodes (tiny root worms). Its mother parent, IAPAR 59, is itself a Sarchimor: Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10 × Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2.

sections.title: In the cup
body: Its breeders rated its cup equal to or better than Mundo Novo's, and WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as very good.

records.name: Ja'adi
records.summary: A Haraaz name for curly-leaved, tightly clustered Yemeni trees.
records.lede: Ja'adi comes from the Arabic ja'd, curly or rough; farmers link it to wavy leaf edges or to cherries packed in tight clusters. In a 2022 survey it was specific to Sanaa governorate, especially Haraaz, and most sampled trees (83%) were in the New-Yemen (Yemenia) group. Like other Yemeni names, it's a local label rather than a defined variety.

facts.label: of sampled Ja'adi trees (15 of 18) were New-Yemen types
of names cited in Haraaz, the most there
(5,600–8,550 ft) where Ozone Coffee says Haraaz coffee grows

cup.text: Ozone Coffee, which sells a single-farm Ja'adi from East Haraaz, describes dried fruit like dates, figs and raisins, warm spices such as cardamom and clove, and a dark-chocolate and molasses base. That's one roaster's view, and because the name covers mixed genetics, lots can differ.
cup.watch: Ozone warns that dark roasting tends to burn off its spice.

sections.title: Growing it
body: Ozone Coffee describes Haraaz farms on hand-built stone terraces with under 400 mm of rain a year, fed with manure and ground stone rather than chemical fertiliser. Almost all Yemeni coffee, Ja'adi included, is natural-processed: whole cherries dried in the husk, on rooftops and, more and more, on raised beds.
The beans tend to be small, hard and often irregular, and there is no working seed sector, so verified Ja'adi seedlings are hard to get.

family.parentsText: A farmers' name; most sampled trees were New-Yemen types, with a few Typica/Bourbon and SL34

grownIn.text: Sanaa governorate, concentrated in Haraaz.

records.name: Jackson
records.summary: An Indian rust-tolerant selection that became common in Rwanda and Burundi.
records.lede: Jackson traces to trees a Mr. Jackson found resisting leaf rust on his farm in Mysore, India, in the early 1900s. In the 1920s seedlings went to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania, and today it's common in Rwanda and Burundi. Its rust tolerance has since been lost, and genetic tests place it in the Bourbon group.

facts.label: from very vigorous, tall trees
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (3,950 ft)
the genetic group tests place it in

cup.text: Sample Coffee's Burundi lots featuring Jackson have been described with strawberry and orange, or with rich chocolate, green grape and soft florals. Those are notes on single lots, not a variety-wide profile.

plant.altitude: above 1,200 m (3,950 ft) near the equator

story.text: Mr. Jackson spots rust-tolerant trees on his farm in Mysore, India.
Seedlings go to research stations in Kenya and Tanzania.
It reaches Rwanda, possibly through the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo (set up in the 1930s) or with Kenyan settler farmers in the 1940s.

sections.title: The family
body: Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and are likely late descendants of the seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India in 1670. The Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) is listed as the breeder of today's Jackson 2/1257.

family.parentsText: Farmer selection from rust-tolerant trees in Mysore, India (Bourbon-related)

grownIn.text: Common in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Java
records.summary: An Ethiopian landrace once mistaken for Typica, later brought to Central America.
records.lede: Named for the Indonesian island, but World Coffee Research says DNA fingerprinting indicates it's a selection from an Ethiopian landrace population called Abyssinia, not the Typica it was once taken for. The Dutch took it from Ethiopia to Java in the early 1800s; it was later selected in Cameroon for tolerance of coffee berry disease and brought to Central America in 1991.

facts.label: CIRAD breeder Benoit Bertrand brought it to Costa Rica
Panama recognized it officially, first in Central America
of coffee berry disease, but susceptible to leaf rust
fertilizer needs, a fit for smallholders

story.text: The Dutch take it from Ethiopia to the island of Java.
It reaches Cameroon through the seed company Vilmorin, where breeder Pierre Bouharmont notes partial tolerance of coffee berry disease.
Released in Cameroon after about 20 years of selection.
CIRAD brings it to Costa Rica for smallholders; seed goes to other Central American countries but isn't released there.
Panama becomes the first Central American country to recognize it officially.

sections.title: Growing it
body: A tall tree with bronze new leaves and large beans, first cropping in its third year. World Coffee Research rates its quality potential very good at high altitude, above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator, and presents it as a hardier alternative to Gesha for small farmers.

sections.title: Java and AB3
body: World Coffee Research lists another Ethiopian selection grown on Java separately: AB3, picked in Ethiopia by P. J. S. Cramer and brought to Indonesia in 1928, released in 1995 and grown on a small scale on Java's state plantations.

family.parentsText: A selection from the Ethiopian landrace population Abyssinia, by DNA fingerprinting; once thought to be a Typica
family.line: Taken from Ethiopia to Java, later selected in Cameroon

grownIn.text: Java (Indonesia), Cameroon and Central America, including Costa Rica and Panama

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: K7
records.summary: A 1930s Kenyan selection that tolerates coffee berry disease.
records.lede: K7 is a Kenyan selection from French Mission coffee. World Coffee Research credits it to R.H. Walker and says it was released in 1936 after five generations of selection by Scott Agricultural Laboratories. It tolerates coffee berry disease (CBD), a fungal disease of the cherries, and is found mainly in Kenya and Tanzania, where breeders have used it widely.

facts.label: released in Kenya
WCR's rating for coffee berry disease
(3,300–5,250 ft) where it does best near the equator
beans on tall trees with medium yield

cup.text: 1Zpresso's Kenya guide describes floral aromas with citrus and berry flavors, delicate sweetness, bright acidity and a full mouthfeel. WCR rates its cup potential up high as good.

plant.altitude: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: Rust and berry disease
body: World Coffee Research rates it susceptible to leaf rust, but a 2014 review of Kenyan varieties says K7 resists some rust races and partly resists CBD, and 1Zpresso calls its rust resistance moderate. 1Zpresso suits it to mid and lower altitudes.
You can spot it by its spreading young side branches, while older main branches tend to droop.

family.parentsText: Selection from French Mission (Bourbon-like)
family.line: Credited to R.H. Walker; refined over five generations at Scott Labs.

grownIn.text: Mainly Kenya and Tanzania.

records.name: Kent
records.summary: India's early rust-tolerant selection, parent of S795 and KP423.
records.lede: Kent is an old Indian Arabica that World Coffee Research traces to a single tree Mr. L.P. Kent selected on his Doddengooda Estate in Mysore in 1911. It's known as the first coffee selected for tolerance to leaf rust, a tolerance that has since broken down. Its descendants, such as S795 in India and Indonesia and KP423 in Tanzania and Uganda, are now more common than Kent itself.

facts.label: selection date per WCR; India's Coffee Board says the 1920s
taken to Tanzania and other parts of East Africa
Indian planters favoured it for being less prone to rust
the most popular Indian Arabica selection of the 1940s, developed from Kents

cup.text: Homegrounds describes a mild, naturally sweet cup with low acidity and medium body, often with nutty or spicy notes, and My Coffee Explorer says Indian Kents tend toward chocolate, nuts and mild fruit. India's Coffee Board still credits it with exceptional cup quality.

story.text: Kent is believed to descend from the first Bourbon-type seeds Baba Budan brought from Yemen to India.
L.P. Kent selects a single tree on Doddengooda Estate in Mysore, the start of Kent and the varieties bred from it.
Kent reaches Tanzania, where Lyamungu Research Station starts a selection program on it.
India releases S795 (S.288 × Kents) in 1945–46, and Tanzania releases the Kent selection KP423.

sections.title: Which family?
body: Sources disagree. World Coffee Research calls Kent a Bourbon-related population and puts its offspring KP423 in the Bourbon group, while Royal Coffee and Homegrounds call it a Typica. WCR also says Jackson, Kent, Coorg and Mysore all come from the same part of India and likely descend from Baba Budan's seeds.

sections.title: Where it's grown
body: India's Coffee Board says Kent is now grown in only a few areas, listing it among the main varieties of the Nilgiris. Royal Coffee calls it an older variety still sometimes found in Kenya, and Tanzania's Acacia Hills farm, at 1,750–1,950 m (5,750–6,400 ft), still grows some Kent.

family.parentsText: A single-tree selection from Mysore, India
family.line: A planter's selection; WCR calls the population Bourbon-related, others call it Typica.

grownIn.text: A few Indian areas, and as an older variety in Kenya and Tanzania.

records.name: Kurume
records.summary: A small-cherried local Ethiopian landrace from around Yirgacheffe.
records.lede: A regional Ethiopian landrace (a local type farmers have kept, not a research release) from the Yirgacheffe area. It's named after a native tree with small fruit, and is known for small cherries and a generous crop. It's common in the Gedeo and Guji zones, often grown alongside other local types such as Wolisho and Dega.

facts.label: and a big crop most years
the zones where it's commonly grown
in the top 30 at Cup of Excellence Ethiopia 2021, both from Oromia
the name is sometimes used for research selections whose trees look similar

family.parentsText: A landrace kept by farmers; no known parents
family.line: From Ethiopia's wild coffee, with seed selected locally by farmers; named after a native tree

grownIn.text: Ethiopia: Gedeo (around Yirgacheffe) and Guji; also named on lots from Gera, in Jimma

plant.yield: good, regular crops of small cherries

records.name: Laurina
records.summary: A dwarf, Christmas-tree-shaped Bourbon mutant from La Réunion.
records.lede: Laurina, also called Bourbon Pointu, is a dwarf mutant of Bourbon generally thought to have been selected from a field on La Réunion, then called Bourbon island, in the early 1800s. Its trees grow in a pyramid, like a Christmas tree. A 2009 scientific review says its beans are known for excellent cup quality, but calls the exact story of its origin ambiguous and debated.

facts.label: selected on La Réunion, by the usual account
and pyramid-shaped, like a Christmas tree
cup quality, per a 2009 review in Euphytica

sections.title: The shape
body: A CIRAD study found that Bourbon and Bourbon Pointu branch off the trunk at about the same angle, around 50°. The Christmas-tree shape comes instead from the Laurina mutation changing how the top of the main stem grows compared with the side branches.

sections.title: The low-caffeine claim
body: Laurina is often sold as naturally low in caffeine. One decaf-focused newsletter puts it at 0.2–0.8% caffeine by weight, against 1.2–1.8% for most Arabica, but it cites no study, so treat that figure as unconfirmed.

family.parentsText: Bourbon (natural dwarf mutant)
family.line: Selected on La Réunion; the details of its origin are debated.

grownIn.text: First selected on La Réunion, the former Bourbon island.

records.name: Lempira
records.summary: Honduras's Catimor, once rust-resistant, now confirmed susceptible there.
records.lede: A Catimor that IHCAFE, Honduras's national coffee institute, selected from the Central American line T8667. Farmers planted it for higher yields and rust resistance, but a new rust race has since got through, and World Coffee Research now lists it as confirmed susceptible in Honduras.

facts.label: WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
to leaf rust in Honduras, confirmed by scientific evaluation
Lempira among the varieties of Honduras's Cup of Excellence winners

story.text: CATIE in Costa Rica receives the Catimor line T8667, which IHCAFE later selected Lempira from.
Rust starts infecting Lempira, one of the cases WCR singles out of resistance breaking down.
Lempira is among the varieties of the winning lots at Honduras's Cup of Excellence, where every winning lot scored at least 86.

sections.title: Its reputation
body: WCR rates its quality potential at high altitude as low and calls it highly similar to Costa Rica 95. Competition results are kinder: Lempira was among the varieties of the 2017 Honduras Cup of Excellence winners, a year when winning lots scored 86 to 91.81.

sections.title: Where it grows
body: Coffeeness names Lempira among the varieties of El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta. WCR recommends it for the warmest zones and for acidic, aluminium-rich soils.

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/1 × Caturra (selected from T8667)
family.line: Pedigree selection by PROMECAFE and IHCAFE in Honduras.

grownIn.text: Honduras, including El Paraíso, Montecillos and Agalta.

plant.rust: rated intermediate, but now confirmed susceptible in Honduras
plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator

records.name: Limani
records.summary: Puerto Rico's compact, rust-resistant Sarchimor, released to farmers in 1994.
records.lede: A compact, rust-resistant variety grown in Puerto Rico, from a cross of the Timor Hybrid and Villa Sarchi. Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas sent the seed to the island's Agricultural Experiment Station in 1982, and after trials it went to farmers in 1994. World Coffee Research warns that plants sold as Limani often don't match the original.

facts.label: released to Puerto Rican farmers
a dwarf tree, planted 5,000–6,000 to the hectare
(3,300 ft+), where WCR says true Limani does well
its first crop after planting

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid 832/2 × Villa Sarchi
family.line: A pedigree selection made by Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station from a Brazilian population of this Sarchimor cross.

grownIn.text: Released in Puerto Rico, where it is still important to the island's coffee.

plant.altitude: above 1,000 m (3,300 ft)

story.text: Brazil's IAC supplied Limani, along with another variety, Fronton, to Puerto Rico's Agricultural Experiment Station.
After trials showed rust resistance and high yield potential, it was released to farmers.

sections.title: The name problem
body: WCR calls true Limani elusive: because the seed has been hard to trace, plants sold under the name often don't match the original reference material.

On the island it has proved itself. A 2021 University of Puerto Rico thesis notes that the experiment station found it outperformed Bourbon, Caturra and Pacas there, and that it remains important to Puerto Rican production for its performance and rust resistance.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as needing a lot of fertilizer, ripening at an average pace, and giving a high outturn, meaning a lot of green coffee from each kilo of cherry.

records.name: Maragogipe
records.summary: A Typica mutation with giant beans, found in Brazil in 1870.
records.lede: A natural mutation of Typica found near the town of Maragogipe, Brazil, in 1870, caused by a single dominant gene. It's known for its very large beans, sometimes called elephant beans, and it's one of the two parents of Pacamara.

facts.label: beans, WCR's yardstick for the biggest size
from tall trees with big leaves and long gaps between leaf pairs
WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)

cup.text: Coffee Hunter describes a mild, smooth cup with gentle, sweet acidity, a fresh oaky note and a dark, syrupy body. World Coffee Research rates its cup good to very good in Central America.
cup.watch: Yields are so low that World Coffee Research calls Pacamara, its big-bean offspring, the better option for farmers.

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

sections.title: Growing it
body: Besides leaf rust, it's susceptible to coffee berry disease and nematodes (tiny root worms). It needs little fertiliser and turns a high share of cherry weight into green coffee. Coffee Hunter says it matures slowly and is most common in Brazil, Guatemala and Mexico.

family.parentsText: Typica (natural mutation)
family.line: A single dominant gene mutation found near Maragogipe, Brazil.

grownIn.text: Most common in Brazil, Guatemala and Mexico, says Coffee Hunter.

records.name: Marsellesa
records.summary: A high-yielding Nicaraguan Sarchimor that WCR notes for high acidity.
records.lede: A Sarchimor selected in Nicaragua for rust resistance by CIRAD and ECOM and released in 2009. World Coffee Research describes a high-yielding plant adapted to medium altitudes, with notably high acidity in the cup.

facts.label: released, after selection in Nicaragua
WCR's cup-quality rating at high altitude
acidity in the cup, WCR notes

cup.text: WCR notes notably high acidity. The importer Coffee Hunter describes a fruity, floral fragrance, a medium, balanced acidity and a medium body, like Caturra but sweeter.
cup.prized: The Costa Rican consultant Jorge Ramírez Rojas told Perfect Daily Grind that Marsellesa and Obatã cup even better than Caturra and Catuaí.

sections.title: Growing it
body: WCR lists it as susceptible to nematodes and tolerant of coffee berry disease, with a high outturn (green coffee per kilo of cherry) and heavy feeding needs. Coffee Hunter says it matures and grows faster than Caturra and Catuaí, holds its cherries in heavy rain, and does best up to 1,300 m (4,250 ft).

family.parentsText: Timor Hybrid CIFC 832/2 × Villa Sarchi CIFC 971/10
family.line: Pedigree selection for rust resistance in Nicaragua by CIRAD-ECOM.

grownIn.text: Selected in Nicaragua.

plant.altitude: low to medium: 1,000–1,600 m (3,300–5,250 ft) near the equator; 700–1,300 m (2,300–4,250 ft) at 5–15° latitude

records.name: Mibirizi
records.summary: Probably Rwanda's oldest coffee, a Typica type with top cup ratings.
records.lede: Probably the oldest coffee variety in Rwanda, and still important to smallholders there and in Burundi. A Belgian coffee historian wrote that Germany's colonial administration brought it from Guatemala in the 1910s, and in the 1920s it went to Catholic missions, including one at Mibirizi in western Rwanda. Genetic tests tie it to the Typica group.

facts.label: WCR's rating for its cup potential up high
and copes with little care and harsh conditions
highly susceptible to the major coffee diseases
where it does best near the equator (5,250 ft)

plant.altitude: high: above 1,600 m (5,250 ft) near the equator

story.text: Germany's colonial administration brings coffee from Guatemala to Rwanda, where it's called "Guatemala"; it was probably Typica, since Guatemala then grew only Typica.
The coffee is handed out to Rwanda's Catholic missions, including the one at Mibirizi, whose well-kept trees later supplied seed to the Mulungu collection in today's DR Congo.
Several Mibirizi lines are compared at the Rubona research station near Huye; it's unclear whether any reached farmers.

sections.title: The family
body: Its history is poorly documented. World Coffee Research says Mibirizi plants were probably mixed with French Mission plants from Kenya, which are Bourbon-type, but recent genetic tests confirm a link to the Typica group.

family.parentsText: Typica-like, possibly mixed with French Mission (Bourbon)
family.line: Probably Typica from Guatemala, kept at Rwandan missions.

grownIn.text: Smallholder farms in Rwanda and Burundi.

records.name: Milenio
records.summary: Sarchimor × Rume Sudan F1 hybrid; a 2023 lot scored 93
records.lede: A first-generation (F1) hybrid from the same parents as Centroamericano: the rust-resistant Sarchimor T5296 and the Ethiopian landrace Rume Sudan. It came from the first wave of Central American hybrids, and WCR rates it very high-yielding and rust-resistant, though its plants are not uniform.

cup.text: Coffee Review scored a Finca Las Lajas lot from Costa Rica's Central Valley 93 in 2023, calling it sweetly tart and citrusy, with bergamot, cedar, persimmon, cocoa and macadamia nut.

story.text: The PROMECAFE–CATIE–CIRAD breeding program that produced Milenio begins.
Coffee Review scores a 100% Milenio lot from Finca Las Lajas 93 points.
CATIE starts supplying Milenio, with Centroamericano and Esperanza, to smallholders in the Trifinio region.

family.line: F1 cross from the CIRAD–PROMECAFE–CATIE consortium; propagated as clones

records.name: Monte Claro
records.summary: A rust-tolerant Venezuelan Arabica bred by INIA in Táchira state.
records.lede: An Arabica variety bred in Venezuela by the national agricultural research institute, INIA, in Táchira state, over roughly 40 years of work; its name was registered with Venezuela's national seed commission in 2013. It is valued for tolerating leaf rust and other diseases, and in 2023 Reuters reported that a Monte Claro took first place among 186 samples at a Caracas coffee show, scoring 90.11 points.

it also tolerates other diseases
